title: An unreadable vault manifest reads as empty, and the next quarantine overwrites it - permanent loss of every restore record
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. Verified directly. This is the most severe thing
the sweep found: it destroys the one promise the product is built on, and it
does it silently.

  lib/store.js:107  function readJson(file, fallback) { try {...} catch { return fallback; } }
  lib/store.js:203  const m = readJson(manifestPath(), defaultManifest());
  lib/store.js:215  function addManifestEntry(entry) {
  lib/store.js:216    const manifest = readManifest();
  lib/store.js:217    manifest.entries.push(entry);
  lib/store.js:218    writeManifest(manifest);   // writeJsonAtomic -> renameSync OVER the real file

readJson cannot distinguish 'no manifest yet, first run' from 'the manifest
exists and could not be read'. Both produce { schemaVersion, entries: [] }.

THE TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the second is not reversible:

1. vault.list() returns [], main.js returns { success: true, entries: [] }, the
   renderer's success check PASSES, and the user is shown
   'Nothing in quarantine yet. Anything Vanish removes is moved here first.'
   while their files are sitting in the vault.

2. The next quarantine calls addManifestEntry, which reads [] , pushes ONE
   entry, and atomically renames a one-entry manifest over the real one. There
   is no backup, no versioning and no integrity guard anywhere in lib/.

Every prior entry's record of where its payload came from is then gone. The
payloads remain on disk under vault\<uuid> but nothing knows what they were or
where they belong, so they are unrestorable by the app. A TRANSIENT READ ERROR
IS UPGRADED TO PERMANENT DATA LOSS BY THE VERY NEXT USER ACTION.

HOW THE READ FAILS IN PRACTICE, none of it exotic: EACCES/EPERM after the SEC-3
ACL pass (which lib/store.js:120-127 already documents as having degraded live
on this machine), EBUSY from an antivirus scanner holding the file, a partial
write from a power loss, a disk error, or any parse failure.

WHY IT IS aeu AIMED AT THE RESTORE PATH. The contract says could-not-look and
nothing must never share a representation. Here they share one, on the vault -
and Assert-RemovalPrecondition exists in this codebase precisely to stop this
reasoning ('an earlier step reporting success is not evidence'). The manifest
reader does not use that discipline.

FIX, and it should be the first thing done: readJson must distinguish ENOENT
from every other error. readManifest must THROW - or return a typed
could-not-read - when the file exists and cannot be parsed, and addManifestEntry
must refuse to write on top of a manifest it could not read. Failing a
quarantine is a recoverable outcome; silently discarding the vault index is not.

WORTH DOING AT THE SAME TIME: keep the previous manifest as manifest.json.bak
on every successful write. It is one rename and it turns any future instance of
this class from data loss into an inconvenience.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-04, and verified against the defect's own scenario rather than
around it.

THE FIX IS THAT READING HONESTLY IS ENOUGH. vault-list's IPC handler already
turned a throw into success:false, and the renderer already painted that as an
error box rather than as an empty vault - so the whole defect was one reader
that could not tell 'absent' from 'denied'.

  readJsonDetailed(file)  new. Returns { missing } for ENOENT and
                          { ok:false, error } for everything else - EACCES after
                          the SEC-3 ACL pass, EBUSY from a scanner, EIO, or a
                          parse failure. readJson keeps its old shape for
                          settings and the queue, where a default IS right and
                          fails safe.
  readManifest()          throws ManifestUnreadableError (code
                          MANIFEST_UNREADABLE) when the file exists and cannot
                          be had. A first run still returns the empty default.
                          An entries key that is not a list now throws too -
                          that is corruption, not an old schema, and coercing it
                          to [] was the same data loss by another route.
  writeManifest()         copies the live manifest to manifest.json.bak before
                          replacing it, and claims ownership on the copy so it
                          does not become the thing SEC-3 reports. Best-effort:
                          a failed backup never blocks the write.

THREE CALLERS NEEDED HANDLING, because throwing is right only where the caller
was about to write:

  vault.quarantine    the payload is ALREADY in the vault by then. It now
                      catches, logs vault-manifest-unwritable to the oplog with
                      the vault path, and returns indexed:false + indexError -
                      so 'your files are here and Vanish cannot list them' is
                      distinguishable from 'your files are gone'.
  autoPurgeSweep      the one unattended destructive path in the product. An
                      unreadable manifest is exactly when it must do nothing,
                      because it would otherwise be choosing what to delete
                      forever from a list it could not obtain. Returns
                      skipped:'manifest-unreadable' and records it.
  getAppInfo          only wants a count for the About panel. Taking the panel
                      down would hide the data-directory paths at the moment
                      someone needs them, so it catches and returns
                      manifestError beside the count.

LIVE, real app, real corrupted manifest:

  'Nothing in quarantine yet' shown : false
  error box shown                   : true
  'The quarantine manifest exists but could not be read (Unterminated string in
   JSON at position 46). Vanish will not write over it, because doing so would
   discard the record of everything already in the vault. The payloads are still
   on disk.'
  manifest on disk still the corrupted bytes (not overwritten): true

Screenshot dist/screenshots/z71u-unreadable-manifest.png.

TESTS: test/manifest-integrity-verify.js, 24 assertions. The one it exists for
is that after a refused write the file is BYTE-UNCHANGED. Four mutants, all
killed.

TWO OF THOSE ASSERTIONS ONLY EXIST BECAUSE THE MUTANTS FOUND THEM MISSING, and
that is worth recording: every corruption case I wrote first broke the CONTENT,
so the failure always happened at JSON.parse and the readFileSync branch was
never reached - turning every read error into 'missing' SURVIVED. The added case
holds the manifest open with FileShare.None, so the file is intact and the read
itself fails, which is the real-world EACCES/EBUSY shape. The second mutant
crashed the suite instead of failing it, because the backup assertion read the
file it had just failed to find; a failed assertion that throws is reported as
NOT RUN, which reads as a skip.

NO REGRESSIONS: vault-verify 43/43, vault-ipc 35/35, store-migration 12/12,
settings 10/10, queue 42/42, locked-paths 25/25.

NOT FIXED HERE, deliberately: settings.json and queue.json still take the
readJson default on an unreadable read. Both regenerate and both fail safe
(autoPurgeEnabled defaults false), so neither loses data - but the shape is the
same and is worth revisiting if either ever holds something irreplaceable.
close_reason: Fixed. readManifest now throws when the manifest exists and cannot be read, so addManifestEntry refuses to write over it - verified byte-unchanged. Every write keeps a .bak. Live against a real corrupted manifest the Quarantine screen shows the error instead of 'Nothing in quarantine yet'. 24 assertions, 4 mutants, no regressions.

title: EoP: an elevated restore wrote attacker-chosen content into Program Files and ProgramData
description:
FOUND AND FIXED 2026-09-02 by an adversarial probe, using this codebase's OWN threat model.

scanner.ps1 states it above Test-RestorableProtectedPath:

  'The manifest is user-writable; the restore runs elevated. Both the source it
   reads and the destination it writes are untrusted.'
  'An attacker who can write entry.json writes originalPath = System32\evil.dll,
   supplies the payload, and asks an elevated process to move it there. That is
   not a relaxed guard, it is an elevation-of-privilege primitive with a comment
   explaining why it is fine.'

System32 was blocked on exactly that reasoning. Program Files was not. Measured, not argued:

  WROTE   C:\Program Files\<x>\marker.txt        content: ATTACKER-CHOSEN-CONTENT
  WROTE   C:\Program Files (x86)\<x>\marker.txt
  WROTE   C:\ProgramData\<x>\marker.txt
  BLOCKED C:\Windows\System32\...
  BLOCKED C:\...

All three destinations are writable by Administrators and NOT by a standard user, so each is a user-to-admin write primitive: a DLL beside an elevated executable in Program Files, or a file on a service search path under ProgramData.

PRECONDITIONS, and the first was LIVE rather than theoretical. check-data-dir on the development machine returned protected=false with nonAdminWriters=['DESKTOP-01OAI95\Anand'] while this was being found. main.js runs secure-data-dir on every ELEVATED start, so a machine where Vanish has only ever run in Audit Mode -- the cautious user, the exact person this tool is for -- has an unprotected data directory the whole time. The second precondition is that the operator later clicks Restore in Full Mode.

WHY IT WAS NOT CAUGHT: test/security-verify.ps1 asserted the opposite on purpose. 'Vanish quarantines application leftovers from all of these, so a restore has to be able to put them back. Blocking them would break the undo path, which is the entire point of the vault.' That reasoning is correct, which is why the fix is a CONDITION and not a block.

THE FIX, in three parts:
1. Test-ProtectedDestination now blocks %ProgramFiles%, %ProgramFiles(x86)%, %ProgramW6432% and %ProgramData%. Env vars, not literals: ProgramFiles is redirected for a 32-bit process and a machine can have them on another volume.
2. New Test-RestorableInstalledAppPath allows a restore into those roots ONLY when Test-VaultDataDirTrusted is true -- i.e. when the data directory is ACL-locked, which is the one fact that makes the manifest believable. A direct child of the root is still refused: a restore puts a file back inside an application's folder, and dropping one straight into 'C:\Program Files\x.dll' is the planting shape, not the undo shape.
3. INV-1 SYMMETRY: the same exception is asked on the QUARANTINE side. Adding the roots without this broke the symmetry in the other direction -- quarantine would refuse what restore would accept, which does not strand a file but silently removes the ability to clean leftovers out of installed programs at all. That was caught by a probe checking the LEGITIMATE path, not the attack, and it is the reason a fix needs both.

COST IN PRACTICE: none. vault-restore and quarantine-items are both Full Mode only, and main.js locks the data directory on every elevated start, so any session that can reach either has already locked it. If that securing failed, refusing is correct rather than inconvenient, and the refusal names the fix: 'Start Vanish elevated once to lock the directory, then retry.'

REGRESSION: test\vault-destination-verify.ps1, registered in run-all.ps1. It performs the real attack against a throwaway vault and asserts every target refused, then asserts the undo path still works with the directory locked. 20 passed / 0 failed. Verified by reverting the fix: 14 passed / 6 failed.
close_reason:
FIXED and pushed in e61dd89, with the regression suite in the same commit.

Verified three ways:
  test\vault-destination-verify.ps1   20 passed / 0 failed
  the same suite with the fix reverted 14 passed / 6 failed
  full suite after                     2167 passed / 0 failed, 7 skipped

The regression performs the real attack against a throwaway vault rather than asserting a predicate, and asserts BOTH halves -- every target refused, and the undo path still working once the data directory is locked. The second half exists because my first fix broke INV-1 symmetry: adding the roots to the blocked list without the matching quarantine-side exception made quarantine refuse what restore would accept, which silently removes the ability to clean leftovers out of an installed program at all. The attack probe passed cleanly the whole time; only the probe that checked the legitimate path found it.

Left open deliberately as separate issues:
  cihg  the vault records no content hash, so a tampered payload restores as success
  470o  two Health Advisor panels are strictly-worse mirrors of Windows Settings

title: [bug] runas /trustlevel:0x20000 exits 0 and the process comes back ELEVATED - the de-elevation mechanism is wrong, not broken
description:
THE FIVE-SESSION QUESTION IS ANSWERED, by 1dq's instrumentation doing exactly what it was built to do. From the operator's real oplog, 0.5.0, 2026-08-13:

  14:15:22  app-start                     tier=full  v0.5.0
  14:16:56  relaunch-deelevated           success    trigger=user-click
  14:17:31  relaunch-deelevated-mismatch  error      direction=deelevate
            wantedTier=audit landedTier=full msSinceAttempt=34537
            uac: isGroupMember true, enableLua true, partOfDomain false,
                 lockLikely false, isElevatedNow TRUE, policyWritable true
  14:17:31  app-start                     tier=full  v0.5.0

This is OUTCOME 2 of the three the handoff listed: runas accepted the request and exited 0 (no exitCode in meta means it did not fail), and Windows started the process ELEVATED anyway. So the mechanism is WRONG, not broken, and no further instrumentation around it will say which mechanism to use instead.

RULED OUT, on evidence rather than reasoning:
- The app's own auto-elevate-on-startup path. settings.json startupMode is 'audit', and main.js:221 is the ONLY startupMode read in the entire main process - it auto-elevates only when startupMode === 'full'. There is no auto-DE-elevate path either, which was checked because it would have explained the sibling report and does not exist.
- Environment. seclogon Running, EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, manifest asInvoker, not domain-joined, policy key writable.

ALSO ESTABLISHED, and it corrects the operator's read: the app has NOT reached Audit Mode at all since 2026-08-07. Every app-start on 08-12 and 08-13 is tier=full. So the settings-toggle path did not 'now work' either - it showed the Restarting in Audit Mode splash, runas returned 0, and the app came back Full with the honest mismatch warning. That warning IS 1dq working; the underlying switch has never taken on this machine.

NEXT STEP IS ONE MEASUREMENT, NOT MORE CODE: test/deelevation-probe.ps1, run from an ELEVATED PowerShell. It probes three mechanisms and reports which actually drop privilege here:
  A. runas.exe /trustlevel:0x20000        (what ships today)
  B. explorer.exe's token via CreateProcessWithTokenW  (the documented way to run as the logged-on user from an elevated process; a direct call, NOT the Shell.Application COM trick that was already tried and found unreliable)
  C. a scheduled task registered with RunLevel Limited
It refuses to run unelevated, because from an unelevated shell every mechanism would 'succeed' with no privilege to drop.

Whichever of B or C comes back DROPPED PRIVILEGE is the replacement for scanner.ps1's relaunch-deelevated case.
close_reason:
FIXED in 0.5.2, by measurement rather than by another theory.

test/deelevation-probe.ps1, run by the operator from an elevated shell 2026-08-13:

  runas.exe /trustlevel:0x20000              NO RESULT (exit 1)
  explorer token, CreateProcessWithTokenW    NO RESULT (child died 0xc0000142)
  scheduled task, RunLevel Limited           DROPPED PRIVILEGE
                                             Medium Mandatory Level, S-1-16-8192

runas /trustlevel is the Windows-DOCUMENTED mechanism for this exact operation and it does not work on this machine. In the app it did something worse than fail: it exited 0, so the app reported a successful de-elevation and came back Full Mode. That is why five sessions found nothing - the mechanism was not erroring, it was lying, and every layer above it faithfully reported the lie.

FIX: scanner.ps1 gains Invoke-DeelevatedViaScheduledTask, which registers a task with -RunLevel Limited -LogonType Interactive, starts it, waits for a new process, and unregisters in a finally. relaunch-deelevated calls it FIRST; runas remains as a fallback because it is documented and may work where SAFER policy is intact, but it no longer gets the benefit of the doubt.

A LAUNCH IS NO LONGER A SUCCESS UNTIL A PROCESS EXISTS. Both mechanisms now call Wait-ForNewProcess and report the PID. An exit code proved nothing - that is exactly how this survived - and is not accepted as evidence by either path.

TWO THINGS THAT WOULD HAVE BITTEN LATER, both asserted:
- ExecutionTimeLimit is [TimeSpan]::Zero (unlimited). The DEFAULT is 72 hours, after which Task Scheduler would terminate Vanish out from under someone who left it open.
- The task is always unregistered. A leftover task would show in the user's Task Scheduler as something Vanish installed, which is the residue this app exists to object to. Asserted to be gone after both the success and failure paths.

THE RECORD NOW SAYS WHICH MECHANISM RAN. The 14:17:31 entry said only 'success'. Both the relaunch-intent marker and the oplog now carry method, newPid, and on total failure the reason from BOTH attempts rather than only the last.

VERIFIED: test/deelevation-mechanism-verify.ps1 20/20; the launch path is exercised for real (registering a task for your own user needs no elevation, so it launches and returns a live PID even unelevated, and leaves no task behind). Full suite 691 passed, 0 failed. Packaged scanner.ps1 sha256-identical to source and carries the new mechanism.

REMAINING, and it is the operator's to confirm: that the de-elevated instance comes up in Audit Mode with a visible window. The probe proved the process runs at Medium integrity; only a round trip proves Vanish paints its UI from there.

title: De-elevation reports success without verifying it happened - the round trip never reached Audit Mode
description:
FIRST HARD EVIDENCE in four sessions of investigation, from the operator's round trip on 2026-08-13. It falsifies both standing theories, including mine.

THE OPLOG, verbatim:
  04:30:55  app-start              tier=full
  04:35:50  relaunch-deelevated    outcome=success  tier=full   (user clicked Restart now)
  04:37:20  app-start              tier=FULL                    <- came back ELEVATED
  04:37:29  relaunch-deelevated    outcome=success  tier=full   (tried again)

There is NO relaunch-elevated entry on 2026-08-13 at all.

WHAT THIS MEANS: the failure is not re-elevation. It is DE-elevation. The app never reached Audit Mode, so there was never anything to re-elevate and the 'Restart as administrator' button was never even on screen - it does not render in Full Mode. The operator's read ('it didnt reelevate') and my own framing were both describing a symptom one step downstream of the actual fault.

ROOT CAUSE, in scanner.ps1's relaunch-deelevated case:

    $null = Start-Process -FilePath 'runas.exe' -ArgumentList @('/trustlevel:0x20000', $commandLine) -ErrorAction Stop
    @{ success = $true }

success=true means 'runas.exe was launched'. It does NOT mean a de-elevated Vanish started. runas.exe's exit code is never captured, its stdout/stderr goes to a console window that closes immediately, and Start-Process without -Wait returns as soon as the process is created. Every failure mode of runas itself is therefore invisible and reported as success. This is the same class of defect 6lg was built to catch for the elevation direction - and 6lg only instruments THAT direction, so the mirror case had no detection at all.

ENVIRONMENT RULED OUT on this machine, so this is app code, not Windows:
  seclogon (Secondary Logon, which runas.exe requires): Running
  EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, PromptOnSecureDesktop=1 - normal
  package.json requestedExecutionLevel: asInvoker - Windows is not force-elevating it
  settings.json startupMode: 'audit' - the startup auto-elevate path requires 'full' and did not fire

THE FIX, which is the operator's own instinct ('should we try to get the state of elevation every time') and the answer is yes:

1. Capture the outcome, not the launch. runas.exe must be run so its exit code and error text are readable, and a non-zero exit must be reported as a failure with the real reason instead of success.
2. Bidirectional intent verification. 6lg writes an elevation-attempt marker and compares tier on the next boot; do the same for de-elevation. Every relaunch records the tier it INTENDED, and the next launch compares intent against reality and surfaces a mismatch either direction.
3. State the tier transition honestly in the UI at the moment it fails, rather than relaunching into a silent contradiction.

Filed P0 because it makes a shipped, operator-facing control (the startup-elevation toggle's Restart now) claim it worked when it did not - the precise class of dishonesty this app exists to avoid.
design: Do NOT fix by guessing at runas alternatives again. dtd already burned one attempt on Shell.Application that looked right and failed live. The durable fix is verification: whatever mechanism drops privilege, the app must confirm the resulting tier and say so when it does not match. Build the verification FIRST, then diagnose runas with it in place - the verification is what makes the next attempt conclusive instead of another guess.
acceptance_criteria: A de-elevation that does not result in an Audit Mode launch is reported to the user as a failure with the reason, and logged as a mismatch; a de-elevation that succeeds is silent. Same for elevation. Both directions covered by tests.
close_reason:
Detection and honest reporting shipped. The runas mechanism itself is NOT yet proven fixed - that needs one more operator round trip - but the app can no longer claim a tier switch happened when it did not, which was the actual defect.

WHAT CHANGED:
1. scanner.ps1 relaunch-deelevated: was Start-Process without -Wait, reporting success the moment runas.exe existed as a process. runas then ran, and whatever it decided went to a console window that closed. Now -Wait -PassThru with stdout/stderr redirected: a non-zero exit is a failure carrying runas's own reason, and success means exit code 0 rather than 'a process was created'.
2. main.js: the relaunch intent marker now records its DIRECTION, and the next boot compares the tier it landed in against the tier that direction wanted. 6lg only ever asked 'did we ask to elevate and land in Audit', so the mirror case had no detection at all - which is exactly why two failed de-elevations on 2026-08-13 produced no evidence anywhere. Logged as relaunch-deelevated-mismatch with wantedTier/landedTier.
3. renderer/core.js: a message for the de-elevation direction ('reported success but this session started with them anyway - nothing was lost, you are still in Full Mode, but the switch did not take'), and the immediate failure path now shows runas's exit code and reason instead of one sentence covering every cause.

Markers written before this change have no direction field and are treated as elevations, which is what they were - tested.

Verified: npm test 565/0, 21 new assertions. The decision logic is pinned in test/elevation-intent-verify.js as main.js evaluates it, plus structural checks that catch someone reverting main.js to a single-direction test - the specific regression that kept this invisible for four sessions.

NEXT ROUND TRIP will now be conclusive either way: if de-elevation still fails, the toast names it and the oplog carries relaunch-deelevated-mismatch with the runas exit code. Environment already ruled out on this machine: seclogon Running, EnableLUA=1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=5, manifest asInvoker, startupMode audit.

title: Confirm elevated-relaunch fix in the portable build
description: Operator hit a blank navy window after clicking 'Restart as administrator' from the portable exe. Root cause: attemptElevatedRelaunch (main.js) used process.execPath, which for a portable build is a temp-extracted copy that can be cleaned up mid-relaunch, racing the new elevated process reading its own resources. Fixed by preferring process.env.PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE (the stable path electron-builder sets for exactly this case), plus show:false/did-fail-load so a future failure surfaces an error instead of a silent blank window. Commit e00f252. This is a live-UAC path and cannot be verified by any automated harness in this environment.
acceptance_criteria: From the rebuilt dist/Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe, click Restart as administrator from an unelevated launch. The elevated window shows real content, not blank. If it still fails, capture the error dialog text (did-fail-load now shows one) and report it.
close_reason: Live sandbox test, 2026-08-10 (operator): launched dist\Vanish-0.3.0-portable.exe unelevated, clicked Restart as administrator, accepted UAC. Elevated window showed the real app - sidebar, program list, everything - not a blank navy rectangle. Exactly one instance running. Confirms commit e00f252's PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE fix holds in the packaged build, not just in theory.

title: Real-data test harness: the missing gate that let all of the above ship
description:
THE PREVENTION ITEM. Every defect in this epic was invisible to a 312/312 green suite because every UI test runs against test/fixtures/stub-preload.js: ONE app, clean fields, instant responses. Real conditions - 163 apps, varied shapes, multi-second scans, partial states, Windows-component entries, scrollbars - are untested end to end.

This is not 'add more tests.' It is a second harness class that runs the real preload + real backend against the real machine, and asserts on what a user would actually see. The pattern already exists and works: several throwaway diagnostics this session (dashboard stats, the search-filter race) did exactly this and each found a real bug within minutes. They were deleted instead of kept. Make it permanent.

Must cover, at minimum, per screen: does the primary action button pass a hit test with a REAL-length list; does the screen render real data without visual breakage; does an action actually change what a rescan reports.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT learned the hard way (see AGP-3 in the pitfalls retrospective): a diagnostic that require()s main.js also spawns main.js's real visible window as a side effect, which reached the operator's screen and confused them once already. Any permanent real-data harness must handle this explicitly - suppress the window, or run headless, or make it unmistakably not-the-real-app.
acceptance_criteria: A committed real-data harness (separate from the stub suites, runnable on demand, not necessarily in npm test's default path) that loads the real preload against the real backend and asserts per-screen: primary action buttons hit-testable with a real-length list, real data renders, actions change subsequent scan results. It must reproduce at least two of this epic's defects BEFORE they are fixed - that is the proof it would have caught them. Spawns no window that could be mistaken for the real app.
close_reason: Real-data harness landed: test/real-data-verify.js + test/fixtures/real-machine-truth.ps1. Reproduced 6 real defects before any fix - details-panel action buttons 250px below the window bottom at the app's real 1080x720 size (7oo.1), Storage renders 0 of 2 fixed drives (7oo.8), 60 of 151 registry entries never reach the renderer (7oo.3), 15 genuinely-broken entries missing from Force Uninstall (7oo.2), orphaned startup items with no control on any row (7oo.4), and a 180s context-menu scan with no progress (6g2/7oo.5). main.js gained VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1 so no diagnostic can spawn a window mistakable for the app.

title: System-component filter too broad: protects all Microsoft products, not just what Windows needs
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'system installs are discouraged to touch, meaning software windows needs to survive, not every ms product. but this is just ridiculous.'

Current logic (scanner.ps1 Get-InstalledApps) skips SystemComponent=1 and ParentKeyName entries wholesale, which conflates 'Windows will break without this' with 'this happens to be published by Microsoft.' A user must be able to uninstall Office, Teams, Edge, OneDrive, Visual Studio etc. - these are ordinary applications. Only genuine OS components should carry the protected treatment.

Needs a real classification pass: what is actually load-bearing for Windows vs what is merely Microsoft-published. Per Rule 24, whatever protection remains must state WHY an item is protected, not just grey it out.
acceptance_criteria: Ordinary Microsoft applications (Office, Teams, Edge, OneDrive, VS) appear as normal uninstallable entries. Genuine OS components remain protected AND state the specific reason. Verified against the real installed list on the operator's machine (163 apps), not fixtures.
close_reason: Fixed together - all three were the same root cause. Inventory now classifies every uninstall entry (application/component/update) with a stated reason instead of dropping 60 of 151. Force Uninstall reads the same classified inventory rather than a second sweep that reapplied the old drops. Redundancy groups by product family keyed on vendor. Verified on the operator's real machine: 77 applications / 73 components / 1 update, Edge+Office+OneDrive+VSCode+WSL all ordinary applications, 1 protected entry with a reason, 0 false-positive broken entries, detection proven with a planted HKCU entry, 4 real redundancy groups down from 6. npm test 312/0.

title: Force Uninstall: lists wrong/un-actionable entries and omits real ones
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'force uninstall simply shows wrong entries which cant be uninstalled, still not displaying all entries.'

Two distinct defects in one surface: (a) false positives - entries listed as force-uninstallable that cannot actually be acted on, (b) false negatives - genuinely broken entries missing from the list. The detection heuristic in scanner.ps1 Find-BrokenEntries needs re-derivation against real registry state, not the planted fixtures test/force-verify.ps1 uses (19/19 passing against fixtures - see the epic's root cause).

Related: vanish-uninstaller-1qp (REQ-20 VM acceptance) is the same surface; likely resolve together.
acceptance_criteria: On the operator's real machine: every entry listed is genuinely broken AND genuinely actionable (force-uninstall completes and the entry leaves Programs and Features). Every genuinely broken entry present on the machine appears in the list. Verified against real registry state, not planted fixtures.
close_reason: Fixed together - all three were the same root cause. Inventory now classifies every uninstall entry (application/component/update) with a stated reason instead of dropping 60 of 151. Force Uninstall reads the same classified inventory rather than a second sweep that reapplied the old drops. Redundancy groups by product family keyed on vendor. Verified on the operator's real machine: 77 applications / 73 components / 1 update, Edge+Office+OneDrive+VSCode+WSL all ordinary applications, 1 protected entry with a reason, 0 false-positive broken entries, detection proven with a planted HKCU entry, 4 real redundancy groups down from 6. npm test 312/0.

title: Uninstall wizard: action buttons partially occluded by another element
description:
Operator, 2026-08-06: 'opening an item to uninstall results in poor ui, where the choice buttons are partially hidden behind another element.'

CRITICAL CONTEXT: test/ui-interaction-verify.js exists specifically to catch this class of bug (its own header documents a prior occlusion defect where 'buttons rendered perfectly and did nothing'), and it PASSES green. So the existing hit-test coverage does not reproduce the real condition - likely because the fixture renders 1 app in a short list while real data renders 163 with a scrollbar, different container heights, and a details sidebar in a different state. Reproduce with real data first, then fix, then extend the hit-test suite so the REAL geometry is covered, not just the fixture's.

Files: index.html wizard screens, index.css (.wizard-*, z-index/stacking), renderer.js showScreen().
acceptance_criteria: With the real app and real data loaded (163 apps), every wizard action button on every wizard screen passes a document.elementFromPoint hit test at its own centre. Regression test reproduces the real layout condition (list long enough to scroll, details sidebar open), not the 1-app fixture.
close_reason: Root cause was not the wizard: the details panel scrolled as a whole while its two action buttons relied on margin-top:auto, so with real registry paths the buttons rendered at y=969/1036 in the app's own 1080x720 window - 250px below the bottom edge. Fixed by making the info list the scrolling element and the actions structure, with panel chrome sized in vh. Verified by test/real-data-verify.js at 800x600, 1080x720 and 1440x900. Wizard footer buttons themselves were sound at every screen once the harness stopped mistaking Audit Mode's deliberate pointer-events:none for occlusion.

title: EPIC: Shipped surfaces are aesthetic shells - make every existing screen actually work
description:
Operator audit 2026-08-06, verbatim verdict: 'we have an aesthetic product with poor UX and minimal functionality, this is the worst of all worlds. implode the fluff, build a robust software.'

ROOT CAUSE (agent process failure, recorded so it is not repeated): every UI test in this repo runs against test/fixtures/stub-preload.js, which returns ONE fake app with clean well-formed fields. Real state on the operator's machine is 163 apps of wildly varied shape, plus real scan latency, real partial states, real Windows-component entries. Result: 312/312 tests passing while the app is visibly broken on screen. The hit-test suite that exists SPECIFICALLY to catch occluded buttons passed green while real action buttons sit occluded in the real app. Fixture-shaped testing validated fixture-shaped reality.

Prior sessions fixed defects one-at-a-time as the operator reported them, never doing a systematic screen-by-screen pass with real data. That reactive loop is what produced an app that looks finished and is not. See D:\Depthworks\Projects\ideations\agent-verification-pitfalls\RETROSPECTIVE.md (AGP-1) - the pattern was documented twice this session and still not applied where it counted.

BINDING RULE for all children of this epic: no child may be closed on a stub-test pass alone. Each requires verification against the REAL app with REAL data (the operator's machine or the Sandbox), because that is the only environment where these defects are visible at all.

STRATEGIC CONTEXT (changes priorities): operator confirmed commercialization intent - B2B paid, personal use free. This supersedes the MS Store Convenience Edition assumption recorded on vanish-uninstaller-22n. A B2B buyer will not tolerate any defect on this list. Robustness of existing surfaces now outranks new stage scope.
close_reason: All ten original children fixed and verified against the real machine, not fixtures. Measured: context-menu scan 300s+ -> 0.7s; Storage 0 -> 2 of 2 drives; inventory 91 of 151 entries visible -> all 151 classified with reasons; uninstall actions 250px off-screen -> on screen at 800x600/1080x720/1440x900; Force Uninstall now reads the same classified inventory as the app list (detection proven with a planted HKCU entry); redundancy 6 groups -> 4 real; startup orphans 3 -> 1 real (2 were false positives from quote handling); live scan progress where there was none; Windows optional features listed (135); quarantine entries state what happens if left alone. Gate: test/real-data-verify.js 152/0 across 11 sections; npm test 314/0; geometry sweep 262/0. 7oo.11 detached as deliberate follow-up scope, not a defect.

title: SEC-1 (CRITICAL): elevated command injection via registry UninstallString in uninstall-native
description:
Found by /cso audit 2026-08-03 (TASK-18). Report: .security-reports/2026-08-03-160528.json finding 1.

main.js:247 passes uninstallString straight to node:child_process exec(), which on
Windows runs it through cmd.exe /d /s /c. The string originates in the registry:
Get-InstalledApps (scanner.ps1:56,97) enumerates
HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* and copies
UninstallString verbatim; Find-BrokenUninstallEntries (scanner.ps1:2889,2906) does
the same for the broken-entry repair flow. HKCU is writable at medium integrity.

Because a shell is attached, cmd metacharacters (&, |, &&, ^) are honoured. This
path has no Get-UninstallerTrust check, no live registry re-read, and no
executable/argument split -- all three of which lib/queue.js runOne does apply.
The Vuln 3 remediation hardened only the queue path.

EXPLOIT
1. Medium-integrity code creates HKCU\...\Uninstall\FreeVideoToolbar with
   DisplayName "Free Video Toolbar" and
   UninstallString = C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c "net localgroup administrators
   attacker /add & powershell -enc <payload>"
2. User launches Vanish and elevates to Full Mode (documented FLOW-01 path).
3. The planted entry appears in the app list -- an entry named like adware is
   exactly what an uninstaller's user wants to remove.
4. User clicks Launch Native Uninstaller (renderer.js:902) or Scan traces ->
   Run its uninstaller (renderer.js:2682).
5. exec() spawns cmd.exe as administrator with the attacker's command line.

IMPACT
One-click local privilege escalation from medium integrity to administrator, with
a shell. Registry write plus a UI click; no memory corruption, no race.

FIX
Delete the exec() path. Change the IPC contract so uninstall-native accepts a
registryPath, never a command string, then route through the queue's pipeline:
read-uninstall-entry (live re-read + Get-UninstallerTrust) -> resolve-uninstall-args
(Split-UninstallString) -> run-uninstaller (Start-Process -FilePath/-ArgumentList,
no shell), with the trust.risky acknowledgement gate in front.
acceptance_criteria: uninstall-native accepts a registryPath, never a command string; no exec()/shell anywhere in main.js; the path re-reads the live registry, splits executable from arguments, and applies the Get-UninstallerTrust risky gate; test/security-verify.ps1 plants an HKCU entry with cmd metacharacters and asserts refusal; run-all.ps1 stays green.
close_reason: Fixed: uninstall-native now takes a registry pointer and runs read-uninstall-entry -> trust gate -> resolve-uninstall-args -> run-uninstaller (Start-Process, no shell). exec removed from main.js. UWP branch calls Remove-AppxPackage as a cmdlet via the new remove-appx action. Invoke-Uninstaller gate widened from userWritable to risky. Regression tests added to test/security-verify.ps1 (elevated) and tier-verify.js (both tiers). Suite: 164 passed / 0 failed unelevated; the new elevated assertions still need an elevated run.

title: Health Advisor says 'All 6 checks read successfully' when two of them failed
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04, verified directly. The landing page's verdict can
state a provable falsehood in the exact wording this project exists to prevent.

TWO SECTIONS RESOLVE ON FAILURE AND MANUFACTURE THE NEGATIVE FACT:

  main.js:1628  get-startup-items catch -> { items: [], total: 0, orphans: 0, error }
  main.js:1808  redundancy      catch -> { groups: [], hasRedundancy: false, error }

Note what those return: not just an empty list, but total:0 and orphans:0 and
hasRedundancy:false - the negatives asserted as facts. The startup one has no
success field at all.

THE RENDERERS NEVER LOOK. Verified: renderStartupTable reads
startup.items ?? [], startup.total ?? items.length, startup.orphans ?? 0 and
never touches .error. Because the promise RESOLVES, renderer/audit.js takes the
draw path and the .catch that would call auditReportBlind never fires.

WHAT THE USER SEES: a green check and 'Nothing extra starts with Windows on
this PC', or 'No programs here appear to overlap with each other'. Then the
draw callback calls auditReportWork(0, ...) - so the section reports NO WORK
and NO BLINDNESS - and the page-level verdict reads:

  'Nothing on this page needs a decision - All 6 checks read successfully and
   none of them found anything to act on.'

Two of the six did not read successfully. The verdict machinery itself
(renderer/audit.js) is correct and refuses to name a state mid-flight; it is
being fed a lie by two sections.

FOUR SECTIONS ON THE SAME PAGE DO THIS RIGHT, which is what makes it a bug
rather than a design gap: renderListeners, renderNetworkActivity,
renderWindowsUpdates and loadBrokenEntries all check success before rendering a
negative.

FIX: the two handlers should return success:false with the error rather than a
well-shaped empty, and the two renderers should call auditSectionFailed /
auditReportBlind on that - the helpers already exist and the other four
sections already use them.
close_reason: Folded into qkgu. Same root: a failure represented as a well-shaped success. The two handlers are named there and the fix is the same two adapters.

title: Registry restore has no integrity check and no destination guard - cihg is files-only
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. Found independently by two reviewers and verified
directly. This is the unfixed half of a security fix that already shipped.

cihg was built because 'quarantine a file, overwrite the payload inside the
vault entry folder, restore' returned success and put back
TAMPERED-BY-SOMETHING-ELSE. The fix records contentHash / hashAlgo / hashNote on
every FILE row (scanner.ps1:4113-4116) and refuses on mismatch at restore.

THE REGISTRY ROW HAS NEITHER HALF. Verified: the quarantine row shape is
index / keyPath / regFile / status / error / mode - no hash of any kind. And the
restore path goes straight from 'the file exists' to running it as admin:

  if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $regFile)) { ...missing...; continue }
  $null = & reg.exe import "$regFile" 2>&1

So the exact attack cihg was written for still works against the registry half
of the same vault entry.

NO DESTINATION GUARD EITHER. There is no registry analogue of
Test-ProtectedDestination anywhere in the engine. reg.exe import applies
whatever the file says, as administrator. The only constraint is
Resolve-SafeVaultPath, which checks the .reg sits INSIDE the entry folder - it
says nothing about what the file contains.

FAILURE SCENARIO: a standard user writes
<dataDir>\vault\<uuid>\registry\1.reg containing
[HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run] plus a
matching row in manifest.json. lib/vault.js reads the entry from the manifest
and passes it verbatim to the engine. The operator clicks Restore in Full Mode
and an HKLM Run key is written as admin.

THE PRECONDITION IS LIVE, not hypothetical - it is the same one al45 was filed
on. scanner.ps1 records check-data-dir reporting protected=false with
nonAdminWriters=[the user] on the development machine. And SEC-3's ACL is
applied only from the first ELEVATED start, so anything planted while the app
had only ever run in Audit Mode survives the lock: the ACL protects the
directory going forward, it does not validate what is already in it.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY IN THE EXCEPTIONS: Test-RestorableProtectedPath and
Test-RestorableInstalledAppPath both consult Test-VaultDataDirTrusted. The
GENERAL restore path never asks it, so a non-protected destination restores
from an untrusted manifest without complaint.

WHAT THE TESTS COVER: security-verify.ps1 tests a TRAVERSING regFile
(..\..\evil.reg). An in-bounds, attacker-authored .reg is untested, and the
independent test-quality review flagged the same gap and noted there is no
mutant for this path either.

FIX: hash the .reg at quarantine exactly as files are hashed, verify at
restore, and add a key-path guard so a restore cannot write outside the
key it claims to be restoring.

title: open-external-link hands an unvalidated URL to shell.openExternal, un-gated, from an elevated process
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. Verified directly.

  main.js:2308   ipcMain.on('open-external-link', (event, url) => {
  main.js:2309     shell.openExternal(url);
  main.js:2310   });
  preload.js:147 openExternalLink: (url) => ipcRenderer.send('open-external-link', url)

Zero validation of scheme, host or path. Registered with ipcMain.on, so it is
not in the fullModeOnly table and never reaches the oplog - it is invisible to
the elevation audit.

THE ONLY LEGITIMATE CALLER in the whole app is renderer/updates.js:160, which
passes the literal 'ms-settings:windowsupdate-history'. One caller, one
constant, and the channel accepts anything.

WHAT A COMPROMISED RENDERER BUYS. shell.openExternal on Windows is
ShellExecuteW in the MAIN process, which in Full Mode is elevated, so the
launched process inherits High integrity. In one call it bypasses every
fullModeOnly gate, the entire SEC-1 trust pipeline (user-writable check, HKCU
check, LOLBin block, the acknowledged:true requirement) and the oplog.

HONEST ON REACHABILITY, and this matters for the priority: the reviewer did not
execute it, so whether 'file:' specifically survives this Electron build is
unconfirmed. Even if file: is filtered, every URI scheme registered on the
machine stays reachable - the ms-msdt:/Follina shape is exactly this. Rank it
as 'the worst thing a renderer compromise buys' rather than a standalone RCE:
the CSP has no unsafe-inline and esc() was audited clean this sweep, so the
initial compromise is genuinely hard.

RELATED, SAME FILE, and it makes the above worse: createWindow (main.js:81-125)
sets no will-navigate handler and no setWindowOpenHandler. The meta CSP is a
property of the DOCUMENT. Navigate the window to a remote origin and the new
document carries the attacker's CSP while still holding the preload and every
window.api channel. connect-src 'none' does not restrict top-level navigation.

FIX, smallest possible: an allowlist. The app needs exactly one scheme prefix
today ('ms-settings:'), so validate against that and refuse everything else
with a logged reason. Add will-navigate and setWindowOpenHandler while there.

NOT COVERED by test/security-verify.ps1 - no test mentions this channel.
close_reason: Channel now takes a KEY, not a URL. No string a renderer can send reaches shell.openExternal. 9 assertions in updates-verify.

title: Rescue module ranks cheap FIRST, and the caption tells the user the opposite
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02 while profiling the hygiene panel. Two facts that are individually defensible and together defeat the panel's core claim.

FACT 1 -- THE RANKING. lib/findings.js rankFindings sorts ASCENDING by costRank, and COST_ORDER is:

  cheap -> moderate -> expensive -> irreplaceable -> unknown

Demonstrated with five synthetic findings, one of each class:
  1. cheap  2. moderate  3. expensive  4. irreplaceable  5. unknown

So the cheapest-to-rebuild findings are at the TOP and the irreplaceable ones are fourth of five.

FACT 2 -- THE CAPTION SAYS THE REVERSE. renderer/hygiene.js, the render-cap notice shown whenever a module has more than HYGIENE_RENDER_CAP = 100 findings:

  'They are the first 100 for a reason -- everything here is ranked by what it
   would cost to get back, so the ones you cannot rebuild are at the top and
   the ones a command regenerates are at the bottom.'

That is false as written. The ones a command regenerates are at the top.

WHY THIS IS P1 AND NOT A WORDING BUG. duplicate-content is registered with -module 'rescue', the SAME module as local-only-credentials and gitignored-unique. The rescue module is the one whose stated job is 'what a delete would destroy'. Measured on this machine, duplicate-content alone returns

  4,040 findings, every one costClass 'cheap', 46 unreadable, 36.8 s standalone

against a 100-row per-module cap. So any irreplaceable finding in the rescue module ranks below four thousand cheap ones and is not rendered, in the module that exists to show it, under a caption promising it is at the top.

WHAT IS PROVEN AND WHAT IS NOT, stated separately on purpose:
  PROVEN  the ordering, the caption text, the shared module, and the 4,040 count.
  INFERRED  that a credential would actually be buried. It could not be
            observed here because local-only-credentials returns 0 findings on
            this machine today -- the ho2 probe's '4 candidates' are files
            matching the credential patterns, and the finder then filters to
            gitignored AND on no remote, which none of the four passed. The
            mechanism is demonstrated; the instance is not.

WHAT THE FIX IS NOT. Do not just flip COST_ORDER. Cheap-first is arguably correct for a RECLAIM list, where the question is 'what is safe to delete' and leading with irreplaceable items would put the most dangerous offers first -- which is exactly what the 'unknown sorts last' comment in lib/findings.js is defending against. The two modules want opposite orders because they ask opposite questions:

  rescue   'what would I lose' -> irreplaceable first
  reclaim  'what is safe to remove' -> cheap first

So the candidate fix is a per-module sort direction, plus a caption generated from the direction actually used rather than written by hand. A caption that is a literal string can always drift from the sort; one derived from it cannot.

SECOND QUESTION THIS RAISES, worth its own issue if the answer is yes: should duplicate-content be in 'rescue' at all? 4,040 findings of which the sampled ones are 514-byte scraps under .gemini/antigravity/brain/ is the same noise problem as the 77 Visual C++ rows that 7oo.3 exists to remove, and it is 97.5% of everything the panel reports.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-02 in 623acde. Both halves.

THE ORDERING. lib/findings.js now carries two cost orders and picks by module:
  reclaim  cheap -> moderate -> expensive -> irreplaceable -> unknown
  rescue   irreplaceable -> unknown -> expensive -> moderate -> cheap

'unknown' is deliberately not a mirror: last in reclaim (an unmeasured cost is not a cheap one and must not head a list of things to delete), second in rescue (it might be irreplaceable, and burying it under things known to be cheap is the same mistake reversed). Both put the unmeasured case where being wrong costs least.

rankFindings sorts by module first so the comparator stays a valid total order -- two findings in different modules are ranked by different directions and comparing them directly is not a consistent ordering, which Array#sort is entitled to misbehave on. Cross-module order is never displayed: renderer/hygiene.js and lib/hygiene-report.js both slice the ranked list by module rather than re-sorting.

THE CAPTION. costOrderCaption() generates the sentence FROM the order array, and renderer/hygiene.js calls it instead of carrying a literal. The words and the sort can no longer disagree because there is only one of them. This is the half that was a lie rather than a defect.

THE THIRD COPY. The module order now decides ranking as well as layout, so lib/hygiene-report.js derives MODULE_KEYS from findings.js rather than keeping its own, and test/hygiene-report-verify.js asserts renderer/hygiene.js's HYGIENE_MODULES order matches -- it cannot derive, because those entries carry the on-screen title, icon and lede.

VERIFIED BY BREAKING IT, three ways:
  one order for every module again        7 failures
  order reversed, caption words unchanged 4 failures
  panel module order reordered            1 failure

And end to end in the panel: 141 rescue findings, 140 cheap and one irreplaceable, past the 100-row cap. The irreplaceable one is row 1, under 'the ones you cannot rebuild are at the top'.

  Seam decider (5p5)      85 passed, 0 failed
  Hygiene report (z22)    42 passed, 0 failed
  Hygiene panel (5p5 UI) 159 passed, 0 failed
  TOTAL 1931 passed, 0 failed, 13 skipped [Audit Mode]

Audit Mode because this session lost elevation partway through. Adequate for this change: every file it touches is tier-independent, and the Full-Mode-only suites are untouched by it.

NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately: whether duplicate-content belongs in 'rescue' at all. That is 9caq. The practical harm is now much reduced either way -- with rescue ranking loss-first, 4,040 cheap duplicates sink below anything irreplaceable instead of burying it -- but 97.5% of the panel's output still coming from one check is its own problem.

title: A clean machine cannot build some test preconditions, and three suites call that FAIL
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30 in the FIRST unattended clean-machine run, which is the whole
point of having one. Windows Sandbox, Full Mode:

  TOTAL: 1980 passed, 3 failed, 14 skipped   [Full Mode]

None of the three failures is a product bug. All three are one defect:

  A SUITE THAT CANNOT CONSTRUCT ITS PRECONDITION REPORTS FAIL INSTEAD OF SKIP.

  1. Walker invariants -- "come from more than one check". Windows Sandbox
     ships without git, so gitignored-unique, repo-health and
     local-only-credentials could not run and only reclaim-node was left to
     compare. The INVARIANT itself passed. FIXED 2026-08-30: it now skips with
     the reason when git is absent, and still fails when git IS present and a
     walker has gone missing, which is the case that means something.

  2. Data-dir ownership (isp) -- "NEGATIVE CONTROL: with the fix off, one
     manifest write breaks protection". The sandbox account is an
     Administrator with UAC off, so the ACL protection this control needs to
     break cannot be broken. NOT FIXED.

  3. Live elevated relaunch (69a) -- "and it was genuinely UNPRIVILEGED,
     otherwise this proves nothing". The sandbox account is ALWAYS
     Administrator, so an unprivileged context cannot exist there. NOT FIXED.

WHY THIS IS P1 AND NOT HOUSEKEEPING. docs/PRE-RELEASE.md Rule 10 makes a clean
VM pass a release gate. The first time that gate was actually run it produced
three red lines that mean "this machine cannot host these tests", and a gate
whose failures have to be individually explained away is not a gate. The next
person to run it either investigates three non-bugs or learns to ignore red,
and both outcomes are worse than not running it.

THE RULE TO ENFORCE, and it is the same one 686 needs for its silent variant:
  * cannot build the condition  -> Write-Skip, with the reason
  * built it and it behaved wrong -> Assert-True $false
  * never assert false for the first case, and never quietly skip the assertion
    without recording a skip (686: GPU payload shape drops 14 -> 10 assertions
    with no skip line at all)

SANDBOX SPECIFICS WORTH RECORDING, since they will recur every run:
  * no git.exe on PATH (the credentials suite already skips wholesale for this)
  * WDAGUtilityAccount is an Administrator and UAC is off, so nothing
    unprivileged and no enforceable Deny ACE
  * these are properties of the image, not of the build under test
notes:
PARTIALLY FIXED 2026-08-30 in commit 85e3acd. All three suites now skip instead of failing when the machine cannot build the precondition, and both files gained the helper they lacked (assertOrSkip in data-dir-ownership-verify.js, Write-Skip in relaunch-live-probe.ps1). Host after: 2056 passed, 0 failed, 9 skipped [Full Mode].

NOTE ON THE COMMIT MESSAGE: 85e3acd refers to 'bd vanish-uninstaller-1uy9'. There is no such issue -- I wrote an id from memory instead of looking it up. THIS issue, 392o, is the one it means.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN HERE: the rule now holds in the three places that broke, but nothing enforces it. 686 records the silent variant of the same problem (GPU payload shape drops 14 -> 10 assertions between runs with no skip line at all), which no amount of fixing individual suites prevents. The generic form would be a runner-level check that a suite's assertion count is stable across runs in the same tier, or that any drop is accounted for by a recorded skip.
close_reason:
FIXED and verified by the run that found it. The clean-machine gate now passes unattended: TOTAL 1992 passed, 0 failed, 17 skipped [Full Mode], exit 0, Windows Sandbox.

All three red lines are now skips that name what the machine could not do:
  walker invariants - 'only 1 check(s) could run because git.exe is not on PATH'
  data-dir ownership (isp) - the negative control skips: an Administrator with UAC off cannot break the ACL it must break
  live relaunch (69a) - 'the de-elevated stage came back STILL elevated. EnableLUA is 0 - with UAC off there is no standard-user token to drop to'

Took three sandbox runs (3 failed -> 1 failed -> 0 failed). The middle failure was a mangled registry path in the fix for the first, not a new defect.

Also fixed on the way, because it made the gate unreliable to run at all: start-sandbox.ps1 reported 'Starting Windows Sandbox' whether or not it started one. Windows Sandbox permits a single instance and fails SILENTLY on a second launch - no dialog, no exit code, no log - and vmmemWindowsSandbox outlives the window by minutes, so a launch in that gap fails the same way. It now detects both, waits 5 minutes, and throws with the reason.

The rule this issue asked for is enforced generally, not case by case: cannot build the condition -> Write-Skip with the reason; built it and it behaved wrong -> Assert-True $false. run-all.ps1 names every skip at the bottom and the assertion-count baseline guard (686) catches a suite that quietly asserts less without recording a skip.

Remaining and NOT part of this issue: Rule 10 wants four cells (Win10/Win11 x Full/Audit). This fills one. Windows Sandbox mirrors the host OS family (guest 10.0.26100 against host 10.0.26200) so the Windows 10 half needs a real VM, and the sandbox image ships EnableLUA=0 so its Audit Mode half needs UAC enabled in-guest plus a restart.

title: Audit Mode silently fails to save settings once SEC-3 has locked the state directory
description:
REPRODUCED 2026-08-28, unelevated, on the operator's machine.

  node -e "fs.appendFileSync('%APPDATA%\Electron\vanish-state\settings.json','')"
  BLOCKED   settings.json  (EPERM)
  BLOCKED   queue.json     (EPERM)
  BLOCKED   oplog.jsonl    (EPERM)
  BLOCKED   (a new file in the directory)  (EPERM)

WHAT THE USER SEES. They flip a toggle in Settings. The checkbox moves, because
that is what a checkbox does on click. Nothing else happens: no toast, no error.
Next launch, the setting is back where it was.

THE CHAIN:
1. Set-VanishDataDirAcl (SEC-3) grants Users ReadAndExecute only. Correct: the
   elevated engine reads settings.json (scan mode, auto-purge), so a standard
   user rewriting it IS the threat SEC-3 exists for.
2. store.writeSettings -> writeJsonAtomic -> fs.writeFileSync throws EPERM.
3. ipcMain.handle('set-settings') has no try/catch, so the handler REJECTS.
4. renderer/settings-about.js saveSettings() has no try/catch either, so the
   rejection propagates and the line after it - toast('Setting saved.') - never
   runs, and neither does syncSettingsPanel(). The user gets silence.

This is the exact defect class this application exists to prevent: an action
that appears to work and did nothing.

NOT CAUSED BY isp, BUT MADE RELIABLE BY IT. Before the isp fix the protection
decayed on the first write, so an unelevated run would often still be able to
write - the failure was intermittent and depended on when secure-data-dir last
ran. It is now consistent, which is how it surfaced: an unelevated run-all.ps1
printed 'oplog append failed: EPERM' from the harness on 2026-08-28.

THE POLICY QUESTION, WHICH COMES FIRST. Audit Mode being unable to write
settings is arguably CORRECT - settings are elevated-engine input. If so the
app must SAY so instead of pretending, exactly as it already does for every
destructive control: disable the settings controls in Audit Mode on a secured
directory and name the reason. If instead some settings are renderer-only and
safe, they need a separate store outside the locked directory - and deciding
which is which is a security judgement, not a convenience one.

DO NOT fix this by loosening the ACL. Granting Users write access to the
directory the elevated engine reads its instructions from is the escalation
path SEC-3 was written to close, and it would undo isp on the same day.

ALSO IN SCOPE: appendOplog swallows its own failure to stderr, so in Audit Mode
on a secured machine the audit trail records NOTHING and says nothing about it.
A missing audit trail that reports itself as working is its own problem.
close_reason:
Fixed in 363fddf, three parts.

1. Controls locked UP FRONT. get-tier carries settingsWritable + settingsLockReason from a real write probe (create a temp file, delete it) rather than reasoning about an ACL. Not derived from isAdmin: a machine where Vanish never ran elevated is unlocked and an unelevated session saves fine. The panel shows a notice naming the reason, the fix, and why the lock exists, and disables every input/select it finds rather than a hand-kept list.

2. A failed write is reported anyway. set-settings never rejects; returns { settings, saved, reason } where settings is what is ON DISK, so the control snaps back. All four call sites now route through applySettingsPatch() in core.js - previously each assigned the reply straight to appSettings, which would have silently stored the new wrapper.

3. The activity log says it has stopped. appendOplog swallows its own EPERM to stderr, so on a locked machine the trail records nothing and said so nowhere.

Did NOT loosen the ACL - that is the escalation SEC-3 closes and would have undone isp the same day.

Proof: test/settings-lock-verify.js 22/0 (new; asserts the UNLOCKED case too, since disabling the panel for everyone would satisfy every did-not-lie assertion while breaking the feature). Verified against the real main process on the genuinely locked directory: get-tier settingsWritable=false, set-settings saved=false, and the reply reported Moderate when Safe was asked for. Regression suites re-run green: ui-interaction 100/0, ui-interaction-full 114/0, settings 10/0, store-migration 12/0, tier 14/0.

FOLLOW-UP NOT DONE, and it is a judgement call rather than a defect: some settings are engine input (defaultScanMode, autoPurge*, startupMode, confirmBeforeQuarantine, preferSilentUninstall) and some are purely local memory (hasSeenTour, pingConsentGiven, speedTestConsentGiven, processRefreshSeconds, networkRefreshSeconds, redundancyWaivers). The second group is locked today for no security reason. Splitting them into a separate writable store would restore them in Audit Mode - but deciding which side each one falls on is a security judgement, and getting it wrong puts engine input somewhere a standard user can rewrite.

title: Machine Hygiene: a full scan takes over ten minutes
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-28 on the operator's machine, from the live probe and a direct engine timing run.

  hygiene module alone (5 checks)   89 s
  one whole module, clicked          94 s
  all 13 checks, sequential         > 10 min (a per-finder timing loop did not finish 13 finders inside a 10-minute window)

The 0.9.0 panel makes this LEGIBLE rather than fixed: each check is its own
engine call, bounded at three at a time, and results render as they land with a
per-check status list. That is the right shape and it is not a fix. Nobody runs
a ten-minute scan twice.

WHERE THE TIME GOES, not yet measured per finder. A per-finder timing loop was
started and was still running after 15 minutes, which is itself the finding. The
suspects, in order:
  - the walkers default to $env:USERPROFILE with maxDepth 6 and no exclusions,
    so they descend into AppData, node_modules trees and OneDrive placeholders
  - duplicate-content hashes file CONTENT across trees, which is correct and is
    the single most expensive thing here
  - each finder is a fresh powershell.exe that re-enumerates the same tree the
    previous one just walked; nothing is shared between them

CANDIDATE DIRECTIONS, none chosen:
  - one walk, many finders. Enumerate once into an index and hand it to every
    finder, instead of thirteen independent walks of the same disk.
  - honest default roots. USERPROFILE is where the work is, but AppData\Local
    and OneDrive placeholders are not, and excluding them is a judgement to make
    explicitly rather than by tuning maxDepth.
  - size-gate the content hashing before it hashes.

DO NOT fix this by scanning less and saying nothing. A check that quietly stops
looking below depth 4 reports 'nothing found' about a place it did not go, which
is aeu with a performance justification attached.
close_reason:
Fixed and measured. All thirteen checks now run in 103.7 s wall clock as the panel runs them (3 concurrent engine calls), from 'over ten minutes with duplicate-content never completing'. Summed engine time 264.6 s, and the floor is now one check: duplicate-content at 56.4 s.

MEASURED FIRST, per finder, in one process with each in its own runspace under a 240 s cap - the earlier attempt spawned a process per finder and never reached the end, so it could not say which check was the problem. The profile contradicted every prediction in this issue.

  finder                    before      after
  duplicate-content       >240000*     85995   * capped, never completed
  redirect-variables        59592      12835
  reclaim-package-caches    52252      25504
  reclaim-node              38708      38805
  reclaim-archives          21458      17169
  local-only-credentials    21224      13607
  reclaim-gradle            20405      18430
  reclaim-flutter           20305      19211
  repo-health               15374       8321
  gitignored-unique         14633       7987
  duplicate-installs         1299       1056
  path-hygiene                176        112
  profile-list                163        168

THREE causes, none of them the one guessed here:

1. Six near-identical directory sizers, four byte-for-byte identical, all Get-ChildItem -Recurse building a FileInfo PSObject per file to read .Length. One memoised sizer in finders/_contract.ps1 over DirectoryInfo.EnumerateFiles replaces them. The memo was the bigger half: redirect-variables was the slowest check in the suite while examining FIVE things, because ANDROID_HOME and ANDROID_SDK_ROOT name the same default path when neither is set, so it sized 129,198 files twice.

2. duplicate-content enumerated the whole profile unpruned and materialised every FileInfo before grouping. Now uses the same pruned stack walk as its siblings - and records every pruned subtree ONCE as reason 'not-searched' with a detail saying a duplicate spanning it will be missed, because this finder reports PAIRS and pruning can hide a real finding. No findings plus a prune = could-not-look, not nothing.

3. 4,035 findings appeared once it could finish. Each module now renders 100 and states the real total; safe only because rankFindings is cost-first.

Commit 29b8a5d. Proof: finder-sizer-verify.ps1 19/0 (new - compares byte total AND file count against the exact expression replaced, proves the memo by changing the disk between two calls, proves a junction is not followed, proves a partial walk returns the partial sum and names the directory), finder-dedup-verify.ps1 36/0 (+6 prune-honesty), hygiene-panel-verify.js 42/0 (+4 render cap), plus contract 83, hygiene 78, reclaim 43, gitignored 35, credentials 24, hygiene-report 39 - all 0 failed.

Follow-up filed for the remaining structural item: four reclaim finders each walk the same tree and each hit the same 15,000-directory cap.

title: [bug] SEC-3 data-dir protection is not self-sustaining: a vault write re-creates manifest.json owned by the interactive user
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-27/28 on the operator's machine, elevated, with before/after evidence.

THE CHAIN:
1. secure-data-dir sets the state directory's owner to BUILTIN\Administrators recursively, strips inheritance, and grants Administrators + SYSTEM FullControl with Users ReadAndExecute. Verified working: check-data-dir returned protected=true, foreignOwners=[].
2. A test run then wrote to the vault.
3. check-data-dir immediately afterwards returned protected=FALSE, with foreignOwners naming vault\manifest.json as owned by S-1-5-21-...-1001 (the interactive user).

WHY: Windows' default owner for a newly created object is the OBJECT CREATOR, not the Administrators group - HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\nodefaultadminowner is unset on this machine, which is the Windows default. So even an ELEVATED process running as an administrator creates manifest.json owned by 'Anand'. The DACL is inherited correctly; the OWNER is not, and an owner permanently retains WRITE_DAC - it can hand itself write access back whatever the DACL says. That is exactly the escalation SEC-3 was written to prevent, and Set-VanishDataDirAcl's own comment says so.

CONSEQUENCE: the protection decays on the first vault write after it is applied. Everything gated on Test-VaultDataDirTrusted then silently switches off - which today means the z3s narrow exception (restoring a cached installer into %SystemRoot%\Installer) stops working, fails closed, and reports 'the vault could not put it back afterwards'. It is a feature outage rather than a vulnerability, because it fails in the safe direction. But the guard becomes a coin flip on when secure-data-dir last ran, which is not a security control.

WHY IT LOOKED INTERMITTENT: this feature was proven end to end earlier in the same session and then failed in the elevated full run. Same code, different history - the difference was purely whether anything had written to the vault since the last secure-data-dir.

CANDIDATE FIXES, not yet chosen:
- Set the owner explicitly on write. lib/vault.js writes manifest.json through fs; the engine could take ownership of the file it just wrote, or the write could be routed through the engine which already knows how.
- Re-run the ownership half of secure-data-dir after each vault mutation. Cheap (one file), but it makes every write a privileged operation.
- Have Test-VanishDataDirAcl distinguish 'owned by an administrator who is also the current elevated user' from 'owned by a standard user'. NOTE THIS IS PROBABLY WRONG - the whole point is that the same SID unelevated can still exercise WRITE_DAC, so it would weaken the control to make a test pass.

The first option looks right. Do not pick by convenience: this guard is the only thing standing between a user-writable vault and an elevated restore into a system directory.

NOTE ON THE HARNESS: the test suite reaches this through %APPDATA%\Electron\vanish-state, because it runs via npx electron and app.getPath('userData') resolves on the app NAME. The operator's real app directory (%APPDATA%\vanish-uninstaller\vanish-state) currently reports protected=true. The bug is the same in both; the real directory simply has not been written to since it was last secured.
notes:
REPRODUCED LIVE IN SEQUENCE, 2026-08-28, elevated. This is the clean before/after the issue was missing.

BEFORE the run - check-data-dir on %APPDATA%\Electron\vanish-state:
  {"protected":true, "foreignOwners":[], "nonAdminWriters":[], "inherited":false}

The suite then ran, writing 58 cleaner purges into the vault.

AFTER, same directory, same command:
  {"protected":false, "foreignOwners":["...\vault\manifest.json is owned by S-1-5-21-479141868-1469886205-2683390752-1001"]}

The state directory itself is STILL BUILTIN\Administrators. Only manifest.json flipped, and it flipped while the writing process was ELEVATED - which is the whole point: Windows gives a new object to its CREATOR, not to Administrators, unless nodefaultadminowner is set. The DACL inherits; the owner does not.

The 7v3 leg, which runs after those 58 writes, therefore finds the gate shut on a directory that was correctly secured minutes earlier. That is the intermittency, and it is fully explained: not the machine, not elevation, just whether anything has written to the vault since secure-data-dir last ran.

SEPARATELY, and worth recording so the next person does not repeat it: the operator's REAL installation is currently fine - %APPDATA%\vanish-uninstaller\vanish-state and its manifest are both BUILTIN\Administrators, check-data-dir returns protected=true, and protected-destination-probe returns dataDirTrusted=true, restorable=true. An earlier diagnosis in this session claimed that directory was user-owned; that was wrong. The probe had been called with vaultRoot pointing at the STATE directory, and Test-VaultDataDirTrusted takes Split-Path -Parent of what it is given, so it checked %APPDATA%\vanish-uninstaller - the parent, which is user-owned and is not the data directory. Passing the actual vault directory returns true. The product was right; the instrument was aimed one level too high.
close_reason: Fixed at the write (option 1). store.js takes ownership for BUILTIN\Administrators after each atomic write, after the vault mkdir, and on the append that creates oplog.jsonl. Off by default; main.js enables it once the tier is known so Audit Mode pays nothing. Commit cdfc12e. Proof: test/data-dir-ownership-verify.js 12/0/0, carrying a negative control that reproduces the decay with the fix off before asserting the fix defeats it. Side effect: phase4-ipc-verify went 53 passed/7v3 SKIPPED to 60 passed/0 skipped - the z3s protected restore round trip now runs end to end.

title: [bug] test/phase2-verify.ps1 was DELETED from the working tree during a full-suite run, and that is why it reported NOT RUN
description:
OBSERVED ONCE, 2026-08-27, not reproduced. Recording it because an unexplained deletion of a tracked file in a repository whose product deletes things for a living is not something to let pass.

WHAT HAPPENED: after a full test/run-all.ps1 run, 'git status --porcelain' showed ' D test/phase2-verify.ps1'. The runner had reported that suite as NOT RUN with 'did not report a result (needs Full Mode, or it crashed)'. Those are the same event: powershell -File could not find the script because it was gone. The log for that suite (test/logs/DESKTOP-01OAI95/task-manager-unlocker-2.log) ends cleanly after TASK-08's last assertion with no Result line. Restored with git checkout; the file is intact and byte-identical.

WHAT WAS RULED OUT, with evidence:
- The suite deleting itself. It confines all filesystem work to $env:TEMP\vanish-phase2-verify and its two Remove-Item calls both target that path. Running the suite alone afterwards did NOT delete the file.
- Windows Defender remediation. This was the strongest hypothesis, because the suite deliberately spawns a decoy process whose command line is 'vssadmin delete shadows /all' (a textbook ransomware indicator) at the exact point the log stops. Get-MpThreatDetection and Get-MpThreat both return nothing, so there is no record of a detection or a quarantine.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and the honest answer is 'unattributed':
The deletion happened during a window when six agents were writing test fixtures concurrently, several of which build and tear down temp trees with Remove-Item -Recurse -Force and manipulate ACLs with icacls. A cleanup routine computing a wrong root is the most plausible remaining cause, but no evidence points at a specific one and they are no longer running.

SECOND, SEPARATE OBSERVATION: a solo run of this suite on this machine exceeded 7 minutes without completing, where the VM logs (test/logs/68A2CEC3, test/logs/D0B08B54) show it finishing at 23 and 17 assertions. That may be machine load or may be a real hang, and it is unmeasured. A re-run on a quiet machine is queued.

WHY P1: not the deletion by itself, but that run-all.ps1 reports a MISSING SUITE FILE identically to a suite that crashed. Those want different responses, and 'NOT RUN' currently covers both. The skip-naming work of 2026-08-20 fixed the skipped-versus-passed confusion; this is the same shape one level over.
close_reason: CAUSE FOUND, and it was an antivirus doing its job. The operator's Kaspersky System Watcher flagged PDM:Trojan.Win32.Generic on test/phase2-verify.ps1 and quarantined it. MY EARLIER 'no record of a detection' WAS WRONG IN METHOD: I queried Get-MpThreatDetection and Get-MpThreat, which report on Microsoft Defender, and never established which antivirus was actually running on this machine. The hypothesis was right and the instrument was aimed at the wrong product - a confident answer about something adjacent to the question. ONE CAUSE, TWO SYMPTOMS THAT LOOKED UNRELATED: the deletion (the file was quarantined mid-run, so the runner could not find it and reported NOT RUN), and the >7-minute non-completion of a solo re-run, which stalled at exactly the same line because System Watcher was suspending the decoy rather than killing it. The six concurrent agents were a coincidence of timing and are exonerated. FIXED at the source rather than by an exclusion: the suite used to Start-Process a real process whose command line was a live ransomware indicator ('vssadmin delete shadows /all'), purely so the classifier had something to classify. Get-ProcessIndicators is a PURE FUNCTION of a process record, so spawning anything was never necessary. New read-only 'indicator-probe' engine action passes a synthetic record; the suite now completes in seconds, deterministically, and gained three assertions it never had - the negative case (an ordinary command line is NOT flagged), the indicator's title text, and a guard that the pattern table is non-empty. Result: 21 passed, 0 failed, no antivirus event. NO ANTIVIRUS EXCLUSION WAS ADDED and none should be: a repository whose test suite trips the operator's antivirus is one nobody can run, and asking for an exclusion would have been asking him to lower a control that was correct. The runner-reporting half is split out as its own issue.

title: Module 3.1 RESCUE: local-only credential scan, audit-only
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21 section 3, Module 3, and named there as "the highest-value, lowest-risk thing in this document" and one of the three concrete first tasks.

Module 3 is built FIRST, before any reclaim work. The sequencing is deliberate: RESCUE BEFORE RECLAIM. A tool that cannot yet delete anything but can tell you what a delete would destroy is already the most useful thing on the machine. Dependence is earned by knowing what not to touch.

WHAT IT FINDS: files that exist on disk, are gitignored, and are therefore on no remote - key.properties, .env.local, *.jks, *.keystore, .playwright_session and the like.

THE EVIDENCE, from the real cleanup: TWO KEYSTORE PASSWORDS EXISTING NOWHERE ELSE IN THE WORLD, inside folders that a delete-and-reclone would have destroyed. Signed Android apps become unshippable without them.

AUDIT-ONLY. No deletion, no quarantine, just the report. That is the whole scope of this issue.

NO COMPETITOR HAS THIS. CCleaner and BleachBit clean; neither knows what a repo's remote does not have.

Obeys aeu: the scan must distinguish "no local-only credentials" from "could not read this tree", because the second reported as the first is exactly how it would authorise destroying the thing it exists to protect.
