MEASURED, not inferred. Four A/B runs against the real index.html in a visible, foregrounded window (an occluded window stops compositing and reads 0%, which is why a first attempt measured nothing). Per-process GPU via '\GPU Engine(*)\Utilization Percentage' counters summed over all electron pids, phases alternated twice, first 2 samples of each phase discarded as straddling the switch:

  as shipped, idle, no user input     ~27-34%  (mean ~30%)
  scale removed from @keyframes float ~29%   -- NO CHANGE
  blur(100px) replaced by a gradient  ~26%   -- NO CHANGE
  backdrop-filter disabled everywhere ~21%   -- about a third off
  ambient animation stopped            0.0%  -- every sample, every run

Two hypotheses were tested and BOTH WERE WRONG: it is not the animated scale (a scaled blur layer re-rasterising), and it is not the blur radius (a pre-soft radial gradient with filter:none costs the same). What the data actually says is blunter: the cost is that a continuous animation exists at all, over large areas. The app's ~10 backdrop-filter surfaces (glass panels, and the h0i sticky table headers at blur(12px)) amplify it by roughly a third, because a moving backdrop forces each of them to re-read and re-blur every frame - but removing them still leaves ~21%.

Stopping the animation takes idle GPU to EXACTLY zero. So this is 100% of Vanish's idle GPU draw, on a machine doing nothing, forever, on every tab, for a background the changelog itself describes as 'deliberately subtle'.

Source: index.css:117-165 (.orb x3, 400-600px, filter: blur(100px), animation: float 25s infinite) and index.css:68-83 (body::before, ambient-drift 75s infinite).

Related, and a bug on its own regardless of what is decided here: the prefers-reduced-motion block at index.css:85-87 only stops body::before. .orb is not covered, so a user who has explicitly asked their OS for reduced motion still gets three continuously animating layers.

Fix options, cheapest first: (a) drop the animations, keep the orbs static - 0% measured, and at 0.18 opacity a 25s drift is close to imperceptible anyway; (b) pause on window blur/occlusion - keeps the look while focused but the operator saw 51% WHILE USING IT, so this does not solve the reported problem; (c) keep motion only under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference and accept the cost. Recommend (a), plus fixing the reduced-motion gap either way. This is a look-and-feel decision, so it wants an operator call, not a unilateral change.

Battery and thermals on a laptop are the real-world cost here, not just a number in Task Manager.
design: Measurement harnesses are in the session scratchpad (gpu-ab.js through gpu-ab4.js): they load the real index.html with test/fixtures/stub-preload.js in a visible alwaysOnTop window and toggle one CSS override between phases, so only the variable under test changes. Re-runnable if the fix needs verifying.
acceptance_criteria: Idle GPU with the app open and untouched is near zero, measured the same way (foregrounded window, GPU Engine counters, alternating phases); prefers-reduced-motion stops .orb as well as body::before.
close_reason:
eex: ambient orbs and the body::before wash are now static, and the prefers-reduced-motion block covers .orb/.pulse (it previously stopped body::before and nothing else, so a user asking their OS for less motion still got three animating layers). Functional indicators - the loading spinner and the indeterminate wait bar - are deliberately left animating: freezing a progress indicator does not read as less motion, it reads as a hung app. Dead @keyframes float removed. Measured after the change with the same harness that found it: 0.00% mean, 0.00% peak, 40 samples, zero nonzero samples (was ~30% continuous). The comment on body::before carries the measurement and the two falsified hypotheses so nobody re-adds an always-on animation without reading why it stopped.

kct: the ping tile and the one-time consent dialog now say 'your router (192.168.1.1)' instead of a bare IP, and only while the destination IS the detected gateway - editing it to anything else drops the claim, and retyping the gateway earns it back (compared against the live gateway, not latched off on first edit). 5 new assertions in the Audit-Mode UI suite drive the real DOM through detected -> edited -> restored.

npm test 442/0 (was 437/0).

title: Guided tour welcome step: no dim behind tooltip, blends into busy background
description: Operator screenshot, default post-install window size: tour step 1 of 7 (Welcome to Vanish) has no spotlight target, and positionTourSpotlight's no-target branch set .tour-spotlight to 'is-hidden' (opacity:0), which killed the box-shadow that does the dimming - so the CSS comment's promised 'plain full-screen dim' for the welcome step never actually rendered. The tooltip card (--bg-dark-card, only 40% opaque by design) sat directly over the full-brightness app list behind it with nothing dimming it, reading as low-contrast/'converging with background'.
close_reason: Root cause: positionTourSpotlight's no-target branch added the 'is-hidden' class, whose CSS set opacity:0 on the spotlight element - which silently killed its own box-shadow (the mechanism that dims everything outside the spotlight's box). The comment above .tour-spotlight promised 'a plain full-screen dim' for the welcome step but the code never produced one. Fixed by keeping the spotlight visible (opacity:1, still using the same box-shadow dim as every other step) and just collapsing its box to 0x0 at viewport center, so there is no meaningful cutout but the dim still renders. Removed the now-dead, actively-wrong .is-hidden CSS rule. Verified both by computed style (opacity 1, box-shadow present) and an actual captured screenshot of the welcome step showing the background properly dimmed. npm test 371/0.

title: Network Activity verdict overclaims certainty - says idle while 15 programs have open connections including a known-active one
description: Operator screenshot: verdict reads Nothing on this PC is using the network / idle badge, while the detail line shows 15 program(s) with a connection open and 566 Bytes/s down / 258 Bytes/s up - and the operator confirms Claude Code itself was actively making real network calls during this exact session. The busy/idle verdict is computed from one very short (400ms-1s) sample window (Get-NetworkActivity, scanner.ps1) - if that window happens to land during a quiet gap in bursty traffic (like an LLM API call between exchanges), it legitimately measures near-zero bytes/s at that instant even though the process is genuinely active. The verdict text conflates 'byte-rate during a brief sample was low' with 'nothing is using the network', which are different claims - operator explicitly: honesty is important. Also requests seeing machine-wide network availability/usage, not just Vanish's own brief-query snapshot.
design: Options for next session: (a) weight the verdict more heavily on connection COUNT (15 open connections is real evidence of usage even at near-zero instantaneous bytes/s) rather than only the byte-rate sample, (b) lengthen or repeat the sample window to reduce the odds of catching a quiet gap, (c) reword the quiet-verdict text to explicitly state what was measured and its limits (e.g. 'low observed traffic in a 1-second sample; N programs have connections open') rather than the flat, more certain-sounding 'Nothing on this PC is using the network'.
close_reason: Split the 'quiet' verdict on processes.length (open connections), matching design option (a)+(c): a low byte-rate sample with 0 open connections keeps the original 'Nothing on this PC is using the network' wording; a low byte-rate sample WITH open connections gets new wording ('Low traffic in this sample - not necessarily idle') that names the sample duration, the open-connection count, and states explicitly that a brief sample can miss bursty traffic - no longer conflates 'byte-rate was low' with 'nothing is using the network'. Also fixed an adjacent bug hit while verifying: rate() routed a genuine 0 B/s reading through formatBytes(0), which returns the 'Unknown' label meant for untracked sizes (same bug class as xw2) - a truly idle connection read 'Unknown/s' instead of '0 B/s'. Verified both branches via direct renderNetworkActivity calls in an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0. Connection-count vs byte-rate threshold logic in scanner.ps1 (Get-NetworkActivity) is unchanged - this was a display/wording fix, not an engine change.

title: System Clean: Scan all and Clean all buttons visually far apart, should be adjacent
description: Operator screenshot: Scan all sits near the panel title, Clean all is pushed to the far right of the header row - looks odd, should be side by side. Regression from this same day session (Clean all was added right after Scan all in index.html; some header flexbox rule - likely justify-content: space-between on .panel-header with only 2 children plus title - is spreading them apart). Quick CSS fix: group both buttons in their own flex container.
close_reason: Wrapped Scan all / Clean all in .panel-header-actions flex group (gap:12px) so the shared .content-header's justify-content:space-between only spreads title vs. button-group, not both buttons individually. Verified via offscreen electron geometry check: buttons now 12px apart. npm test 371/0.

title: Uninstall completion messaging overclaims success when 0 items actually succeeded
description: Same screenshot as the Left-in-place bug: 0 item(s) moved to quarantine, 1 could not be moved - this is a full failure of the one item attempted, but the screen shows Unknown for Freed on your drive (inconsistent with 0 succeeded - should read 0 or N/A) and the overall framing reads more positive/neutral than warranted. Operator explicitly: honesty is important. Review the completion-screen copy/color logic in renderer.js (uninstall wizard finish state) so a 0-success outcome cannot read as anywhere close to a success, regardless of whether SOME step (restore point, scan) nominally completed.
close_reason: Added an explicit full-failure branch (quarantined===0 && problems.length>0) in renderPurgeSummary: 'Nothing was moved to quarantine' title, failed/red hero styling, and freed-space set explicitly to '0 B' instead of routing through formatBytes(0), which returned the misleading 'Unknown' label. Partial-success (some succeeded, some failed) framing is unchanged - verified via direct renderPurgeSummary calls in an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0.

title: Uninstall wizard completion screen: Left in place list not visible, dialog appears fixed-size
description: Operator screenshot: uninstalling BingSearch, completion screen shows Moved to quarantine, with some items left in place, a Left in place (1) collapsible/section that is cut off - not scrollable or otherwise accessible. The wizard-modal / completion-screen CSS likely has a fixed height without overflow:auto on this failure-detail section. Needs to actually show WHY the 1 item could not be moved (the error), not just that it happened.
close_reason: Root cause was CSS, not missing error detail - the per-item error reason was already rendered (renderer.js renderPurgeSummary), but #scr-complete had no overflow-y, so .wizard-screens' overflow:hidden clipped the failures box off the bottom of the fixed-height wizard modal with no way to scroll to it. Added overflow-y:auto scoped to #scr-complete. Verified computed overflowY=auto and the failure reason text is present in the DOM via an offscreen electron harness. npm test 371/0.

title: Startup latency investigation: 5-8s reported on both regular and elevated launch
description: Operator reports both a regular start and restart-as-administrator take 5-8 seconds. Measured empirically: a single runPowerShell call through the real 4994-line scanner.ps1 costs ~340-590ms (vs ~300ms for a trivial script through the same invocation shape - most cost is process spawn, not parse). get-desktop-apps/get-uwp-apps (loaded in parallel at every startup since All Apps is the default active tab) now measure ~350ms combined - the historical 10-15s Get-UwpApps folder-size walk was already removed in a prior session (2026-08-07) but a stale comment in renderer.js still described the old behavior; comment corrected. Headless dev-mode boot (VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS=1, isolates main.js own JS+PS chain from Electron/Chromium startup and from portable-exe extraction) measured 1252ms unelevated. Summed JS/PS-controllable cost is roughly 1.2-2.5s (more when elevated: check-data-dir + secure-data-dir add ~2 more sequential PS spawns gating window creation) - real, but does not add up to the reported 5-8s alone.
design: Considered moving check-data-dir/secure-data-dir (elevated-only directory hardening, security review 2026-08-03 Vuln 2 - closes a privilege-escalation path where a standard-user process could rewrite manifest.json/queue.json before the elevated engine trusts them) off the blocking path to shave ~600-1200ms off elevated launches, mirroring the fire-and-forget pattern already used for autoPurgeSweep/releaseStaleNetworkHold a few lines below. NOT done: widening the gap between window-creation and directory-lock is a real, if narrow, security tradeoff on a path tied to a named privilege-escalation vuln, and deserves a security-focused pass, not a perf-driven edit bundled into this session. Leading hypothesis for the unexplained remainder (roughly 3-6s) is the portable exe self-extraction to a fresh TEMP folder on every single launch (electron-builder portable format, already documented elsewhere in main.js re: the elevated-relaunch race) - structural to that packaging format, not fixable in app code. Not verified directly - would require launching the actual packaged portable exe (a real visible window) without the operators live confirmation first.
acceptance_criteria: Either confirm with the operator whether the NSIS/installed build launches meaningfully faster than the portable exe (would confirm the extraction hypothesis), or get permission to instrument and launch the packaged portable build once to measure directly.
close_reason: Root cause confirmed via a clean, single-script live timing test (launch to real main window, both same methodology, both under the operators actual startupMode=full auto-elevate path): NSIS-installed build 4165ms, portable exe 20433ms - a ~5x difference. This isolates the portable packaging format (self-extraction to a fresh TEMP folder on every launch, likely compounded by real-time antivirus scanning the newly-extracted files - Kaspersky avp.exe confirmed active on this machine) as the dominant cause of the reported 5-8s+ startup wait, not app code. No further code fix exists on the Vanish side - this is inherent to the portable packaging format. Recommendation for the operator: default to the NSIS-installed build for regular use; keep portable for no-install/USB scenarios where the tradeoff is accepted.

title: System Overview grid: guarantee single row unconditionally (real fix, not width-guessed)
description: First attempt (7d8, closed) tuned auto-fit minmax bounds to guess a width. Still wrapped on the operators actual laptop, plus auto-fit left visible dead space on both sides (tabbed margin). Replaced with repeat(6, minmax(0,1fr)) - unconditionally one row, full width, no guessing, since the card count is fixed at exactly 6.
close_reason: Replaced auto-fit width-guessing with repeat(6, minmax(0,1fr)) - unconditional single row, full width, no side margins. index.css:1602.

title: Never show raw PowerShell stderr/exit-code text in the UI; recover missing scanner.ps1 automatically
description: main.js:271-327 runPowerShell() rejects with the raw 'PowerShell exited with code N. Error: <stderr>' string on non-zero exit; main.js:768-774 list-processes handler passes error.message through unmodified; renderer.js:2758-2769 Task Manager panel renders res.error verbatim (only HTML-escaped). Observed case: portable-build temp extraction race leaves resources\scanner.ps1 missing, and the user sees the raw PowerShell parameter-binding error text in Task Manager. Fix: (1) enginePath()/runPowerShell add an fs.existsSync guard before spawning and return a distinct, recognizable error code/shape when the engine script is missing; (2) on that specific condition, attempt an automatic recovery (re-resolve/re-extract the resourcesPath copy, or relaunch through the same PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE-aware path already used by attemptElevatedRelaunch) instead of surfacing the raw text; (3) renderer never renders raw PowerShell stderr for ANY panel -- map unrecognized/engine-missing errors to one friendly 'Vanish needs to restart to finish repairing itself' message with a retry action, keep raw text only in devtools console for diagnosis.
notes: IMPLEMENTED, partially verified. main.js: runPowerShell() now fs.existsSync-checks the engine script before spawning (rejects with a friendly ENGINE_MISSING error and offers a native restart-via-relaunch dialog, reusing the same PORTABLE_EXECUTABLE_FILE-safe exePath logic as attemptElevatedRelaunch, instead of ever spawning powershell.exe against a missing -File arg); the process-exit-code and JSON-parse failure paths were also rewritten to keep raw stderr in console.error only, never in the Error surfaced to a renderer. node --check clean; npm test 371/0 and npm run verify 177/0 both pass, which does exercise module load and the check-admin/tier-resolution boot path without erroring. NOT deliberately reproduced (temporarily renaming scanner.ps1 and launching would pop a real native dialog with no way to click it from this session, risking an orphaned blocked process) - needs a human to actually trigger the missing-engine path once (e.g. rename scanner.ps1, launch Vanish, confirm the dialog and friendly text appear, confirm Restart re-extracts and recovers) and confirm the Task Manager panel specifically no longer shows raw PowerShell text.
close_reason:
VERIFIED 2026-08-18, 19 assertions, 0 failed. It sat in_progress for nine days on the note that it 'needs a human to trigger the missing-engine path once, because it pops a real native dialog with no way to click it from this session'. That was true of the DIALOG and not of the BEHAVIOUR: the dialog is a single dialog.showMessageBoxSync call, and patching that one call before requiring main.js makes the whole path testable. The reported bug - a user seeing raw PowerShell parameter-binding text inside the Task Manager panel - never depended on a human clicking anything.

test/engine-missing-verify.js renames scanner.ps1 to provoke the real condition rather than mocking fs.existsSync, and restores it in a finally plus process exit and uncaughtException handlers, then asserts the engine is back. Verified restored after every run.

ASSERTED, against list-processes specifically because that is the panel the operator saw it in: the call fails rather than resolving with empty data that would read as an idle PC; the error handed to the renderer matches none of ten raw-shell patterns (powershell, 'exited with code', 'at line:N', CategoryInfo, FullyQualifiedErrorId, ParameterBinding, 'Cannot bind', the ~~~~ caret line, System.Management.Automation, or the scanner.ps1 path itself); no other field in the payload smuggles it through; and the message says what to DO. get-startup-items, get-listeners and find-broken-entries take the same path and are asserted too, so this is the class rather than the one reported instance.

The recovery offer: exactly ONE dialog with a Restart button, carrying no raw text or internal path, and stating that nothing on the PC was changed - which is the actual question at that moment. Three consecutive failures still produce one dialog, which matters because Task Manager re-polls every couple of seconds and a re-arming modal would be unusable; later failures still return the friendly error rather than falling back to raw text.

ONE HONEST LIMIT, recorded rather than papered over: the suite does NOT statically prove every renderer escapes error strings. Two regexes were tried and both were wrong - the first matched whole innerHTML statements and its greedy quantifier ran past the esc() call, giving false positives against correct code; the tightened version then flagged every error interpolation in the app including plain toast() strings that are not HTML sinks. Deciding whether an interpolation reaches innerHTML is a parsing job. The guarantee asserted instead is stronger and is the one the bug was about: no raw shell text crosses the IPC boundary at all, so no panel can render any. Plus the shared failure sink (toast) is pinned as escaping, and esc() is pinned as a real escaper.

title: Elevation-toggle info text can show stale state if settings save is rejected (e.g. Audit Mode)
description: index.html:658-674 'Always start with administrator rights' toggle; renderer.js:932-934 change handler calls saveSettings() which POSTs to main; renderer.js:989-1000 syncSettingsPanel renders the '#set-startup-elevated-state' Next start line from appSettings.startupMode -- but only after the save round-trip resolves. If save-settings is rejected or fails silently (e.g. under a mode that blocks writes), the checkbox's own DOM checked state can visually diverge from the persisted appSettings.startupMode the info text reflects, showing an ON toggle next to 'opens read-only next start' or vice versa. Verify whether save-settings is gated by fullModeOnly/isFullMode; if so, either allow this specific preference to persist regardless of current tier (it only affects a future launch, not this session) or make failure visibly revert the checkbox and toast why, so the two never contradict.
close_reason: Root cause found and fixed: applyStartupElevatedCopy() now runs synchronously on the checkbox's own change event (renderer.js), before saveSettings()'s awaited IPC round-trip - closing the race where a native checkbox flips instantly but the 'Next start' text used to wait for set-settings to resolve. That gap, not an Audit-Mode write block (set-settings is NOT fullModeOnly-gated - checked main.js:705), was the real mechanism: any real latency in writeSettings' disk I/O could catch a screenshot mid-gap with the toggle already ON next to the OFF-state text. Wording also restated (ON/OFF prefix) so the two can't be misread as describing different states even without the race. npm test 371/0 unaffected (Settings validation suite covers this path unelevated); not interactively re-clicked in a live window from this session.

title: UAC diagnostics: distinguish decline vs UAC-unavailable/non-admin account
description: Windows did not grant administrator rights banner gives no reason. Check-AdminStatus in scanner.ps1 only reports IsInRole(Administrator); relaunch-elevated collapses every Start-Process -Verb RunAs failure into the same declined:true. Need to read EnableLUA registry policy, check Administrators-group membership independent of current elevation, and distinguish Win32 1223 (real cancel) from other failure causes, then surface a cause-specific message instead of one generic banner.
design: scanner.ps1: add Get-UacDiagnostics (EnableLUA, isAdminGroupMember, isElevated via WindowsIdentity/WindowsPrincipal). Merge into check-admin response. relaunch-elevated: inspect $_.Exception (Win32Exception.NativeErrorCode -eq 1223 => declined) vs other causes; return cause: declined|not-admin|uac-disabled|unknown. main.js: thread uacInfo through get-app-info. renderer: FLOW-01 modal / audit banner text varies by cause.
notes: IMPLEMENTED, needs console/VM verification (same class as jhh/bfh.2/dmu/etc). scanner.ps1: Get-UacDiagnostics (EnableLUA registry read, Get-LocalGroupMember-based Administrators check independent of token elevation state) merged into check-admin and relaunch-elevated's catch block; distinguishes Win32 1223 (real UAC decline) from not-admin (account isn't in Administrators) and uac-disabled (EnableLUA=0) causes. main.js threads cause/uac through attemptElevatedRelaunch and get-app-info. renderer.js elevationFailureMessage() gives cause-specific copy in the FLOW-01 toast. PS syntax validated (Parser.ParseFile, 0 errors); npm test 371/0 and npm run verify 177/0 both unaffected (unelevated paths only). NOT YET verified: an actual UAC decline, an actual UAC-disabled machine/VM, and a genuinely non-admin account all producing the correct distinct cause - needs a human at a real console/VM, per this project's own established pattern for anything elevation-dependent.
close_reason:
VERIFIED 2026-08-18 as far as one machine can verify it: 29 assertions, 0 failed, and the limits printed by the suite itself rather than buried here.

WHAT IS PROVEN. Get-UacDiagnostics reports this machine's real facts, cross-checked against the registry and the current token independently rather than restated from the implementation (enableLua=true matches EnableLUA=1; isElevatedNow=false matches the token). All three fields are asserted to be BOOLEAN OR EXPLICITLY NULL - never a silent false - because 'unknown' and 'off' are different answers and the difference decides what the user is told.

THE MAPPING, which is where the actual bug was: relaunch-elevated used to collapse every Start-Process failure into the same declined:true, so a non-admin account, a UAC-disabled machine and a real 'No' click were indistinguishable. Eight cases are driven directly - decline; decline outranking everything else; not-an-administrator; UAC off locally; UAC off and likely policy-enforced; and three that must stay 'unknown', including the two that matter most: an UNREADABLE group membership must not harden into 'your account is not an administrator', and an unreadable policy key must not be reported as UAC being off. The engine's own branch order is then asserted against source (1223 first, explicit -eq $false comparisons, declined now DERIVED from cause) so the model in the test cannot silently drift from the engine.

THE COPY: all four causes have distinct messages, asserted distinct by set comparison. not-admin names the fix. uac-disabled offers the fix a personal machine has. uac-disabled-locked deliberately hedges ('likely', 'probably') because Windows does not record whether a value came from Group Policy, and it must NOT tell a managed user to change a setting that reverts at the next policy refresh - asserted both ways.

WHAT CANNOT BE PROVEN HERE, and no amount of code changes it: an actual UAC decline (this machine now has ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0, so elevation is silent and there is no prompt to decline), a genuinely non-administrator account, and a machine with UAC off. Those need different machines, not a different test, which is exactly why this sat in_progress for nine days. The mapping that WOULD run on them is exercised directly above, so what remains unverified is the environment rather than the logic. Closing on that basis; if a second machine ever runs this, the three environment cases are the ones to watch.

One self-inflicted finding worth keeping: the first version of the copy assertion failed against correct code because it matched 'turn UAC back on' inside the CODE COMMENT explaining why that branch must not say it. Comments are now stripped before user-facing copy is tested.

title: Confirm the network hold applies and fully reverts (elevated)
description: bfh.2 shipped the hold: Delivery Optimization background bandwidth capped to 1% by policy, plus Suspend-BitsTransfer on transfers that were running. Unelevated coverage is complete - capture is read-only and works, apply and revert refuse by tier, applying without a captured record is refused outright, and a refused hold leaves the policy key untouched. What has NOT run is the elevated path, which is the only path that writes.
design: Ordering is the safety property: capture (read-only) -> main.js writes the record to network-hold.json -> apply. A crash between capture and apply leaves a machine nobody touched; a crash after apply leaves a file that says what to put back, and releaseStaleNetworkHold() at the next elevated start puts it back unasked. A partial release deliberately KEEPS its record so the next start retries rather than stranding the leftovers.
acceptance_criteria: Elevated: hold with a Windows Update download in flight; confirm DOPercentageMaxBackgroundBandwidth=1 exists under HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Policies\\Microsoft\\Windows\\DeliveryOptimization and the BITS jobs report Suspended. Release; confirm the value is GONE (it did not exist before, so revert must delete rather than zero it), the policy key itself is removed if Vanish created it, and the jobs resume. Then repeat and kill Vanish while held - the next elevated start must release it on its own and write network-release-stale to the oplog.
close_reason: CONFIRMED ELEVATED 2026-08-18, 6/6 checks passed. Before: policy key absent, DOPercentageMaxBackgroundBandwidth absent. Capture returned a record; hold applied; the value read 1 while held; release succeeded; the value is GONE after release (revert DELETES rather than zeroing, which is the whole point - a zeroed policy is still a policy); and the policy key Vanish created was removed too. The independent end-of-run safety net then confirmed the Delivery Optimization value was absent, as it was before. Transcript: TEMP\vanish-elevated-confirmations\transcript.txt

title: Size ATTRIBUTION, not another treemap: whose bytes are these, and is that program still installed
description:
RESCOPED 2026-08-12 on operator direction. The previous scope ('build the WinDirStat half') was redundant nonsense by our own standard and is dropped.

WHAT IS ALREADY SOLVED, by better tools than we would write: 'what is big on this disk'. WinDirStat (GPL-2.0), WizTree, TreeSize, and Windows' own Settings > System > Storage all answer it. A Vanish treemap would be a worse fourth copy.

WHAT NOBODY SOLVES: whose bytes those are. Every disk-usage tool shows you C:\ProgramData\Package Cache at 12GB and stops, because none of them has an uninstall database. Vanish already has the three things needed to finish that sentence:
  1. the installed-programs map (scanner.ps1, HKLM/HKCU uninstall hives + UWP),
  2. corrections.json, the verified publisher/path table,
  3. the leftover scanner's path heuristics, already used post-uninstall.

The output is not a treemap. It is: '12.4 GB, last written March, belongs to a program that is NOT in your installed list' - orphaned bytes grouped by their former owner, each one quarantine-able through the vault that already exists. That is the product story in one screen: the uninstaller that shows you what your uninstalls left behind, sized.

MECHANISM, and why it is free: enumeration via the NTFS Master File Table (FSCTL_ENUM_USN_DATA / MFT_ENUM_DATA, documented Microsoft API - learn.microsoft.com). This is the technique that makes WizTree seconds-fast instead of minutes, and it is a TECHNIQUE, not code: no license attaches. Requires local NTFS + admin, both of which Vanish already has in Full Mode, with the standard directory-walk fallback for network/non-NTFS/Audit Mode.

Explicitly still refused, unchanged from the original scoping: no auto-proposed deletions, no one-click clean, no temp-file heuristics. Finding and attributing is the feature; removal goes through the same ticked-checkbox quarantine path as everything else.
design:
RESUME POINT, written 2026-08-12 after zrw shipped (git da1004a). zrw's groundwork is DONE and bu2 should build on it rather than re-deriving anything.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS AND SHOULD BE REUSED:
- lib/snapshot.js attributionPaths(diff) already returns added directories per monitored install, and main.js's snapshot-finish handler already writes them to the oplog as action='install-snapshot-diff' with items.paths. That is the ground-truth attribution table. Read it back with the same oplog reader the app already uses; do not invent a second store.
- scanner.ps1 Get-InstallSnapshot already enumerates top-level Program Files / ProgramData / LOCALAPPDATA / APPDATA directories. bu2 needs SIZES for those, which that function deliberately does not compute (a snapshot must stay sub-second).
- The installed-programs map (Get-InstalledApps) and corrections.json are the other two join inputs, both already engine-side.

BUILD ORDER:
1. Engine 'size-scan': MFT enumeration via FSCTL_ENUM_USN_DATA for local NTFS volumes, standard Get-ChildItem recursion as the fallback for non-NTFS, network paths, and Audit Mode. Return path + sizeBytes + lastWriteTime, rolled up to a configurable depth. VERIFY THE FALLBACK PRODUCES THE SAME ATTRIBUTION AS THE FAST PATH - that is the assertion that matters, because the two code paths are easy to let drift.
2. lib/attribution.js, pure and testable the way lib/snapshot.js is: given (sized paths, installed programs, corrections, recorded install deltas) return each path labelled owned / orphaned / unknown. Test the classifications, not the walk.
3. UI: a size-ranked list where every row above a threshold is labelled with its owner or explicitly flagged as belonging to no installed program. NOT a treemap.

BINDING CONSTRAINTS, do not relax:
- No auto-proposed deletions, no one-click clean, no temp-file heuristics. Finding and attributing IS the feature; removal goes through the existing ticked-checkbox quarantine path.
- 'unknown' must be a visible third state. A path Vanish cannot attribute must never be shown as orphaned - that is the confident-wrong-answer failure this whole app is built against, and it is the single most likely way to get this feature wrong.
- MFT enumeration needs admin + local NTFS. In Audit Mode the fallback must still work, just slower, and the UI must say which path was used rather than silently being slow.
acceptance_criteria: A size-ranked view where every entry above a threshold is labelled with the program it belongs to, or explicitly flagged as belonging to no installed program; orphan entries are quarantine-able and restorable; MFT path and fallback path produce the same attribution.
notes: Prerequisite zrw closed 2026-08-12 (git da1004a). npm test baseline at handoff: 465/0.
close_reason:
Shipped. Not a treemap: 'what is big' is answered by WinDirStat, WizTree and Windows' own Storage page, and the half none of them can answer - whose bytes these are - is the whole feature.

DESIGN DEVIATION, recorded in lib/attribution.js's header: the plan called for MFT enumeration via FSCTL_ENUM_USN_DATA. USN records carry FileReferenceNumber, ParentFileReferenceNumber, FileName and FileAttributes but NOT size, so sizing that way means parsing raw $MFT records off the volume. Inverted the design instead - attribution is milliseconds and measurement is the expensive part, so classify FIRST and measure ONLY what classification could not explain. The fast path stopped being necessary rather than being reimplemented.

Honesty rule enforced by the module and by 36 assertions: 'unattributed' and 'orphaned' are different claims. Orphaned is positive - we watched the install and the program is gone - and is ONLY ever made on zrw's recorded evidence. A recorded path whose owner was never resolved (an installer that writes no uninstall entry) stays unattributed; calling it orphaned would invent the fact that makes the word mean anything. Unmeasured folders report null and a reason, never 0 B.

Two defects found by running it live against this machine rather than by testing:
1. 134 of 233 directories came back unexplained. Two matching gaps: a program registered BENEATH a publisher folder (Brave installs to BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\Application, so the scanned directory is an ancestor of the registered location), and concatenated folder names that do not split into tokens. Added contains-install-location (certain) and name-prefix (likely, with a 4-char floor so short names cannot match everything). Unattributed 134 -> 107, owned 66 -> 93.
2. Measurement took 62 seconds, dominated by a 12GB WSL tree and an npm cache of hundreds of thousands of tiny files. Added a 20s budget in Measure-Paths; anything past it returns unmeasured WITH a reason rather than being silently truncated or reported as small. 62s -> 20s. Orphans are now ordered first in sizeCandidates because the budget decides what goes unmeasured, and spending it on an unexplained dev cache would leave the reclaimable headline wrong.

Engine: Measure-Paths uses a manual stack walk, not Directory::EnumerateFiles with AllDirectories - EnumerationOptions is .NET Core only and does not exist in PS 5.1's .NET Framework, and the recursive overload aborts the whole walk on the first UnauthorizedAccessException. Per-directory try/catch means one unreadable subtree costs that subtree. Reparse points are skipped (their bytes are not this folder's, and following one can loop). Reports skippedDirs/partial/timedOut so a floor is never presented as a total. Get-TopLevelProgramDirs extracted and shared with zrw's snapshot so the two features cannot disagree about scope.

Also fixed in zrw as a prerequisite: snapshot-finish now resolves the PROGRAM name from the added uninstall keys at the only moment it is knowable, and records it. Without that every recorded path would have been permanently unattributable.

Verified: npm test 501/0 (was 465/0), 36 new assertions. Live on this machine: 233 directories, classify 6ms, measure 20s, 93 owned / 107 unattributed / 33 system, with BraveSoftware correctly resolved via contains-install-location. 0 orphaned is the CORRECT answer here - no installs have been watched yet on this machine, and the UI says exactly that rather than guessing.

title: Confirm the three startup actions elevated (remove / manual / disable)
description: 7oo.11 shipped three write actions on the Health Advisor startup list. Unelevated coverage is complete: the engine refuses each verb by tier, refuses targets outside its own surface, and every row renders an inert, labelled, hit-tested control. What has NOT run is the elevated path - the actual registry value removal, service reconfiguration and task disable, each of which must be undoable afterwards. Registry and service actions export a manifest-only .reg to the vault first; the restore is what proves the action was safe to offer.
acceptance_criteria: Elevated: (1) remove a harmless Run value, confirm it is gone from the registry and from msconfig, restore it from Quarantine and confirm the value returns byte-identical; (2) set one non-Microsoft auto service to manual, confirm Start=3, restore; (3) disable a scheduled task, confirm State=Disabled, re-enable from the same button. Nothing else on the startup list changes in the process.
close_reason: CONFIRMED ELEVATED 2026-08-18, in two halves, because one harness could not reach both. ENGINE HALF (test/elevated-confirmations.ps1): 12 passed / 0 failed - a planted Run value removed and verified gone, a planted Automatic service set to Manual (Start=3) and restored to Automatic, a planted scheduled task disabled, State=Disabled confirmed, and re-enabled from the same verb. VAULT HALF (test/startup-action-ipc-verify.js, new): 27 passed / 0 failed - the restore manifest is exported BEFORE the mutation, the returned entryId is a real vault entry attributed to startup/registry-remove and startup/service-manual, its row references a .reg file on disk, the Run key and the service key both survive their own export, the restore is byte-identical including quotes and spaces, and an item that cannot be saved is REFUSED with the value left untouched. title: Elevated restart: ~5 seconds of nothing on screen

title: System Clean: left-over Store (UWP/MSIX) app data sweep
description: Uninstalling a Store app routinely leaves %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<PackageFamilyName> behind - sometimes hundreds of MB - and Windows never cleans it up. Vanish has no surface for this at all today. Add a System Clean cleaner that reports (a) Packages folders with no matching registered package and (b) registered packages whose install location is gone (audit only). Removal goes through the existing quarantine pipeline, which currently only handles registry-kind findings.
design: New Find-UwpLeftovers in scanner.ps1 behind the existing cleaner-scan dispatch. Comparison set is the UNION of Get-AppxPackage and (elevated) Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers family names, so ambiguity always resolves toward not removing. cleaner-purge in main.js gains a file-kind branch feeding vault.quarantine({files}).

description: test/real-data-verify.js has only ever run unelevated. Every section is read-only by design, so an elevated run does not by itself exercise a destructive path - but it DOES change what the harness can observe: tier-locked controls stop being pointer-events:none (so the hit tests assert the real thing rather than the geometry fallback), Get-InstalledApps sees HKLM entries a standard user cannot read, and the 2 stub suites currently reported as NOT RUN (Vault IPC, System Clean purges) can run. Needs a human at the console for UAC by design - no agent-side workaround exists or should be built. Related: 0xt (VM matrix), 1qp.

(148 vs the 152 of the unelevated --plant run is exactly the 4 assertions --plant adds; the runs agree.)

WHY THE ELEVATED RUN IS THE STRONGER EVIDENCE: unelevated, every data-destructive control carries pointer-events:none by design, so the harness falls back to asserting geometry only and labels it '(inert in Audit Mode - geometry checked)'. Elevated, those labels are gone: 'Clean Uninstall is clickable', 'Add to bulk queue is clickable', 'scr-leftovers-tree: #btn-wiz-purge is fully clickable' are now REAL document.elementFromPoint hit tests on live controls. 7oo.1 is therefore proven against actually-clickable buttons, not just correct boxes.

ELEVATION DELTAS OBSERVED (all expected, all in the direction of showing more): 231 loaded entries vs 229 unelevated, 157 rows vs 155 - HKLM entries a standard user cannot read; 48 startup items vs 41 - services visible only when elevated. Storage 2 of 2 both ways. Inventory 151 of 151 both ways.

ALSO STILL TRUE: an elevated run does not mean an uninstall was performed. Every section here is read-only by design. No real uninstall, purge or restore has been executed end to end by any automated run.

The first elevated run scored 164/2 and both failures were real product defects, now fixed: #btn-launch-native's bottom edge was under DIV.wizard-footer, and 0 of 46 startup action buttons carried a hover title. title: Startup items: genuine disable/remove through the quarantine pipeline
description: 7oo.4 made the startup panel honest: it states that it only reports, and every orphaned row names where its kind of entry is managed (taskschd.msc, services.msc, the Run value path). The next step is doing it in-app. Registry Run values can reuse the PATH cleaner's proven pattern in main.js purgePathEntries - export the whole key as a manifest-only vault entry, then rewrite the value - so removal stays reversible under INV-1. Scheduled tasks and services need their own reversible verbs (Disable-ScheduledTask, sc.exe config start= demand) rather than deletion. Rule for this epic applies: no button ships unless the action verifiably resolves the finding and it disappears on rescan, verified against the real machine via test/real-data-verify.js --only=startup.

Scheduled tasks and services can be disabled from the app and re-enabled from the quarantine surface. After acting, a rescan no longer reports the finding. Verified on a real machine, not fixtures.
