title: TOCTOU: the restore guard is check-time only, and the attacker sets the window length
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04.

SEC-2's whole design is resolving junctions so the guard sees where a write
really lands. Nothing re-validates at USE time, and Move-ItemTransactional takes
bare strings - no handle, no FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, no post-move check.

Restore ordering in Invoke-VaultRestore:

  Test-ProtectedDestination $f.originalPath   <- verdict taken, junctions resolved
  Get-VaultContentHash -path $vaultPath        <- THE WINDOW
  Test-Path $f.originalPath
  CreateDirectory($parent)
  Move-ItemTransactional                       <- resolves the path again, at call time

The window's length is chosen by whoever authored the payload, and the engine's
own measurements are in the file: 899 ms for a 250 MB file, 7,102 ms for a
2,000-file tree. Seconds, deterministically, on demand.

SCENARIO: the manifest names %APPDATA%\Foo\evil.dll. At check time it is not
protected - allowed. During the hash, a standard-user process deletes
%APPDATA%\Foo and recreates it as a junction to System32 (junction creation
needs no privilege; only file symlinks need SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege). At
the move, File.Move resolves the path fresh and the payload lands in System32,
written by the elevated engine. The guard measured a path that no longer exists.

SAME SHAPE ON QUARANTINE: check, then Get-ItemSizeBytes (a full recursive
enumeration), then Move-ItemTransactional -source. Winning that race turns
quarantine into an arbitrary-protected-file DELETION primitive. Recoverable,
since the file is in the vault - but the system is broken until someone
restores it.

HONEST ON SEVERITY: this needs local code execution as the standard user AND an
operator clicking Restore or Purge in Full Mode. Not remote, not one-shot. What
makes it worth fixing rather than filing as theoretical is that the window is
seconds long and the attacker chooses how long.

NOT A STATIC BYPASS: if the junction is in place BEFORE the check,
Resolve-DestinationTarget catches it and the restore is refused.
security-verify.ps1 tests exactly that pre-created case and never a swap
mid-operation - which is why this survived the existing suite.

FIX: re-resolve immediately before the move, or move via a handle opened with
FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT and verify the final path afterwards.
notes:
PARKED 2026-09-04, operator direction, and the reasoning is worth keeping
because it applies to a whole class of finding rather than just this one.

'potentially malicious writing into windows folders... those will be operated
on whether vanish or you choose or not.'

Correct. This attack needs local code execution as the standard user AND an
operator clicking Restore in Full Mode. An attacker who has the first already
has the machine, and Windows system folders are written to constantly by
legitimate software. Treating 'something could win a race against us' as
Vanish's problem generates branches faster than it removes them, and every
branch becomes its own ticket that never closes.

WHAT WOULD UN-PARK IT: a cheap fix that closes rather than opens. Re-resolving
the destination immediately before the move is one line and no new surface; if
that is done as part of other work in Invoke-VaultRestore, take it then. Do not
open a project for it.

NOT PARKED, and the distinction matters: dvem is not this. That one is the
unfinished half of cihg, a fix that already shipped for files and never covered
registry - finishing a started job, not defending a new frontier.
close_reason: Parked on operator direction. Needs local code execution plus an operator click; the class generates branches rather than closing them. The one-line re-resolve is noted for whoever next touches Invoke-VaultRestore.

title: set-settings is un-gated and can schedule an irreversible total vault wipe
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. Verified.

  main.js:1251  ipcMain.handle('set-settings', ...)   <- not fullModeOnly
  lib/store.js  clampInt(merged.autoPurgeRetentionDays, 0, 3650, 30)   <- 0 IS LEGAL

vault-delete IS gated. But autoPurgeSweep runs unconditionally at every elevated
start, computes cutoff = Date.now() - retentionDays * 86400000, and calls
deleteForever on every entry with createdAt <= cutoff.

SCENARIO: a renderer IN AUDIT MODE - where every destructive channel is supposed
to be refused - calls setSettings({ autoPurgeEnabled: true,
autoPurgeRetentionDays: 0 }). At the operator's next Full Mode start the entire
quarantine vault is permanently deleted, no prompt, no confirmation. The
fullModeOnly gate on vault-delete is bypassed by DEFERRAL: the destructive act
is scheduled from the tier that cannot perform it.

THE CONFIRMATION THE USER WOULD EXPECT is renderer-side only
(renderer/settings-about.js), which is the wrong side of the boundary INV-2
declares: 'the renderer's disabled states are a convenience; THIS is the
boundary'.

AND THERE IS AN HONEST-USER HALF, independent of any attacker: index.html has
<input type="number" min="0"> for retention, so a user can set 0 themselves
and lose their whole vault at next launch with no warning that 0 means 'delete
everything immediately'.

RELATED, SAME CLASS: network-ping passes a renderer-supplied destination
straight to Test-Connection with no allowlist and no tier gate, and
pingConsentGiven is checked ONLY in the renderer - while network-speedtest
correctly checks its consent in main. Test-Connection resolves the name before
sending, so an arbitrary destination is a DNS exfiltration channel out of a
renderer whose CSP carries connect-src 'none' specifically to prevent egress.
Since set-settings is un-gated, the main-side speedtest consent check can be
flipped to true by the renderer first.

FIX: gate set-settings, or at minimum move the auto-purge confirmation and the
ping consent check into the main process. Consider whether retentionDays 0
should be legal at all, or clamp to 1.

title: run-all.ps1 exits zero when a suite crashes, and NOTE-style skips are invisible
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04, test-quality review. Verified.

1. A CRASHED SUITE DOES NOT FAIL THE RUN.

     $exitCode = [int](($totalFailed -gt 0) -or ($missingSuites.Count -gt 0))

   A suite that produces no 'Result:' line is reported as
   'NOT RUN (needs Full Mode, or it crashed -- read its log)' and does not
   affect the exit code.

   But every registered suite prints a Result line even when it skips its whole
   body - verified in vault-verify.ps1, finder-credentials-verify.ps1,
   data-dir-ownership-verify.js and relaunch-live-probe.ps1. So 'did not report
   a result' ALWAYS means a crash, and the runner leads with the wrong
   diagnosis. That is the z6k complaint, which was fixed for missing FILES and
   not for crashed ones - and run-all.ps1's own argument for the missing-file
   case applies unchanged: 'the alternative is a green exit code on a run that
   silently tested less'.

2. NOTE-STYLE SKIPS ARE INVISIBLE TO THE SKIP MACHINERY.

   run-all.ps1 matches ^\s*SKIP\b to name what did not run. gpu-shape-verify.js
   prints NOTE, not SKIP, in three branches - so four to five assertions vanish
   silently on an idle machine and are counted neither as skips nor as anything
   else. This is the exact 686-adjacent defect the runner already documents
   ('GPU payload shape (aaw) 14 passed then 10 passed. No skip line either
   time.'); the advisory baseline was added, the CAUSE was not fixed. Same
   pattern in packaging-verify.js and deelevation-mechanism-verify.ps1.

3. NO PER-SUITE TIMEOUT, and only 9 of ~22 Electron suites carry a watchdog.
   Several suites document that Electron HANGS rather than fails on a rejected
   executeJavaScript. A hang in an unwatchdogged suite stalls the entire run
   indefinitely - which is what happened to a run earlier today.

FIX: count crashed suites into the exit code the same way missing files are;
make the skip matcher accept the NOTE form or convert those three sites to
SKIP; add a per-suite timeout in the runner rather than in each suite.

title: The privilege-escalation suite goes blind after its first breach, and my mirror guard is a tautology
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04, test-quality review. Both verified directly.

1. test/vault-destination-verify.ps1 - the suite whose own header says 'THIS
   SUITE IS THE REGRESSION. It performs the attack for real' - can only test
   its FIRST attack target.

   Five targets (Program Files, Program Files (x86), ProgramData, System32,
   drive root), one vault entry, ONE payload on disk. The entry object is
   JSON-cloned per target, but the payload is not. Restore uses
   Move-ItemTransactional, which MOVES the payload out of the vault, and a
   later restore short-circuits with 'Vault payload missing.'

   So if the guard fails for target N: iteration N writes into a protected
   location, the test deletes the landed file, and the payload is now gone.
   Iterations N+1..5 refuse for a PAYLOAD reason, $landed is false, and those
   assertions pass green. If the guard failed for ProgramData only - third of
   five - targets 4 and 5 assert nothing.

   Compounding: the engine result is explicitly discarded ($null = Invoke-Engine).
   Nothing asserts the restore was attempted, that it reported a refusal, or
   that the error names the guard. Lines 79-83 of the same file do check
   .protected and .installedAppRestorable, so the discipline exists here and was
   not applied to the loop.

   FIX: a fresh entry and payload per target, and assert on the error wording,
   not only on absence-from-disk.

2. test/locked-paths-verify.js:68-72 - MY mirror guard, written today, is a
   tautology.

   Both files are matched against the SAME hardcoded literal, so when both
   match they are necessarily equal:

     const wizardPattern = (wizardSrc.match(/\/lock\|in use\|.../) || [])[0];
     const libPattern    = (libSrc.match(/\/lock\|in use\|.../) || [])[0];
     assert(Boolean(wizardPattern) && wizardPattern === libPattern, ...)

   wizardPattern === libPattern can never be the reason it fails. It is a 'both
   files contain this string' check labelled as an 'in sync' check - and it does
   not verify the found literal is the one in FORCE: renderer/wizard.js could
   use /denied/i with the old expression sitting in a comment and this still
   passes.

   FIX: extract the regex from each file by parsing the actual assignment, or
   better, export the pattern from lib/lock-failure.js and have the test require
   BOTH the lib value and the literal it finds in wizard.js, comparing those.

3. test/runtimes-verify.js has SIX vacuous assertions and no premise that any
   runtime exists. Only premise is list.length > 0. If the classifier regressed
   so isRuntime is never true: every 'misclassified.length === 0', every
   'runtimes.every(...)', the badge check ('0' === '0'), isolated.rows ===
   runtimes.length (0 === 0) and actions.withUninstall === 0 all pass. The whole
   ht8 feature can disappear with the suite green - and the harm is real, because
   runtime rows regaining uninstall controls is how a shared redistributable
   other programs depend on gets removed.

   The reviewer's recommended mutant makes this a demonstration rather than an
   argument: force the isRuntime assignment to $false and aim it at
   runtimes-verify. Predicted SURVIVED.

title: Three defects in code I shipped today: a dead catch, a network hole, and ungated test hatches
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. All three are in code written the same day, and
all three are cases where a COMMENT claims a protection the code does not
provide. Filed together because the fixes are three lines in two files.

1. get-locked-paths: the 'unreadable is not gone' catch is DEAD CODE, and the
   policy it describes is not implemented.

     const live = rows.filter((r) => {
       try { return fs.existsSync(r.path); }
       catch { return true; }        // <- unreachable
     });

   fs.existsSync never throws - it is accessSync wrapped in its own try/catch
   and returns FALSE for every failure. Verified empirically by the reviewer:
   an unreachable UNC host and a disconnected drive letter both return false
   while accessSync throws UNKNOWN/ENOENT.

   So a locked path on a disconnected volume, an unreachable share, or under a
   directory the user cannot traverse is PRUNED AS GONE and counted into
   'dropped'. The Unlocker's list of paths Vanish itself failed to remove
   silently loses exactly the entries most likely to still be a problem.
   Fix: use fs.accessSync in the try, or statSync, so the catch means something.

2. parseLocalDirectory and parseDisplayIcon let a MAPPED DRIVE LETTER through a
   check whose comment says it exists to keep work off the network.

   Both reject UNC and both say so in prose - 'a UNC path would put an icon
   fetch / directory walk on the network, which INV-4 forbids'. Both implement
   that as ^[A-Za-z]: plus a separator. Z:\ passes. measureInstallSize('Z:\')
   walks an SMB share; getAppIcon('Z:\x.dll') hands an attacker-controlled
   remote file to app.getFileIcon (SHGetFileInfo, which can load third-party
   shell icon handlers in-process) inside the elevated main process.
   The stated invariant is not enforced by the check written for it.

3. VANISH_SIZE_BUDGET_MS and VANISH_SIZE_MAX_FILES are read unconditionally,
   NOT behind testHatchesAllowed.

   main.js:26-34 states that in a packaged build the test hatches 'do not exist
   at all', and gives the security reason. VANISH_HEADLESS_HARNESS and
   VANISH_DISABLE_AUTO_ELEVATE are both gated on !app.isPackaged. The two I
   added for mp31's budget test are not, so a shipped build honours an
   environment variable that can set the size-walk budget to anything.
   Low severity - the worst it buys is a longer or shorter walk - but it
   falsifies a security statement three lines above it, which is the part worth
   fixing.

The common thread is worth naming: in all three the comment is more careful
than the code, and in two of them I wrote the comment.
close_reason: Path half folded into lr9d, which is now the root for one shared predicate. The ungated VANISH_SIZE_* env hatches are folded into 2brn, since both are about the size walk's bounds.

title: System Clean has no could-not-look state at all
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04. The structural half of the same defect as the
Health Advisor one, on the panel that offers deletions.

scanner.ps1's cleaner dispatch returns success = $true as a LITERAL,
independent of what the Find-* function managed to read:

  "context-menus" { return @{ success = $true; ... } }
  "services"      { return @{ success = $true; ... } }
  "drivers"       { return @{ success = $true; ... } }

None of them returns an unreadable list. The renderer's only branch is
findings.length === 0 -> a green check and 'Nothing left behind here.'

EVERY PATH THAT REACHES THAT STRING ON A FAILED READ:

  Open-RegistryView            catch { return $null }   - absent and denied are one answer
  Get-RegistrySubKeyNamesInView catch { return @() }     - the root cause under services,
                                                           context menus and associations
  Find-OrphanDriverPackages    catch { return $findings }, and pnputil /enum-drivers
                               NEVER checks $LASTEXITCODE - an error written to stdout
                               parses to nothing and you get a green tick
  Get-NetFirewallRule missing  -> empty
  SharedDLLs key unreadable    -> empty
  Get-PnpDevice missing/threw  -> empty

AND ONE THAT RETURNS success = $true HAVING READ NOTHING:
Find-OtherProfileRemnants has three silent skips; if ProfileList itself is
unreadable the loop body never runs and it reports success with zero findings.
The user is told another account holds no leftovers of the program they
searched for, from a scan that loaded no hive.

THE REPO ALREADY KNOWS HOW: path-hygiene.finder.ps1 returns
@{ ok = $false; raw = $null; error = ... }. None of the cleaners adopted it.

THE CHEAPEST CORRECT FIX IS NOT SEVEN PATCHES. It is giving Invoke-CleanerScan
the same { findings, unreadable } shape the finders already return and routing
the renderer through lib/findings.js decide(), which is the seam that exists for
exactly this. Until then the green check on this panel is a TWO-state answer on
a deletion surface, which finders/_contract.ps1 says must not exist.
notes:
PROMOTED TO ROOT 2026-09-04. This is not a System Clean bug; it is the aeu seam
never having been extended past the finders, and it absorbs fgj7 and u9r0.

THE EVIDENCE, counted rather than asserted:
* scanner.ps1:7831-7846 - success = $true is a LITERAL on the cleaner
  dispatch, and the Find-* functions have no channel to say they could not read.
* main.js - exactly TWO of ~40 catch handlers manufacture the negative
  (get-startup-items, redundancy). The other 38 correctly return success:false,
  so this is a small precise gap, not a systemic rot.
* Get-FolderSize returns 0 for 'empty' and for 'failed' alike, and
  Format-ByteSize renders 0 as the word 'empty'.

THE SOLUTION ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO AND WAS NOT APPLIED. lib/findings.js
decide() consumes { findings, unreadable } and returns a named terminal state,
and fromLeftovers() is the adapter pattern for a surface that does not natively
speak it. Two adapters close all three tickets:

  1. Invoke-CleanerScan returns { findings, unreadable } instead of a literal
     success, with the Find-* helpers reporting what they could not read - the
     shape path-hygiene.finder.ps1 already uses.
  2. The two main.js handlers return success:false and their draw functions
     call auditSectionFailed / auditReportBlind, which already exist and which
     the other four Health Advisor sections already use correctly.
  3. Get-FolderSize gains the null-plus-reason that Measure-Paths already has,
     so a floor is never rendered as a total.

fgj7 and u9r0 are closed into this.
close_reason: Fixed at the root: the registry helpers' catch blocks. Two new suites (70 assertions) plus 12 in findings-verify. Full suite 2525/0.

comments.author: QuantumMonkey
comments.text:
FIXED at the root, and the root was two five-line functions.

Open-RegistryView / Get-RegistrySubKeyNamesInView / Get-RegistryValueInView all
ended in 'catch { return @() }'. OpenSubKey RETURNS $null when a key is not
there and THROWS when it is there and denied - opposite facts - and that catch
turned both into an empty list. Everything else in the issue is downstream of
those two lines.

Channel: a script-scoped blind-spot list, $null when nobody is collecting, so
the helpers cost nothing for the other ~40 engine actions. Invoke-CleanerScan is
the only opt-in. Cap 200 enforced in the loop with the remainder COUNTED, plus
de-duplication (one denied key gets hit by 2 views x 6 roots x every value
lookup underneath it).

Invoke-CleanerScan is now a wrapper; the ten-branch switch is Get-CleanerFindings.
Ten places to remember to merge is ten places to forget one. State is computed
by the same three rules as New-FinderResult, restated rather than shared because
finders/ is Test-Path-guarded for trimmed installs and coupling would convert a
documented degradation into a crash.

Every site named in the issue, covered:
  Open-RegistryView catch                 -> key-denied
  Get-RegistrySubKeyNamesInView catch     -> subkeys-denied
  Get-RegistryValueInView catch           -> value-denied
  Get-CachedRegistryBaseKey (and its cache, which never retries) -> hive-unreadable
  pnputil catch AND $LASTEXITCODE        -> tool-failed
  Get-NetFirewallRule missing / query     -> cmdlet-unavailable / query-failed
  Get-PnpDevice missing / threw           -> cmdlet-unavailable / query-failed
  Find-OtherProfileRemnants, all three    -> profile-list-unreadable,
                                             hive-would-not-mount,
                                             profile-hive-unreadable
  Find-CleanerMlFindings                  -> definition-unparsable (it already
                                             counted these, in PROSE inside the
                                             note, where nothing could act on it)

Also folded in from the same root:
  main.js get-startup-items / get-software-redundancy manufactured
  { items: [], total: 0, orphans: 0 } and { groups: [], hasRedundancy: false }.
  Those RESOLVE, so renderer/audit.js's already-correct .catch -> section.fail ->
  auditReportBlind path was never reached and the verdict counted a check that
  never ran. Deleted the fabrication; the correct handling was already written.

  Get-FolderSize returned 0 for gone / refused / genuinely-empty alike, and
  Format-ByteSize renders 0 as the literal word 'empty'. Verified live:
  C:\System Volume Information used to read 'empty' in an evidence sentence next
  to a removal offer. Now $null + 'size unknown'. Needed -ErrorVariable, not a
  try/catch: -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue was swallowing per-file denials so
  nothing ever threw. And Format-ByteSize's param had to lose its [long] type -
  [long]$null coerces to 0 silently, which would have made the whole fix invisible.

Coverage: test/cleaner-blindspot-verify.ps1 (37, engine, uses HKLM\SECURITY as a
real denial on every Windows box) and test/cleaner-blindspot-ui-verify.js (33,
the real panel through the real scanCleaner). Plus 12 in findings-verify.

One defect found by the UI suite while writing it: the engine's dropped-remainder
count arrived in 'detail', which renderBlindSpots never renders, so the number
showed as '(more locations) (too-many-to-list)'. Moved to 'path'.

title: get-locked-paths blocks on dead UNC paths - the guard I added twice today and omitted here
description:
FOUND 2026-09-04 by attacking code shipped the same day. This is the same
defect, in the same session, for the third time, and the first two are the
reason it is embarrassing rather than merely a bug.

get-locked-paths (main.js) prunes remembered lock-failure paths by calling
fs.existsSync(r.path) on up to 50 of them, with no check on the path SHAPE
first.

MEASURED on this machine, just now:

  fs.existsSync on a dead UNC path   1,270 ms   (returns false)
  a full list of 50                  63.5 s

...of a synchronous, main-process, single-threaded stall while the Unlocker
modal sits there with an empty quick-pick.

WHY THIS IS THE THIRD TIME. That same ~1,258 ms measurement is written into
Get-InstallFolderCreated's doc comment in scanner.ps1 and into
parseLocalDirectory's in main.js, as the stated reason both of them refuse a
UNC path BEFORE touching the filesystem. I wrote both of those today. Then I
wrote this handler and called existsSync on a caller-independent path with no
shape check at all.

IT IS REACHABLE, and by the likeliest route rather than a contrived one. The
list is built from originalPath values of FAILED quarantine items. A program
installed from or onto a network share, whose file is locked, is exactly the
case that produces a lock failure - so a UNC path in this list is not an
exotic input, it is close to the archetypal one. It only needs the share to be
gone by the time the user opens the Unlocker, which is days later by design:
the whole point of the feature is remembering a failure from last Tuesday.

THE FIX: reuse parseLocalDirectory, which already sits in the same file and
already encodes exactly this rule (drive-letter rooted, not UNC, no relative).
A path it refuses should be dropped from the list without a filesystem call -
and dropped is the right outcome, because a path we cannot even shape-check is
not one list-lockers could answer about either.

WORTH CHECKING WHILE THERE: store.lockedPaths reads the ENTIRE oplog (up to
5 MB, rotated) and parses every line on each Unlocker open, to return at most
50 rows. Not a defect, but it is O(whole log) for a bounded answer, and the
same handler is the one that then blocks on I/O.

REPRODUCE: scratchpad probe adversarial-today.js, section 2.
notes:
PROMOTED TO ROOT 2026-09-04, absorbing scfr's path half. This is not a
get-locked-paths bug; it is that the same path-shape rule is written at each
call site instead of once.

FOUR SITES, THREE IMPLEMENTATIONS, ONE OMISSION:
  scanner.ps1  Get-InstallFolderCreated   drive-letter + explicit UNC reject
  main.js      parseDisplayIcon           drive-letter, no UNC line (redundant)
  main.js      parseLocalDirectory        drive-letter + explicit UNC reject
  main.js      get-locked-paths           NOTHING - calls existsSync directly

AND ALL THREE IMPLEMENTATIONS SHARE A HOLE: they enforce 'no network' as
^[A-Za-z]: plus a separator, so a MAPPED DRIVE passes. Z:\ walks an SMB share
in the elevated main process, which is the thing all three comments say they
exist to prevent.

FIX: one predicate in lib/, exported, used by all four - and it must answer the
question the comments actually claim, which means refusing a drive letter whose
DriveType is Network, not just refusing the \ prefix. get-locked-paths then
drops a path it cannot shape-check rather than calling existsSync on it, which
also removes the 1,270 ms per dead UNC path this issue was originally filed on.

The dead catch from scfr goes with it: once the shape check comes first,
existsSync is only ever called on a local rooted path, and the catch that could
never fire has nothing left to pretend to do.
ROOT FIXED 2026-09-04. One predicate, four call sites, and the mirror that
could not be deleted got a guard that can actually fail.

  lib/path-shape.js         localRootedPath + displayIconPath
  main.js parseDisplayIcon  delegates
  main.js parseLocalDirectory delegates
  main.js get-locked-paths  SHAPE FIRST, then existsSync - which is the fix

The ordering is the whole thing. existsSync on a dead UNC path costs 1,270 ms
and this ran once per remembered path up to fifty, synchronously, in the main
process. A path that fails the shape check is now dropped without a filesystem
call at all.

THE COMMENTS WERE CORRECTED, not just the code. All three copies said they
refused UNC because 'INV-4 forbids putting a walk on the network', and none of
them could deliver that: a mapped drive is a drive letter and is
indistinguishable by shape. The predicate now states exactly what it
guarantees - refuses relative, refuses UNC - and states what it does not.
Reading a share the user mapped themselves is not data leaving the device, so
the residual is small; the comment claiming otherwise was the actual defect,
because the next person would have trusted it.

THE POWERSHELL COPY CANNOT BE DELETED, so it got a BEHAVIOURAL guard rather
than a textual one. test/path-shape-verify.js runs one table of 17 cases
through both implementations - the JS one directly, the PowerShell one through
install-date-probe - and asserts they agree case by case, with a premise that
the engine accepts at least one path so 'agreement' cannot mean 'both refuse
everything'. That is what the tautological guard in locked-paths-verify should
have been, and that one is now replaced with an assertion that can fail.

24 assertions in path-shape-verify, 3 mutants after two were dropped by hand -
one equivalent (the explicit UNC line is redundant against the drive-letter
rule, again) and one mis-aimed by me. Both recorded in the mutation README
rather than left in the set to flatter the ratio.

No regressions: icon-extract 18/18, locked-paths-ipc 21/21 (now with the
live-UNC case), install-size 17/17, manifest-integrity 24/24, queue 42/42.
close_reason: Root fixed: one path predicate in lib/path-shape.js used by all four sites, shape checked before any filesystem call, comments corrected to stop overclaiming, and a behavioural cross-language guard replacing the textual one.

title: measure-install-size's budget bounds nothing inside one wide directory
description:
FOUND 2026-09-04 by attacking code shipped the same day, and the comment that
rationalised it is mine.

measureDirectoryBounded (main.js) checks its 1500 ms time budget and its
200,000-file budget ONCE PER DIRECTORY, at the top of the while loop. The inner
'for (const e of entries)' loop - which does the fs.statSync per file, i.e. all
of the work - has no check in it at all. The comment says:

  'Checked per DIRECTORY rather than per file: Date.now() in the inner loop is
   itself measurable at this file count, and a single directory's entries are
   bounded by what one readdir returns.'

The second clause is not true. One readdir returns however many entries the
directory holds, which is not a bound.

MEASURED, warm, on this machine:

  60,000 files in ONE directory
  walk ran 1,931 ms against a 1,500 ms budget
  budget consulted 1 time
  returned complete = true

431 ms over, and it would be linear past that - 600,000 files in one directory
is ~19 s, and this was WARM. The mp31 measurements put a cold first open at
1.3-2.8 ms per file, so a cold wide directory is minutes.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE OVERRUN. The walk is fully synchronous
(readdirSync + statSync) inside an ipcMain.handle in the MAIN process, which is
single-threaded. While it runs, every other IPC call queues behind it -
including Task Manager's 2-second process refresh. So one row of the program
list can stall unrelated parts of the app, and the budget that exists to
prevent exactly that does not fire.

IT IS REACHABLE WITHOUT ANYTHING PATHOLOGICAL. The walk is driven by the
IntersectionObserver as rows scroll into view, against InstallLocation values
from the registry. Package caches, %WINDIR%\Installer and flat asset folders
routinely hold tens of thousands of files in one directory.

NOT A CORRECTNESS DEFECT: the total returned is right, and the 'never render a
partial total' rule still holds - complete=true here is honest, the walk did
finish. The defect is that nothing bounds how long it takes.

THE FIX IS SMALL and the comment's first clause is the thing to preserve: a
Date.now() per file is real overhead at this scale. Check the clock every N
entries (a counter and a bitmask, so it costs one AND per file), or hoist the
budget test into the inner loop guarded by (files & 0x3ff) === 0. Then correct
the comment, because a comment asserting a bound that does not exist is worse
than no comment.

REPRODUCE: build 60,000 files in one directory and run the shipped loop shape
against it with budgetMs=1500. Scratchpad probe: adversarial-today.js.
notes:
PROMOTED TO ROOT 2026-09-04, absorbing 7cvt and scfr's env-hatch half. One
theme: a bound that is asserted in a comment rather than enforced in code.

  measureDirectoryBounded  the budget is checked ONCE PER DIRECTORY, outside
                           the loop that does the work. Measured: 60,000 files
                           in one directory ran 431 ms past a 1,500 ms budget
                           and still returned complete:true. My comment claimed
                           'a single directory's entries are bounded by what one
                           readdir returns'. They are not.
  lockFailuresFrom         writes an UNCAPPED path list while the reader is
                           capped at 50, so anything past the fiftieth entry is
                           written, never read, and still consumes the oplog's
                           5 MB rotation budget - evicting the elevation history
                           the diagnostic collector needs.
  VANISH_SIZE_BUDGET_MS    read unconditionally, not behind testHatchesAllowed,
  VANISH_SIZE_MAX_FILES    in a file whose own comment says the test hatches
                           'do not exist at all' in a packaged build.

FIX, all three in one pass: move the budget test inside the inner loop behind a
cheap counter mask so it costs one AND per file; cap the write at the reader's
limit and say in the comment that the two numbers move together; gate the two
env reads on testHatchesAllowed like the other two already are. Then correct
the comments, because a comment asserting a bound that does not exist is worse
than no comment.

title: Mutation testing: grow the set into the rest of scanner.ps1 and the renderer
description:
test/mutation/ now covers 27 mutants at 27/27, but that number is a floor on assertion quality in the areas probed, never coverage.

WHAT IS PROBED: lib/findings.js (the seam), finders/_contract.ps1 (the three-state contract), the vault path/identity/integrity guards, Test-ProtectedDestination, never-touch, the reparse skip, column filters, the uninstall queue, platform detection, repo invariants.

WHAT IS NOT PROBED AT ALL, and this is most of the destructive surface:
  - scanner.ps1 registry enumeration and the uninstall-entry parsers
  - the reclaim finders' size arithmetic (piu, lhf, the shared sizer)
  - process and network attribution (bfh.1, ddx)
  - the uninstall and force-uninstall flows (REQ-20)
  - System Clean's cleaner scans (phase4)
  - most of the renderer beyond column filters and the hygiene panel

WHY IT MATTERS MORE FOR THESE: the seam is pure and easy to assert; scanner.ps1 is 8,400 lines that actually delete things. The first pass into it found a real SEC-2 gap (the drive-root rule's junction resolution had no test) that eight months of green suites had not.

TWO PROCESS RULES LEARNED THE HARD WAY, both in test/mutation/README.md:
1. Aim each mutant at the suite that VERIFIABLY covers the code. Three of seven survivors in the first pass were mis-aimed mutants, which look exactly like coverage gaps.
2. Check every survivor by hand before writing an assertion. Three more were equivalent mutants - defence in depth means removing one of two redundant guards changes nothing.

Do NOT chase a kill-rate number. The value is the named gap, not the ratio; a set tuned to score well is a set that stopped looking.
notes:
CLOSING THIS AS A TICKET AND KEEPING IT AS A PRACTICE, 2026-09-04.

THE EVIDENCE FOR THE CHANGE: the set went from 27 mutants to 53 in one session,
and not one of them was added by working this issue. They were added because
every feature that shipped got mutants for its own rules -- xr7j, cihg, s4cx,
9caq, al45, nq21, mp31, 470o, 949, y1j, h55. An issue titled 'grow the set' has
no done-criteria and never will; what actually grew it was the rule that a new
rule gets a mutant.

So the practice is written down in test/mutation/README.md, where the next
person reads it, instead of living in a ticket nobody can close:

  * every new rule gets a mutant aimed at the suite that actually covers it,
    VERIFIED, not guessed -- three of seven 'gaps' in the first pass were
    mis-aimed mutants, and a mis-aimed mutant is indistinguishable from missing
    coverage;
  * check every survivor by hand before writing an assertion for it -- of the
    survivors so far, most were equivalent mutants or harness errors;
  * test the real function, never a replica.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM. The README's own 'What N/N does NOT mean' section
still stands and still names the unprobed areas: most of scanner.ps1's 8,500
lines, registry enumeration, the reclaim finders' size arithmetic, the uninstall
flows, System Clean's cleaner scans, and most of the renderer. That list is the
honest statement of coverage and it belongs in the README next to the number,
not in an open P2 that reads as scheduled work.

DO NOT REOPEN THIS TO CHASE THE RATIO. A set tuned to score well is a set that
stopped looking. If a specific area is worth probing, file THAT area with the
defect you suspect lives there -- which is how every mutant in the set that
ever caught anything got written.
close_reason: Converted from a ticket to a practice. The set grew 27 -> 53 this session entirely through 'every new rule gets a mutant', with none of it done by working this issue. The rule and its three caveats live in test/mutation/README.md; an issue with no done-criteria was never going to close.

title: The vault records no content hash, so a restore cannot detect a tampered payload
description:
FOUND 2026-09-02 by the same adversarial probe that found the Program Files escalation.

MEASURED: quarantine a file containing 'AUTHENTIC-CONTENT'. Overwrite the payload inside the vault entry folder with 'TAMPERED-BY-SOMETHING-ELSE'. Restore. Result:

  restore returned success=True, and put back: 'TAMPERED-BY-SOMETHING-ELSE'

No warning, no error, no difference in the reported outcome.

WHY IT CANNOT DETECT IT: the manifest row records originalPath, vaultRelative, sizeBytes and status. There is no hash. So restore has nothing to compare against and does not try.

Note that even the data it ALREADY HAS is not checked -- the tampered payload was 26 bytes against a recorded sizeBytes of 17, and that mismatch passed silently. A size check is not integrity, but a size check that exists and is ignored is worse than one that was never recorded.

SEVERITY, honestly. This is defence in depth rather than a standalone hole, and it is now largely behind the same door as the escalation issue: anything that can rewrite a vault payload can rewrite the manifest, and the P0 fix means a restore into a privileged location requires an ACL-locked data directory. What is left is that a restore into an ORDINARY user-writable path can still return content the vault did not store, while reporting success -- and the vault's entire promise is 'the thing you deleted is exactly the thing you get back'.

THE FIX, small: record SHA-256 per file at quarantine time alongside sizeBytes, and verify before the move at restore time. On mismatch, refuse rather than warn -- putting back a file the vault cannot vouch for is worse than not putting it back, because the operator believes a restore.

Two things to decide rather than assume:
1. Directories. Hashing a quarantined tree is not free and the sizer already exists; a per-file hash inside the tree may be the wrong granularity.
2. What a mismatch means for the ENTRY. One tampered file in a ten-file entry should probably not block the other nine, but it must be reported per-file rather than folded into a single success flag.

Reproduce: the A3 section of the adversarial probe, preserved in test\vault-destination-verify.ps1's sibling reasoning. The tamper itself is three lines: quarantine, overwrite the file under <vaultRoot>\<entryId>\files\1\, restore.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-03 in 48033f9.

The tamper that used to succeed now returns:
  Refused: the vault payload has changed since it was quarantined. Expected SHA256 098B2953BE1F9E22..., found 68CF2048943BF3FD.... Nothing was written. The file is still in the vault; inspect it before restoring.

Four behaviours, all asserted in test/vault-verify.ps1 (27 -> 43 passed, 0 failed):
  tampered file      refused, nothing written, payload left in the vault to inspect
  tampered directory refused too - trees get a composite SHA256-TREE over sorted path+content
  clean payload      restores, verified=true
  legacy entry       still restores, verified=false, with a note saying WHICH it is

Refuses rather than warns, and per file rather than per entry: one bad payload in a ten-file entry still returns the other nine. Entries predating this restore normally, because refusing them would strand every existing vault.

Both issues the original filing said to decide rather than assume:
  1. Directories ARE hashed, as one streaming composite, capped.
  2. A mismatch fails only that file, not the entry.

Verified by reverting both halves: 6 failures with verification disabled, 10 with the hash never recorded.

  Full Mode  2207 passed, 0 failed
  Audit Mode 1931 passed, 0 failed

COST is measured and recorded in the code: files are effectively free (250 MB adds ~200 ms), trees cost ~3 ms per file, cap 2,000 files for a ~6.5 s worst case. The first implementation used per-file Get-FileHash and was replaced with one streaming incremental hash after measuring 1,642 ms -> 1,234 ms on a 200-file tree.

Left open as its own issue: the identical function is 20x slower inside the engine than standalone, unexplained after ruling out the move, first-read/AV, enumeration, the size loop and StrictMode. The cap is set from the slow number so it cannot hurt anyone.

title: duplicate-content is 97.5% of everything the hygiene panel reports
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02. The panel's full run returns 4,144 findings. 4,040 of them (97.5%) come from one check.

  duplicate-content   4,040 findings, all costClass 'cheap', 46 unreadable, 36.8 s standalone
  everything else       104 findings across twelve checks

Sampled findings are things like three identical 514-byte copies of a file under C:\Users\Anand\.gemini\antigravity\brain\<uuid>\task.md.resolved.7 -- a tool's own internal state, where duplication is what the tool is supposed to produce.

WHY THIS IS A UTILITY PROBLEM AND NOT A TUNING ONE. This project's own standard is 'solve problems that are not solved... do not build redundant nonsense', and 7oo.3 exists specifically because 77 near-identical Visual C++ redistributable rows read as noise inside a list of real programs. Four thousand identical build scraps is the same failure at forty times the scale, and it is in the RESCUE module -- the one whose stated job is 'what a delete would destroy'.

The panel is not wrong. Those files ARE duplicates and the check IS reporting them accurately. It is answering a question nobody asked.

WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not add an exclusion list of directory names. finders/local-only-credentials.finder.ps1 rejects exactly that ('a list that grows by name guess rots the same way an exception list does') and duplicate-content already has a by-name prune that produced 43 of its 46 unreadable records.

CANDIDATE RULES, all needing a decision and none obviously right:
1. A MINIMUM SIZE. Three copies of 514 bytes is 1 KB reclaimed. A duplicate below some threshold is not worth an operator's attention at any count. Cheapest rule, and defensible as 'the finding must be worth the reading'.
2. A MINIMUM COPY VALUE, i.e. rank and cap by bytes-recoverable rather than by count. Ten copies of a 2 GB ISO matter; four thousand copies of a config scrap do not.
3. GROUP BY DIRECTORY. 4,040 findings across a few hundred parent directories is a readable list; the individual files are not. This is the one that changes the SHAPE of the answer rather than filtering it, and is probably the right one.
4. RECLASSIFY OUT OF 'rescue'. Duplicates are a reclaim question ('what is safe to remove'), not a rescue question ('what would I lose'). See vanish-uninstaller-xr7j, which this compounds.

Reproduce:
  $b64 = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('{"finders":["duplicate-content"]}'))
  powershell -NoProfile -File scanner.ps1 -Action hygiene-scan -ParamsBase64 $b64
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-03 in e58663c.

Groups under 16 KB reclaimable (77% of the 4,040 rows, 0.64% of the value) fold into one summary row instead of listing individually. Directory grouping -- my own original proposal in the filing -- was ruled out by the data: 811 directories, still a wall, and the biggest are IDE extension folders (ms-python, redhat.java, vscjava.vscode-gradle) nobody manages by hand.

  before   4,040 findings
  after    925 findings (924 listed + 1 summary standing for 3,116)

Arithmetic reconciles exactly: 924 + 3,116 = 4,040 groups; 1,260.5 + 8.16 = 1,268.7 MB. That reconciliation is what the tests check, in both count and bytes -- a fold that silently dropped rows would make the panel's own totals a lie.

Also moved 'duplicate-content' from module 'rescue' to 'reclaim'. Rescue's lede is 'Nothing here is waste; it is what a delete would cost you', which a duplicate directly contradicts. It was 97.5% of output in the one module whose job is showing what a delete would destroy.

The threshold (minReclaimBytes) is a scan parameter, not a constant -- the existing dedup suite's 777-byte fixtures needed 0 to keep testing what they were written for, which is itself the same lesson 087y already taught with maxDirs.

11 new assertions, verified by reverting both halves: silently dropping instead of summarizing turns 7 red including the reconciliation check (1 vs 4 groups, 40000 vs 40900 bytes); reverting the module move turns 1 red.

  TOTAL: 2235 passed, 0 failed, 8 skipped [Full Mode], single-tier, foreground

Deliberately not -BothTiers for this verification -- see session notes on system load from the interrupted prior run (clean restart, no crash, most likely cause: two full concurrent hash-heavy suites).

title: 58% of program rows carry a real icon path that the renderer throws away
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02 against this machine's real list (scanner.ps1 -Action list-desktop, 150 desktop entries). 87 of 150 (58.0%) carry a non-empty 'icon' field 0 of 150 render one scanner.ps1:320 reads DisplayIcon out of the uninstall key and ships it as 'icon'. main.js passes it through. renderer/core.js uses it NOWHERE -- the only icon markup in the app list is renderer/core.js:1102
${esc(initial)}
so every one of the 152 rows draws a letter tile. 7-Zip shows '7'. Android Studio shows 'A'. AI Noise Cancelation, AMD Radeon Software and Antigravity all show 'A', in a row, which is what a screenshot of the All Programs tab actually looks like. WHY THIS IS THE CHEAPEST THING ON THE 949 LIST. 949 is 'the app doesn't feel modern, advanced or futuristic' with no done-criteria, and this is the largest single visual difference between Vanish and every other program list on Windows -- including the Settings > Apps page it is competing with. The data is already collected, already crosses the IPC boundary, and is already discarded. MECHANISM, no new dependency. DisplayIcon is a path plus an optional index, 'C:\Program Files\App\app.exe,0'. Electron's app.getFileIcon(path, {size}) extracts it natively and asynchronously and returns a NativeImage that toDataURL() turns into something an can show. That is main-process work, so it does not block the renderer, and it should be lazy -- 150 extractions at load would be a worse first paint than letter tiles. DESIGN CONSTRAINTS this codebase already implies: - INV-4 / Rule 6: no network. Icon extraction is local file I/O, so this is fine. - A row whose icon CANNOT be extracted (path missing, exe deleted, index wrong) must fall back to the letter tile silently. An icon is decoration; it never carries meaning here, so a failure is not a could-not-look and must not be reported as one. - Do not cache extracted icons to disk without deciding where. store.js is ACL-protected for SEC-3 reasons and a bitmap cache does not belong in it. RELATED, same screenshot, filed separately because the fix is unrelated: the Date and Size columns say 'Unknown' on 26.7% and 26.0% of rows.
close_reason:
SHIPPED 2026-09-03 in acb8cc4.

Measured before: 87 of 150 desktop entries (58%) carry a DisplayIcon path, 0 of 150 rendered one. After: real icons render, and 39 of 40 sampled extract successfully. A screenshot of the real app shows 7-Zip, AI Noise Cancelation and Antigravity with their own icons, and the rows with no DisplayIcon keeping letter tiles.

LAZY BY MEASUREMENT, not by preference. Extraction is 51 ms per icon, so all 87 up front would be 4.4 s of first paint -- worse than the letter tiles this was meant to improve. An IntersectionObserver with a 200px margin fetches only rows about to be visible; the main process caches by source string, including nulls.

Silent fallback throughout: an icon carries no meaning in this table, so its absence is not a could-not-look. Relative paths, UNC paths (INV-4) and missing files are all refused with success=true and no icon.

THE BUG IT ALMOST SHIPPED WITH is the useful part of this issue. The path check was written /^[A-Za-z]:[\/]/ and landed as /^[A-Za-z]:[\/]/ -- a character class matching only a forward slash. Every Windows path was rejected, the feature silently did nothing, and NOTHING FAILED, because answering null for everything still satisfies every assertion about answering null safely. Caught by probing a real extraction rather than by a test.

test/icon-extract-verify.js is therefore built around what must be ACCEPTED, not only what must be refused. Planting the original bug back turns 5 of its 18 assertions red, including 'at least one real installed program produced an icon (0 of the first 12 tried)'.

18 passed, 0 failed. Registered in run-all.ps1. The stub preload answers with no icon so every existing DOM suite exercises the fallback: ui-interaction 100, column-filter 81, listeners 25, snapshot 23, all green.

title: local-only-credentials spends 78% of its walk on D:\Dependencies and still caps
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02, ho2-profile-probe.ps1, warm, nothing else on the disk.

  2,850 ms   2,986 dirs   4 candidates  12 repos  C:\Users\Anand
     12,547 ms  15,000 dirs   0 candidates   1 repo   D:\Dependencies  <- HIT THE CAP
        591 ms   2,658 dirs   0 candidates   5 repos  the other five roots
     15,988 ms  18,644 dirs   4 candidates            TOTAL

D:\Dependencies is 78% of the check's walk time and 80% of its directory budget, returns zero candidates, and STILL truncates -- so it also emits a scan-capped could-not-look that will never clear no matter how many times it is run.

WHY IT IS A ROOT AT ALL. Get-Ho2DefaultRoots uses a positive test: a drive-root folder earns a spot by demonstrably containing a repo one level down. D:\Dependencies qualified because D:\Dependencies\Flutter has a .git. The SELECTOR therefore knows exactly which child justified the root -- and then discards that and hands the parent to the walker, which re-derives it by brute force through D:\Dependencies\Gradle (163,476 files) and runs out of budget.

087y already fixed the correctness half of this: breadth-first means Flutter is reached (the probe confirms 1 repo found). What is left is pure cost.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX, not decided. Three candidates, in order of how well they fit this codebase's stated principles:

1. CARRY THE SELECTOR'S EVIDENCE. Get-Ho2DefaultRoots already computed which children hold repos. Return them alongside the root so the walker can spend its budget there first. Cheapest, no new rule, and it is information the code already has and throws away.

2. STOP DESCENDING OUTSIDE A REPO. The check looks for credential files INSIDE git repos. A directory that is not in a repo and contains no repo cannot produce a finding. Cap exploration depth outside a repo root while walking fully inside one. This is a rule about the check's own semantics rather than a name list.

3. PRUNE PACKAGE-MANAGER CACHES BY NAME. Rejected unless 1 and 2 fail. Get-Ho2DefaultRoots deliberately uses a positive test precisely because 'a list that grows by name guess rots the same way an exception list does', and adding Gradle/pub-cache/.m2 by name reintroduces exactly that.

Reproduce:
  powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File test\sandbox\ho2-profile-probe.ps1

NOTE ON THE BASELINE. docs/BENCHMARKS.md Run 003 records this check at 34,637 ms with 30,656 dirs, 2 roots capped and ZERO candidates. That number predates 127o (reparse skip) and 087y (breadth-first), and is now stale in both directions: the check is 2.2x faster AND finds 4 candidates where it used to find none. Run 004 should replace it.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-04. Candidate 2 from the description -- stop descending outside a repo -- implemented as a scan parameter, repoSearchDepth, defaulting to 4.

MEASURED BEFORE CHOOSING, full walk to depth 8 with the prune list applied,
every default root:

                     dirs   inside a repo   outside   repos
  D:\Dependencies   81,318           2,285    79,033       1
  C:\Users\Anand     2,999             419     2,580      12
  the other five       659             648        11       5

97% of D:\Dependencies is outside any repo, and a credential outside a repo is
not this finder's claim to make. Its outside-repo dirs by depth: 290 at depths
0-4, then 25,246 / 25,868 / 17,988 / 9,641 at depths 5-8. The package caches
fan out at depth 5 and nowhere shallower.

And every repo on this machine: three at depth 0, three at depth 1, five at
depth 3 (Documents\GitHub\<repo>), seven at depth 4 (.bmad\cache\external-
modules, .claude\plugins). None deeper. So 4 is the shallowest cutoff that
loses no repo here; 3 would lose seven.

RESULT, same probe minutes apart:

  before  16,910 ms  18,658 dirs  4 candidates  1 root CAPPED
  after    7,291 ms   4,570 dirs  5 candidates  0 roots capped

D:\Dependencies alone: 13,306 ms / 15,000 dirs -> 5,137 ms / 2,575 dirs.

Read the candidate column first, as with 127o. The FIFTH candidate is inside
D:\Dependencies\Flutter -- the repo that made the directory a search root, and
which the capped walk was running out of budget before reaching. The old run
said scan-capped, so the contract held and the operator was told the check was
incomplete rather than clean. They were still not told about the credential.
The permanent could-not-look is gone with it.

WHY IT IS SILENT rather than recorded as could-not-look: this is scope, the
same category as Ho2PruneSegments and maxDepth, both of which narrow the search
without comment because they are part of what the check IS. Nothing prevented
us. Recording it would hand every machine a permanent 'incomplete', which is
the defect this issue was filed about, moved one line down. It is a scan
parameter instead, so a deeper layout can raise it.

Candidate 1 (carry the selector's evidence) was not needed once this landed --
the selector's root is walked in full, just not to depth 8 outside a repo.
Candidate 3 (prune caches by name) stays rejected.

TESTS: five new assertions in finder-credentials-verify (37 passed, 0 failed),
including the one that matters -- a credential six levels INSIDE a repo is
still found, so the rule cannot truncate the deep project trees this check
exists for. Two mutants added and both killed: removing the rule, and applying
it inside repos too. Full set 29/29.

docs/BENCHMARKS.md Run 006, which replaces Run 003's figure for this check.
close_reason: repoSearchDepth=4 outside a repo. 16,910 ms -> 7,291 ms, 18,658 -> 4,570 dirs, no root capped, and one MORE credential found - the one inside Flutter that the capped walk never reached.

title: The restore-point test counts net total, so it fails once shadow storage is at its cap
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30. switches-restore-3 failed on the host with:

    FAIL  two back-to-back restore points were actually created (32 -> 33)

after passing an hour earlier on the same commit. Not a regression, and not
flaky in the usual sense - the machine crossed a threshold.

MEASURED on the operator machine at the time of the failure:

    restore points          : 30
    Used shadow storage     : 9.20 GB
    Allocated               : 9.71 GB
    Maximum                 : 9.98 GB     <- 92% of the cap

At the cap, creating a restore point EVICTS an older one. So two creations can
raise the total by one, or by none. The assertion reads the NET COUNT before
and after and expects +2, which is only true while there is headroom.

The preceding assertion in the same suite already passed: 'both consecutive
checkpoint calls succeeded'. So the product did what it was asked; the test's
way of confirming it is what broke.

THE FIX IS TO STOP COUNTING. Capture the restore points by identity before and
after - CreationTime, or SequenceNumber - and assert that two NEW ones exist,
rather than that the total rose by two. That is correct at any storage level
and does not care what Windows evicted.

WHILE IN THERE: the newest six restore points on this machine are all this
suite's own - 'Vanish verify 1', 'Vanish verify 2', 'Vanish verify sentinel',
'Vanish verify absent', 'Vanish protection probe', 'Vanish Pre-Uninstall'. A
full suite run creates several, and repeated runs during a working session
filled most of a 9.98 GB allocation. Worth deciding whether the suite should
clean up the points it creates, and saying somewhere that running it costs
disk. It is the operator's disk and the suite is spending it silently.

RELATED: this is the fourth machine-state-dependent suite found in one day
(686 shared runtimes, bfh.1 network peer count, aaw GPU payload, and now this
one), plus the elevation axis in pnor and the clean-machine preconditions in
392o. The common shape is a test whose result depends on the machine rather
than the build, without saying so.
close_reason: Fixed: the assertion compares restore-point SEQUENCE NUMBERS before and after instead of the net total. At the shadow-storage cap Windows evicts an older point to make room, so two successful creations can raise the total by one or none - which is what produced the failure (32 -> 33) while the assertion immediately before it, that both checkpoint calls succeeded, passed. Identity comparison is correct at any storage level. Verified: 30 passed, 0 failed, reporting '2 new sequence number(s), total 1 -> 3'. Also caught myself passing a third argument to an Assert-True that takes two, the same mistake made in relaunch-live-probe.ps1 earlier the same day.

title: local-only-credentials misses shallow repos when the cap is hit, because the walk is depth-first
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30 profiling o1mj, and separate from the reparse-point fix that
shipped with it.

Invoke-Ho2CredentialWalk uses a Stack, so it is depth-FIRST, and it has a
15,000-directory cap per root. When the cap is reached the deepest branch has
been fully explored and shallow siblings have never been popped.

MEASURED, D:\Dependencies, after the reparse fix:

  8,722 ms   15,000 dirs   0 repos found   CAPPED

D:\Dependencies is a root at all because Get-Ho2DefaultRoots proved it holds a
repo one level down. It does: D:\Dependencies\Flutter has a .git. The walk
never found it. The budget went depth-first into D:\Dependencies\Gradle, which
is 163,476 files (see gkib), and Flutter was still sitting unpopped on the
stack when the cap stopped the run.

So the root SELECTOR and the WALKER disagree about the same directory: one
proved a repo is there, the other reported none. The finder correctly says
could-not-look, so nothing is claimed falsely -- but a repo that was proven to
exist a moment earlier is not examined.

THE FIX IS A QUEUE, not a stack. Breadth-first spends the budget on the
shallowest directories first, which are the ones most likely to be actual
project roots; the cap then costs you the deepest branches rather than
whichever ones happened to sort late. Three lines.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE IN THE SAME COMMIT: the reparse-point change was measured
and has an equivalence check behind it. Changing traversal ORDER in the same
commit would mean a regression could not be attributed to either. Same
reasoning lxl recorded for not extending the shared walk at release time.

WHAT THE FIX MUST PRESERVE, and what to assert:
* repo membership inheritance still works. RepoRoot is carried down the stack
  entries; a queue carries it identically, but a submodule's own .git must
  still replace its parent's for its descendants.
* the cap is still reported as could-not-look with the real path.
* on an uncapped tree the RESULT SET must be identical, order aside. That is
  the control: BFS and DFS visit the same directories when neither is capped,
  so any difference on a small fixture is a bug in the change.

ALSO WORTH DECIDING: whether D:\Dependencies should be a root at all. It earns
one by holding a single Flutter checkout, and the cost is walking a 14 GB
package cache. Get-Ho2DefaultRoots proves a repo is present but says nothing
about what else is in there.
close_reason: Fixed with a queue. D:\Dependencies\Flutter is now found; before it was not, despite being the repo that made the folder a search root. Control: on three uncapped real trees BFS and DFS return byte-identical repo and candidate sets, so only the cap's victims change. maxDirs is now a scan parameter so the cap is testable; the fixture's deep chain is named to sort after the shallow repo because a stack pops last-pushed-first and the test would otherwise pass against the old code. Verified by reverting to a stack: the assertion fails there. ho2 suite 22 -> 26.

title: Machine Hygiene decision bar: one recommended click, chosen by cost not size
description:
BUILT 2026-08-30 on operator request: "a banner/widget on top of machine
hygiene for one click decisions ... some degree of idiot proofing is always
useful."

WHAT IT IS NOT, and this was the first design decision. The obvious build is a
Clean button. Nothing on this panel is removable by Vanish in either mode -
the lede says so and every finder is auditOnly - so a one-click delete would
not be a faster version of this screen, it would be the product this project
exists as an alternative to. Every action opens, filters, scrolls or copies,
and the bar says that permanently in every phase (HYGIENE_NEVER).

THE RULE THAT DOES THE WORK: the recommended click is chosen by COST, never by
size. Ordering is irreplaceable, then unknown, then expensive, then a plain
review. A 14 GB package cache is the biggest number on the screen and the
least consequential thing on it; a megabyte of uncommitted work is the
opposite. lib/findings.js already ranks the LIST this way; this is the same
rule applied to the OFFER.

'unknown' sits second deliberately, matching COST_ORDER: an unmeasured cost is
not a cheap one, and letting it fall through to a bytes-led offer would put
the most dangerous thing behind the safest.

IDIOT-PROOFING, each with a test:
* scanning outranks everything. A has-work decision built from 3 of 13 checks
  offers nothing at all - "a decision from a partial run is not a decision".
* not-trustworthy evidence gets no action computed from it. decide() exposes
  `trustworthy`; with any unreadable location, System Clean is DISABLED and the
  reason ("the total is a floor and not a total") is printed on the page.
* two refusals, two sentences. System Clean is off for two different reasons -
  nothing regenerable found, or an incomplete total - and each prints its own.
  A control off for two reasons that names one is a control that lies.
* disabled, never hidden, and the reason is in the DOM rather than only in a
  title attribute.
* never-run and failed are different phases with different sentences. Those
  are the two states most likely to share a rendering, which is the defect the
  verdict block above it exists to prevent.
* an invariant across all six phases: no enabled action id may match
  /delete|remove|purge|clean-now|free-now|fix-all/, and every phase carries the
  standing promise.

SHAPE: hygieneDecisionActions(decision, ctx) is PURE - no DOM, no globals - so
the rules are asserted directly rather than inferred from rendered HTML.
renderHygieneDecisionBar draws it; refreshHygieneDecisionBar is called from
every path that draws the panel, LAST in renderHygieneAll and with the
decision that was actually drawn.

Tests: test/hygiene-panel-verify.js 66 -> 115.

FOLLOW-UPS worth considering, deliberately not built:
* the primary action scrolls to and outlines the first matching finding rather
  than filtering. Filtering would hide the ranking, and the ranking is the
  argument the screen is making. If a filter is ever added it must not be the
  DEFAULT.
* 'Copy report' uses navigator.clipboard and degrades to "Could not copy". No
  file export - that would need a save dialog and a new IPC channel.
close_reason:
Shipped on master (a5fbbf0), unreleased. Panel suite 66 -> 120, full suite 2043 passing, verified in real screenshots of the running app in all three states it can reach without injected data (invitation, mid-scan, decided).

The headline was wrong in the first version and only a screenshot showed it: it repeated the verdict block's sentence verbatim. Fixed to say what ORDER to work in, with a test that it carries no digits.

title: local-only-credentials is the scan's tail at 40 s, and it shares a walk with nothing
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-29, in a single run with every unit reported:

     40.0 s  local-only-credentials      <- the tail
     35.3 s  duplicate-content
     24.0 s  the four reclaim checks (one shared walk, 3l8)
     19.1 s  reclaim-package-caches
     14.5 s  redirect-variables
     12.6 s  gitignored-unique+repo-health (one shared walk, lxl)

  WALL 59.9 s, summed 148.7 s, 9 engine calls, pool of 3.

This is the check everything else waits on, and it is a SINGLETON unit: it
shares its walk with nothing, so neither 3l8 nor lxl touched it.

WHY IT WAS SKIPPED TWICE. 3l8 noted it walks Get-Ho2DefaultRoots, a
machine-wide root set rather than the home directory, so it could not join the
reclaim group without changing coverage. That reasoning was right and is not
the question here. The question nobody has asked is what it spends 40 seconds
DOING.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH BEFORE PROPOSING ANYTHING, in this order:
1. Profile it the way lhf and 3l8 were profiled -- per phase, warm, alone,
   nothing else touching the disk. Both of those found the real cause
   disagreed with the issue's guess, and so did e6gn and gkib today.
2. How many roots does Get-Ho2DefaultRoots return, and do they overlap? The
   redirect-variables check measured the same folder twice because two unset
   variables resolved to one path (lhf). Same shape, worth ruling out.
3. Does it walk any tree more than once -- once per credential pattern, the
   way Find-ToolchainConsumers walks once per marker (e6gn)? That is the same
   defect three times already.
4. Does it follow junctions? lxl found the two git checks reporting 27 paths
   for 14 real repositories that way. test\sandbox\git-walk-equivalence-probe.ps1
   has the GetFinalPathNameByHandle resolver that settles it.

DO NOT quote a number from another run. The identical 13 checks summed 210.4 s
earlier the same day and 136.8 s later -- 1.5x, same code, same machine, purely
file-system cache warmth. Every figure above comes from one run, and any
comparison must too.
close_reason:
Profiled and fixed. Shipped on master (13851ed), unreleased.

THE ISSUE ASKED FOUR QUESTIONS IN ORDER. Answers:

1. Per-phase profile, warm, alone: 34.6 s total. Two of seven roots exhaust
   their 15,000-directory budget and are 34.0 s of it; the other five cost
   0.6 s together.
2. Root overlap: none. Get-Ho2DefaultRoots takes 80 ms and returns 7 roots,
   none inside another. Not lhf's duplicated-path shape.
3. One walk per root, not one per credential pattern. Not e6gn's shape.
4. Junctions: YES, and this was the whole thing.

THE DEFECT. AppData is in the prune list. Local Settings and Application Data
are junctions TO AppData\Local and are NOT, and the walk had no reparse-point
test -- so it went round its own prune and spent the entire budget in there.

    shipped        23,160 ms  15,000 dirs   9 repos  0 candidates  CAPPED
    skip reparse    2,958 ms   2,991 dirs  12 repos  4 candidates

Not a performance finding. All nine repos it found were alias paths; it missed
all five real ones under Documents\GitHub and reported ZERO credential files
on a machine with four .npmrc files inside repositories. The aeu contract held
-- it said could-not-look, not clean -- and the operator still got that
sentence instead of four real findings.

A NEGATIVE CONTROL WAS RUN before believing the zero: Test-Ho2CredentialMatch
matches .env, id_rsa and .npmrc correctly, and a direct search confirmed the
four .npmrc files exist. The zero was a miss, not an empty machine.

TESTS. Three new assertions, verified to FAIL against the unfixed walker. My
first version called Invoke-Ho2CredentialWalk directly, which this suite
deliberately never does ("a finder that works as a function and is wired up
wrong is a finder that never runs for real"); rewritten to drive hygiene-scan.
2043 -> 2047, all four in this suite, nothing else moved.

FILED FROM THIS WORK:
* 087y (P2 bug) - D:\Dependencies still caps. It is a root because
  D:\Dependencies\Flutter has a .git, but the walk is depth-first and burns
  the budget in a 163,476-file package cache while Flutter is never popped.
  The root selector and the walker disagree about the same directory. A queue
  fixes it; kept out of this commit so a regression stays attributable.
* 127o gains a fourth affected walker: a junction pointing OUTSIDE the root is
  now skipped here with no record, same as everywhere else.

title: One unreadable subdirectory drops a 14 GB reclaimable cache from the findings entirely
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-29 while working e6gn, which was filed believing the tail was
seven redundant directory listings. It is not. The listings are 4.6 s of a
45 s check.

  D:\Dependencies\Gradle    40,307 ms   163,476 files   14.35 GB

That single Measure-FinderPathBytes call is the slowest thing the Machine
Hygiene panel does, and reclaim-package-caches is the unit everything else
waits on (4v8). 40.3 s sizing + 4.6 s consumer search = 44.9 s against the
45.5 s recorded for the whole check.

WHY THE USUAL FIXES DO NOT APPLY.
* Walk sharing does nothing. Nothing else sizes this directory, so there is
  no second walk to remove. lhf's shared sizer already deduplicates across
  finders and this is a single caller.
* Caching across scans is refused by design, and correctly: a second scan
  exists because the operator changed something.
* There is no cheap directory size on NTFS. bu2 already went down this road
  and rejected it: USN records carry names and parents but NOT sizes, so
  sizing that way means parsing raw $MFT records off the volume.

WHAT bu2 DID INSTEAD IS THE PRECEDENT. It inverted the design -- classify
first, and measure only what classification could not explain, under a
20-SECOND BUDGET. The reasoning is in the header of lib/attribution.js.

The same inversion fits here. A package cache is classified by its path: we
already know it is a Gradle cache and that everything in it is re-downloadable.
The exact byte count is evidence for the operator, not an input to any
decision -- costClass is 'cheap' and action is 'audit', so nothing is deleted
on the strength of the number.

PROPOSAL, to be argued not assumed: give Measure-FinderPathBytes a time
budget. On expiry return the bytes counted so far PLUS an unreadable record
naming the truncation, so the finding reads 'at least 10.2 GB, measurement
stopped after N seconds' rather than a total that is quietly short. That is
the aeu three-state contract applied to a measurement instead of a search,
and it lands in the SHARED sizer, so every finder that meets a huge directory
benefits, not only this one.

THE OPEN QUESTION, and why this is not just implemented: a budgeted total is
non-deterministic between runs, and this project's whole position is that it
does not lie about what it knows. 'At least 10.2 GB' is honest. 'You can
reclaim 14.35 GB' when it is really 14.35 GB is more useful. Deciding between
a slow exact answer and a fast honest partial one is a product call, not an
implementation detail -- worth /crew.

CHEAPER THING TO CHECK FIRST: is the 163,476-file enumeration itself
avoidable? Get-ChildItem -Recurse builds a PSObject per file, and lhf already
found PSObject overhead dominating one of these paths. A raw
EnumerateFiles/EnumerateFileSystemEntries loop summing Length may be several
times faster for the same exact answer, which would make the product call
unnecessary. Measure that before designing the budget.
notes:
RE-BASED 2026-08-29 against a single run with every unit reported, after three
cross-run subtraction errors in one day. Pool 3, shared walks, largest unit

title: reclaim-package-caches walks the home directory SEVEN times, one per marker
description:
FOUND 2026-08-29 answering 4v8's "WORTH CHECKING FIRST" note. The answer is
not the one 4v8 guessed. It asked whether reclaim-package-caches could join
the user-tree walk group. The real finding is that the check walks the home
directory seven times all by itself.

finders/_never-touch.ps1, Find-ToolchainConsumers, line ~167:

    foreach ($marker in $markers) {
        $hits = @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $root -Filter $marker -File `
                    -Recurse -Depth $maxDepth -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)
    }

One full recursive listing PER MARKER. reclaim-package-caches then calls it
once per cache spec (finders/reclaim-package-caches.finder.ps1 line ~213):

    npm     package.json                                        1 marker
    Gradle  gradlew, build.gradle, build.gradle.kts             3 markers
    pip     requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py          3 markers

Seven recursive walks of $env:USERPROFILE at maxDepth 4, enumerating exactly
the same directories, to collect seven file names. This is 3l8 and lxl a
third time, and it is the largest instance of the three.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW. reclaim-package-caches is 45.5 s and is the scan's tail
(4v8): a single check that finishes last and that everything else waits on.
Seven walks at roughly 6.5 s each accounts for essentially all of it. Fixing
this removes the tail rather than reordering around it, which is what 4v8
wanted and could not see how to get.

THE FIX IS THE MECHANISM THAT ALREADY EXISTS. Register-SharedWalkHarvest
-markerNames with all seven names, one Invoke-SharedTreeWalk, seven reads of
walk.markers. 3l8 measured harvesting four extra markers in one walk as free
(12.4 s for one, 12.4 s for four): the listing is the cost, not the matching.

TWO THINGS TO CHECK BEFORE ASSUMING IT JOINS AN EXISTING GROUP:
* depth is 4, against 8 for the reclaim group and 6 for the git group. A
  different depth is a different question and must stay a different cache
  key unless deliberately changed. It may be a THIRD group, and that is fine.
* Get-ChildItem -Recurse in PowerShell 5.1 FOLLOWS junctions. So this check
  very likely has lxl's duplicate-reporting bug too: My Documents, Local
  Settings and Application Data would each yield the same consumer projects
  again. lxl found 27 paths for 14 real repos this way. MEASURE IT before
  and after; test\sandbox\git-walk-equivalence-probe.ps1 is the pattern,
  including the GetFinalPathNameByHandle resolver that proves nothing real
  was lost.

Callers are contained: reclaim-package-caches (the finder) and scanner.ps1's
own toolchain-consumers action. Nothing else calls Find-ToolchainConsumers.

NOT a correctness issue for what is OFFERED - consumer evidence only makes
the note attached to a finding richer, and duplicates make it noisier, not
wrong. It is a correctness issue for what the note CLAIMS if junction
duplicates inflate the consumer count.
