title: A junction pointing outside the walk root is skipped with no record
description:
FOUND 2026-08-29 while proving lxl did not lose coverage.

Invoke-SharedTreeWalk (finders/_contract.ps1) does this and nothing else:

    if (($child.Attributes -band [System.IO.FileAttributes]::ReparsePoint) -ne 0) { continue }

Skipping is correct -- a junction is a second name for a directory, and
following one double-counts at best and loops forever at worst. lxl is the
evidence: the two git finders followed junctions and reported 27 repo paths
for 14 real repos, the same work listed up to four times under My Documents,
Local Settings and Application Data.

THE DEFECT IS THE SILENCE, not the skip. When the junction target is INSIDE
the walk root the directory is still visited under its real name, so nothing
is lost and a record would be noise. When the target is OUTSIDE the root
nothing else visits it, and the walk has not looked there -- which is exactly
the state aeu says must be named as could-not-look rather than omitted.
Today it is omitted, so a scan can report 'nothing found' about a tree it
never opened.

Real and ordinary case: a home directory where Documents, or a projects
folder, is a junction to D:\ because C: is a small SSD. Every reclaim check
and both git checks walk straight past it and say nothing.

WHAT IS WANTED. Resolve the child's target, and if it falls outside the walk
root, add New-Unreadable -reason 'not-followed' with the real target in the
detail, so the finder reports could-not-look and the panel names the place.
If it falls inside, skip silently as now -- it is covered under its real
name and a record would fire on My Documents for every user on Windows.

Resolving needs GetFinalPathNameByHandle; there is a working P/Invoke for it
in test\sandbox\git-walk-equivalence-probe.ps1 (Resolve-FinalPath) written
for exactly this comparison, so the mechanism is proven before the fix
starts. Cost is one handle open per junction encountered, not per directory.

AFFECTS BOTH WALK GROUPS and every finder in them; shipped in 0.9.2 for the
reclaim group and 0.9.3 for the git group.
notes: 2026-08-30 findings. (1) duplicate-content.finder.ps1 around line 315 ALREADY implements exactly what this issue asks: it records the skipped junction as New-Unreadable with reason 'not-searched'. That is the reference pattern; three walkers skip silently (Invoke-SharedTreeWalk, Measure-FinderPathBytes, Invoke-Ho2CredentialWalk). (2) Get-Item .Target is NOT usable for the inside-vs-outside test - measured: it returns EMPTY for the system junctions and returned the PARENT of the target for one I created. GetFinalPathNameByHandle is required; a working P/Invoke is in test/walker-invariants-verify.ps1. (3) The inside/outside distinction is not optional. Recording every junction would be WRONG, not just noisy: a junction whose target is inside the root IS searched under its real name, so calling it not-searched is a false could-not-look; and every Windows home directory has three, so unreadableCount would be nonzero on every machine and UI_NOTHING_FOUND - the one state meaning clean - would become unreachable. (4) Add-Type costs ~345 ms so it must be lazy, compiled on first reparse point, not at file scope. (5) DO NOT touch Measure-FinderPathBytes until gkib is fixed: its unreadable list sets hadError, and reclaim-package-caches drops the whole finding when hadError is true, so junction records there would delete the largest reclaim finding on any machine with a junction under a cache directory.
close_reason:
Fixed in 28844c6, unblocked by gkib as predicted. Resolve-FinalPath (GetFinalPathNameByHandle, Add-Type lazy so a machine whose walk meets no reparse point never pays the ~345 ms) plus Test-PathIsInside, wired into Invoke-SharedTreeWalk, Measure-FinderPathBytes and Invoke-Ho2CredentialWalk.

The inside/outside distinction is the whole design and is not optional: a junction whose target is inside the root IS searched under its real name, so recording it would be a FALSE could-not-look, and with three in every Windows home directory unreadableCount would be nonzero on every machine - making UI_NOTHING_FOUND, the one state that means clean, unreachable.

Get-Item .Target confirmed unusable: EMPTY for My Documents, Local Settings and Application Data, and it returned the PARENT of the target for a junction created for the test.

Six assertions in shared-walk-verify.ps1 covering both walkers and both directions, with a premise assertion that the resolver really sees through the junction so the checks cannot pass by accident. 74 passed, 0 failed.

title: No single session can run the whole suite: elevation flips which tests skip
description:
FOUND 2026-08-29 running run-all.ps1 from an ELEVATED shell for the first
time. Both runs are green and neither run is complete.

  unelevated   1739 passed, 0 failed   - skips Vault IPC, Startup actions
                                         IPC, System Clean purges, Data-dir
                                         ownership, live elevated relaunch
  elevated     1980 passed, 0 failed   - runs all of those, and instead skips
                                         NINE access-denied tests

The elevated skips are not flaky and not environmental. They are causal: an
Administrator token reads through a Deny ACE, so the suites cannot BUILD the
condition they exist to test. Their own skip messages say so, e.g.

  "could not construct a directory this account genuinely cannot enumerate
   (icacls /deny did not block this account's own Get-ChildItem, which can
   happen for an elevated or otherwise privileged session)"

Affected, one access-denied assertion each: local-only-credentials (ho2),
gitignored-unique (sgn), content-hash dedup (30i), machine hygiene (pko),
reclaim by marker (piu), shared sizer (lhf), Vault engine (TASK-01),
security regressions, network attribution (bfh.1).

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A SKIP COUNT. could-not-look is the state this
whole project is built around (aeu). The tests that prove a finder reports
could-not-look rather than nothing are exactly the ones an elevated run
cannot exercise -- so the more privileged the session, the less of the
core contract is actually checked. A maintainer who only ever runs elevated
(the natural habit for this app) gets a green suite that never tested the
defect the app exists to prevent.

One suite already handles this honestly and is the model:
  "SKIP  running elevated; guard path is covered by the unelevated run"

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, roughly in order of cost:
1. run-all.ps1 prints its elevation state in the header and in the summary,
   so a log says which half of the suite it was capable of running.
2. The summary names the OTHER half: "9 tests need an unelevated shell; run
   this again without elevation to cover them."
3. Decide whether CI/acceptance requires both runs. Rule 10 already says a
   VM pass is what counts for Complete; this says a VM pass needs to be TWO
   passes, elevated and not.

NOT worth doing: trying to drop privileges mid-suite. Rerunning the process
under a restricted token is a real mechanism but it is a big one, and the
cheap fix (say which half ran) removes the actual danger, which is a green
number that quietly means less than it did last time.
notes: Number correction: the issue body says 'unelevated 1739 / elevated 1980'. Those are not the same code. The elevated run included lxl's 16 new assertions. Like for like it is 1739 unelevated against 1964 elevated -- elevation adds 225 assertions and removes 9. The argument is unchanged; the arithmetic was not.
close_reason:
CLOSED 2026-09-02. All three items shipped.

1 and 2 (say which half ran, name the other half) were already live: run-all.ps1 prints the tier in the header and stamps it on the TOTAL line, then says which tier to run for the rest.

3, the decision, is now a mechanism rather than a note. test\run-all.ps1 -BothTiers runs Full Mode in the elevated shell, then re-runs itself through a scheduled task at RunLevel Limited for the Audit Mode half, and prints both.

The issue said NOT to build this -- 'rerunning the process under a restricted token is a real mechanism but it is a big one'. That was right when it was written and is no longer, because scanner.ps1 already ships the de-elevation mechanism for Audit Mode relaunch (9vp), so this reuses it rather than inventing one. It also exercises the product's own de-elevation path as a side effect.

MEASURED before trusting it: probed RunLevel Limited on this host first -- parent isAdmin True, child isAdmin False. Then the real run:

  Full Mode   2141 passed, 0 failed,  7 skipped
  Audit Mode  1891 passed, 0 failed, 11 skipped
  exit 0, clean committed tree

The two totals are printed side by side and deliberately NOT added. Most suites run in both tiers, so a sum counts the same assertion twice and reads as growth.

IT CHECKS THE CHILD'S OWN ELEVATION rather than trusting the drop. Where UAC is disabled (EnableLUA=0, which is what the Windows Sandbox image ships) there is no standard-user token to drop to and RunLevel Limited comes back elevated; the run then reports the other half as COULD NOT RUN with the reason, instead of counting a second Full Mode pass as coverage. Reporting that as 'both halves covered' would be the exact defect this project exists to prevent.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED IN THE MECHANISM ITSELF, worth recording because it was invisible: the scheduled task has no console, so every Write-Host in the child went nowhere. The assertion-count guard (686) demonstrated this on itself -- it correctly caught repo-invariants dropping 8 -> 6 in the Audit tier, printed the warning to a console that does not exist, then overwrote the baseline so the next run had nothing left to compare against. The child now returns its shrink list and skip names in the JSON payload and the parent reprints them. Verified by planting a baseline of 99:

  suites that ran FEWER assertions than last time in Audit Mode:
    Repo invariants (rkt3/z6k): 99 -> 6

Nine skip names now surface from the audit half that were previously swallowed.

Rule 10 is updated in docs/PRE-RELEASE.md: this makes it one command per machine on a normal Windows install, and changes nothing about the sandbox, whose Audit Mode half still needs UAC enabled in-guest and a restart.

title: gitignored-unique and repo-health run byte-identical walks looking for the same .git directories
description:
FOUND 2026-08-29 while closing 3l8, which named these two as walking the tree
"again for their own reasons". They are not different reasons. They are the
same walk, written twice.

  finders/gitignored-unique.finder.ps1  Find-SgnGitRepoRoots
  finders/repo-health.finder.ps1        Find-PkoGitRepoRoots

Compared line by line: same default root ($env:USERPROFILE), same default
maxDepth 6, same Test-Path on (Join-Path $dir '.git') so a .git FILE counts as
well as a directory, same Get-ChildItem -Directory -Force with .git excluded
from descent, same -ErrorVariable capture into New-Unreadable. The only
difference is that Sgn counts $examined and Pko does not.

Measured in the same run that produced 3l8's numbers:

  gitignored-unique   19.3 s
  repo-health         14.1 s

One walk instead of two should take roughly one of those off the summed engine
time, and both are singleton units today so they can be a walk group with no
new mechanism.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE IN 3l8. Invoke-SharedTreeWalk harvests FILE names and
extensions. '.git' is usually a directory, so it needs a marker kind that
matches container children too -- Register-SharedWalkHarvest -entryNames, and
one extra branch in the child loop. That is a small extension to code that was
just measured and tested, and doing it at release time would have put an
untested traversal change in the same commit as a verified one.

TWO THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE LOST, both already true of the code being replaced:
  * a .git FILE (worktrees, submodules) counts as a repo, not just a directory
  * these two walks have NO maxDirs cap and NO skip list, unlike the reclaim
    group. Sharing them with the reclaim walk is NOT the move: different depth
    (6 vs 8) and different pruning means a different question, and merging them
    would change what is covered rather than how fast it is covered. They share
    with EACH OTHER and nothing else.

local-only-credentials is separately mentioned in 3l8 and does NOT belong here:
it walks Get-Ho2DefaultRoots, a machine-wide root set, not the home directory.
notes: CORRECTION to the close reason's test count. It says 'Tests 1980 -> 1996 (16 new)'. Wrong: 1996 was never observed. The elevated run that reported 1980 had ALREADY picked up this issue's 16 new assertions (its shared-walk suite reported 58, not 42), so 1980 is the WITH-lxl number, not the before. Correct accounting: 1739 unelevated without lxl; 1964 elevated without lxl; 1980 elevated with lxl. Elevation is +225 of that, lxl is +16. Caught by diffing the two elevated runs' per-suite summaries and finding them identical, which they should not have been if one predated the change.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.9.3. The two walks are one walk, and the finding that came out of
it is bigger than the issue was about.

WHAT THE ISSUE ASKED FOR, and got: Register-SharedWalkHarvest gained a third
harvest kind, -entryNames, matching a child whether it is a file or a
directory. Both git finders now call Invoke-SharedTreeWalk and both carry
-walkGroup 'git-repos', so the renderer sends them in one engine call and the
second is served from the memo in about a millisecond.

Both properties the issue named are held:
* a .git FILE still counts as a repo - asserted directly with a linked-worktree
  fixture, and asserted NEGATIVELY too (a marker name would have missed every
  ordinary clone, so the suite checks .git is registered as an entry name and
  is NOT a marker name)
* no maxDirs cap and no skip list - maxDirs is passed as [int]::MaxValue
  rather than left to default to 15,000, which also keeps this out of the
  reclaim group's cache entry. Asserted: reclaim-node's walkGroup differs
  from these two.

WHAT THE ISSUE DID NOT KNOW. The two walkers used Get-ChildItem -Directory
with no reparse-point test, so they followed the legacy junctions every
Windows home directory has - My Documents, Local Settings, Application Data.
They were reporting the same repository once per alias that reached it:

    27 paths reported for 14 real repositories

Five projects under Documents\GitHub listed twice; several under
AppData\Local\Temp listed four times. Depth 6 was the only thing keeping it
finite. Both finders were affected, so repo-health listed the same
uncommitted work four times and gitignored-unique the same never-pushed
files four times, with nothing to say they were one repository.

That is why the timing is 60.0 s -> 6.6 s rather than the ~2x sharing
predicts: three quarters of the 31,921 directories the old walk listed were
the same directories under another name. 8,645 now.

NO REAL REPO WAS LOST, and that is measured, not argued. Every one of the 13
dropped paths is opened with GetFinalPathNameByHandle and resolved to a
directory still in the list -- test\sandbox\git-walk-equivalence-probe.ps1,
which also refuses to pass if it found no repositories at all.

Tests 1980 -> 1996 (16 new). Full suite green.

FILED FROM THIS WORK:
* vanish-uninstaller-127o (P2 bug) - a junction pointing OUTSIDE the walk root
  is now skipped with no record. Inside the root nothing is missed; outside it
  the scan should say could-not-look and stays silent instead. Affects the
  reclaim group shipped in 0.9.2 identically. The resolver is already written
  and proven in the probe.
* vanish-uninstaller-e6gn (P1) - answering 4v8's "check reclaim-package-caches
  first" note: it walks the home directory SEVEN times, one recursive
  Get-ChildItem per marker per cache spec. That is this same defect a third
  time and the largest instance, and it is the scan's tail.

title: Hygiene scan should schedule by measured duration, not unit size
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-29, after 3l8 shipped largest-unit-first scheduling.

The scan schedules walk units biggest-first, where "biggest" is HOW MANY
CHECKS are in the unit. That was the only measure available before the disk
has been walked, and it did help: same run, 92.3 s in registry order against
81.5 s largest-first, with summed engine time unchanged at 222.0 / 220.5 s.
The whole 10.8 s came from not starting the second-largest unit last.

WHAT IT DID NOT DO IS REMOVE THE TAIL. It moved it. Driving the real panel
afterwards:

  58504 ms  duplicate-content        finished at  78.1 s
  50301 ms  the four reclaim checks  finished at  50.6 s
  45478 ms  reclaim-package-caches   finished at 100.7 s   <- scan ends here
  31515 ms  local-only-credentials   finished at  31.8 s

reclaim-package-caches is ONE check taking 45 s. Sorted by unit size it goes
behind a four-check group, lands last, and everything waits on it. The largest
unit is not the longest job.

THE FIX, and why it is not free: schedule by how long each check took LAST
time. That means persisting per-check durations, which raises three questions
this issue exists to answer rather than assume.

  * WHERE. store.js writes to the state directory, which mp4 established is
    locked to administrators once Vanish has run elevated - so an unelevated
    session could not record its own timings. A timing is not engine input and
    does not want that lock. It may belong with the purely-local settings
    named in mp4's close reason.
  * WHAT ON A FIRST RUN. There is no history, so the first scan is scheduled
    by unit size exactly as now. That is a fallback, not a defect, and should
    be visible as one.
  * WHAT WHEN THE DISK CHANGED. A duration is a claim about the machine as it
    was. Clone a large repository and last week's timings are wrong; the
    scheduler should degrade to a worse ORDER, never to a wrong RESULT. Nothing
    about correctness may depend on the estimate.

WORTH CHECKING FIRST, because it may be smaller: reclaim-package-caches walks
its own tree at maxDepth 4 from a different root set, so it did not join the
user-tree walk group. If its roots overlap the home directory in practice, it
may belong in the group - which removes the tail rather than reordering
around it.

NOT A CORRECTNESS ISSUE. Every ordering produces the same 13 results; this is
only about how long the person waits.
notes:

cross-run subtraction errors in one day. Pool 3, shared walks, largest unit
first, WALL 59.9 s, summed 148.7 s:

     40.0 s  local-only-credentials
     35.3 s  duplicate-content
     24.0 s  reclaim-archives+reclaim-flutter+reclaim-gradle+reclaim-node
     19.1 s  reclaim-package-caches
     14.5 s  redirect-variables
     12.6 s  gitignored-unique+repo-health
      1.6 s  duplicate-installs
      0.8 s  path-hygiene
      0.8 s  profile-list

CONTENTION IS NOT THE STORY. Same pass at pool 1 / 2 / 3: summed 136.8 /
143.4 / 145.1 s, wall 136.8 / 78.4 / 58.1 s. Running three at once inflates
each check by 6.1% and cuts wall clock by 2.35x. The pool is fine.

it is compared against is noise.

FOR THIS ISSUE: the defect it describes is still real and now has honest
numbers. Largest-unit-first puts the four-check group (24.0 s) first and leaves
local-only-credentials (40.0 s, a singleton) to land late. Wall 59.9 s against

building timing persistence and arguing with the mp4 settings lock over it.
close_reason:
CLOSED WITHOUT BUILDING IT, on the measurements this issue itself asked for.

The prize is about 10 seconds. Measured in one run with every unit reported: wall 59.9 s against a theoretical floor of max(40.0, 148.7/3) = 49.6 s. That is what PERFECT scheduling would buy, and duration-aware scheduling would not be perfect.

The 10.8 s this issue was filed on does not reproduce. Re-measured after lxl added a second walk group: nine units, 82.2 s in registry order against 81.8 s largest-first - 0.4 s, which is noise on this machine. The original figure was a property of one particular unit count, which is this issue's own point about size being a weak proxy for duration, arriving earlier than expected.

The cost is not 10 seconds of work. It needs per-check durations persisted somewhere, and mp4 established that the state directory is administrator-only once Vanish has run elevated - so an unelevated session could not record its own timings. That is a real design problem to solve for a saving that is inside the run-to-run variance of this machine (the identical 13 checks summed 210.4 s and 136.8 s hours apart, purely file-system cache warmth).

WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED THE SCAN, for whoever reopens this: sharing walks removed real work (3l8, lxl, e6gn), and the tail turned out to be a single check nobody had profiled (o1mj - which was not slow, it was broken). Scheduling was never where the time was.

Reopen only if the per-check profile changes shape - for example if one unit grows past duplicate-content and local-only-credentials, which are 35-40 s each and set the floor.

title: Hygiene finders should share one walk of the disk, not take four
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-28 after lhf. Wall clock for all thirteen checks is 103.7 s at concurrency 3; summed engine time is 264.6 s. What is left is structural rather than per-finder.

FOUR RECLAIM FINDERS WALK THE SAME TREE. reclaim-node (38.8 s), reclaim-archives (17.2 s), reclaim-flutter (19.2 s) and reclaim-gradle (18.4 s) each run their own stack walk from $env:USERPROFILE, and all four hit the SAME 15,000-directory cap and report the same 80 blind locations. That is four passes over one disk to answer four questions about the same directories, ~94 s of the 265 s total.

Plus local-only-credentials and gitignored-unique and repo-health, which walk it again for their own reasons.

THE FIX AND WHY IT IS NOT SMALL: a shared enumeration only helps if the finders run IN ONE PROCESS. They currently get one engine call each - that is what renderer/hygiene.js does deliberately, so results render as they land and one slow check does not hide twelve fast ones. Sharing a walk means going back to one call, which means the progressive UI has to come from progress events instead.

The plumbing exists: runPowerShell already takes an onProgress callback, scanner.ps1 already has Write-ScanProgress, and main.js already parses the @@VANISH-PROGRESS@@ marker off stderr. So Invoke-HygieneScan would emit one progress record per finder and the panel would drive its per-check status list from those instead of from thirteen promises.

DO NOT lose these two properties in the process:
- a partial run is never decided. hygiene-panel-verify.js asserts that a half-finished run names no terminal state; with one call the same rule applies to the progress stream.
- a check that did not run is could-not-look, not absent. Today a rejected per-finder call is synthesised into an unreadable result in the renderer; with one call that has to happen in Invoke-HygieneScan, which already does it for a finder that throws.

SEPARATELY, and possibly first because it is smaller: duplicate-content at 56.4 s is now the floor no concurrency can go below. It is the only check over 40 s.
close_reason:
Done, shipped in 0.9.2.

MEASURED FIRST, and the issue's own framing turned out to be wrong. It said a
shared walk "only helps if the finders run IN ONE PROCESS", so the fix meant
going back to ONE engine call for all thirteen and rebuilding the progressive
UI on progress events. That would have been a regression: summed engine time
is 222 s, and one serial call is 222 s of wall clock against 92 s for the pool.
The concurrency is worth more than the shared walk.

What was actually needed was one call for the FOUR, not for the thirteen. The
progress-event plumbing was never touched.

The four walks were one walk. Same root, same depth 8, same 15,000 cap, and
the same fifteen-entry skip list written in four different orders - differing
only in what each picked up: package.json, pubspec.yaml, gradlew, .zip.

  one walk of the home directory                  12.4 s
  the same walk, all four markers                 12.4 s   (free)
  the four checks, four engine calls              66.2 s
  the four checks, one call, shared walk          28.2 s

  thirteen checks, one call per check             107.2 s   <- 0.9.1
  thirteen checks, shared walk                     92.3 s
  thirteen checks, shared walk, largest first      81.5 s

BOTH PROPERTIES THE ISSUE NAMED ARE HELD, with assertions:

* a partial run is never decided - unchanged; hygieneDecision is still only set
  after every unit settles, and hygiene-panel-verify still asserts it.
* a check that did not run is could-not-look, not absent - and grouping created
  a NEW way to lose this that a one-finder call did not have: three results
  coming back for a call that asked about four. The fourth would be MISSING
  rather than FAILED. The loop is now over the unit rather than over what came
  back, and the shortfall is reported as its own case, distinct from the whole
  call failing.

THE SCHEDULING IS A PARTIAL WIN, stated as one. Largest-unit-first moved the
tail off the group (92.3 -> 81.5 s, same run, summed engine time unchanged) but
did not remove it: reclaim-package-caches, one check at 45 s, is now last.
Unit size is a proxy for duration and this is where it is weak. Filed as
vanish-uninstaller-4v8 with the numbers attached, including the cheaper thing
to check first - whether reclaim-package-caches' roots overlap the home
directory enough to join the walk group outright.

VERIFICATION
  test/shared-walk-verify.ps1          42 passed, 0 failed (NEW)
  test/hygiene-panel-verify.js         66 passed, 0 failed (+24)
  test/finder-reclaim-verify.ps1       43 passed, 0 failed
  test/sandbox/hygiene-scheduling-probe.js   the three-way table (NEW)
  test/sandbox/hygiene-wallclock-probe.js    app-level wall clock (NEW)

The control that matters: every check run BOTH ways - sharing the walk and
owning it - compared on state, counts, byte totals and finding ids. Identical.
With a negative control asserting the fixture produced findings at all, so the
comparison cannot pass by being empty on both sides.

STILL THE FLOOR, unchanged and now the whole story: duplicate-content at 54-60 s.
It hashes file contents, and no amount of concurrency goes below one check.

title: run-all.ps1 reports a MISSING suite file identically to a suite that crashed
description:
Split out of soi, which is now closed with its cause found.

When test/phase2-verify.ps1 was quarantined out from under the runner on 2026-08-27, run-all.ps1 printed 'did not report a result (needs Full Mode, or it crashed)' and listed the suite as NOT RUN. That is the same output it produces for a suite that started and died mid-file. The two want completely different responses - one is 'your working tree is missing a tracked file', the other is 'go read the log' - and the message actively suggests the wrong one first by offering 'needs Full Mode' as the leading explanation.

FIX: Test-Path the suite file before invoking it, and report a missing file as its own state with the path. This is the same shape as the skip-naming work of 2026-08-20: a runner that collapses two different non-results into one line is how a green total came to hide a load-bearing skip.

Cheap, and it would have turned a two-hour investigation into one line of output.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-02, in two places.

AT RUN TIME: run-all.ps1 now Test-Paths each suite file before invoking it. A missing file prints its own state with the path -- 'SUITE FILE MISSING', then 'this is a working-tree problem rather than a test result' -- and the summary lists it as FILE MISSING rather than NOT RUN. A suite that actually started and died still reports 'NOT RUN (needs Full Mode, or it crashed -- read its log)'. The two states no longer collapse into one line, and the line that led with the wrong explanation is gone.

A missing suite also exits NON-ZERO even when nothing failed. A green exit code on a run that silently tested less than its own registration list says is the same defect as an unnamed skip, and worse for being invisible to CI.

AT TEST TIME, which is earlier and cheaper: test/repo-invariants-verify.js parses the suite rows out of run-all.ps1 and asserts every registered path exists. That fails in under a second instead of surfacing 40 minutes into a VM run. Verified by planting the defect: moving test/phase4-verify.ps1 aside produced

  registered but not on disk: System Clean scans (4) -> test\phase4-verify.ps1
  FAIL  every registered suite file exists (55 checked, 1 missing)

and restoring it went green. The row-count assertion guards the guard: if the parser ever stops matching the registration syntax it finds zero rows and fails, rather than passing on an empty set.

title: [bug] Shared runtimes suite (ht8) is flaky on a real machine: 149 of 72 rows about one run in three
description:
MEASURED, not inferred. test/runtimes-verify.js's last assertion - 'turning it off restores the default list' - fails intermittently on the development machine. Three consecutive runs on 2026-08-27 gave PASS (72 of 72), PASS (72 of 72), FAIL (149 of 72). It is not a new regression and it is not caused by the machine-hygiene work: an earlier single run with the new lib/findings.js script tag removed from index.html also passed, but one sample per side is not evidence and the three-run sequence above shows the failure occurs WITH the tag present in only one run of three.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A FLAKY TEST NORMALLY WOULD: 149 is the row count INCLUDING components; 72 is applications only. So in the failing run the table is showing every component after the user unchecked 'Show components'. If that is real rather than a harness artifact, the operator sees 77 Visual C++ redistributable rows reappear in a list they just filtered - which is the exact noise 7oo.3 exists to remove.

WHAT IS KNOWN:
- The two handlers in renderer/core.js (chk-show-components at ~1150, chk-only-runtimes at ~1163) are synchronous and read correctly. showComponents is module-level, so a LATE filterAndRenderApps() would render 72, not 149.
- 149 is therefore the state BEFORE the toggle took effect, which means either the change handler did not run, or a render that started earlier finished later.
- The suite waits a fixed time after load before driving the DOM. That is the AGP-4 / AGP-18 pattern this project has been bitten by repeatedly, and it is the first thing to rule out.
- Earlier assertions in the same suite toggle successfully, so listeners ARE attached by then.
- The VM logs (test/logs/68A2CEC3, test/logs/D0B08B54) show 3 of 3 passing, because a fresh VM has three applications and no components. This can only be reproduced on a machine with a real install history.

DO NOT fix by raising the fixed wait. Per AGP-20, the next change here should add EVIDENCE - instrument what the row count and showComponents value actually are at the moment of the assertion, and whether a render is in flight - rather than be a fourth guess at the cause.
notes:
INSTRUMENTED 2026-09-02, not fixed. Staying open deliberately: the flake has not reproduced since, so there is nothing to verify a fix against.

What changed is that the next failure will name its own cause instead of being a fourth guess. The assertion now records, per step: the row count, the caption, both checkbox states, whether each dispatch was actually HEARD by a listener (counted by our own listener -- dispatchEvent returns true on a node whose startup listener was lost, so the return value proves nothing), whether the checkbox nodes were still the same objects afterwards, and whether a second read 750 ms later settles.

That last one separates the two causes that want opposite fixes and that the old failure line could not tell apart: SETTLED means a read racing a render, which is this test's fault; STILL WRONG means the state is wrong, which is a product bug.

READING OF THE EVIDENCE SO FAR, and it is a hypothesis rather than a finding: 149 rows is exactly the state where runtimesOnly cleared and showComponents did not -- i.e. the FIRST dispatch took effect and the SECOND did not. Both handlers in renderer/core.js are synchronous and renderTable writes innerHTML inline, so a late render cannot produce 149 and raising the fixed wait would only hide it. The leading candidate is that something replaced the chk-show-components node, discarding the listener wired at startup, which is why the node-identity check is in there.

Do not act on that paragraph as though it were established. It is what the instrumentation is there to test.

The assertion-count baseline guard filed under this issue is live in both tiers and was verified this session by planting a baseline of 99, which reported 'Repo invariants (rkt3/z6k): 99 -> 6'. It also caught a real 8 -> 6 drop in the Audit tier -- and exposed that the de-elevated half had no console to print it on, which is now fixed (see pnor).
PARKED ON A REPRODUCTION 2026-09-04, deliberately, and nothing has changed to
justify guessing again.

The instrumentation from 2026-09-02 is in place: the next failure records, per
step, the row count, the caption, both checkbox states, whether each dispatch
was actually HEARD by a listener, whether the checkbox nodes were still the
same objects afterwards, and whether a second read 750 ms later settles. That
last one separates the two causes that want opposite fixes -- SETTLED means a
read racing a render, which is this test's fault; STILL WRONG means a product
bug.

It has not reproduced since. Per AGP-20 the next change here must add EVIDENCE
rather than be a fourth guess at the cause, and there is no new evidence, so
the correct action is none.

This ran green in every full-suite pass this session. That is not proof it is
fixed -- it failed one run in three when it was seen, so a run of passes is the
expected shape of the bug too. It stays open, and it is the ONLY open issue
whose next step is 'wait for it to happen again'.

title: Reclaim: Windows component store via DISM (WinSxS reclaimable packages)
description: From docs/history/HANDOFF-2026-08-21.md Module 1 (RECLAIM) table, deferred out of vanish-uninstaller-piu on purpose - DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /AnalyzeComponentStore and /StartComponentCleanup both need elevation (Full Mode), and the reclaim-*.finder.ps1 pattern used for piu's five finders (fixture directories under a temp root, driven through hygiene-scan) cannot exercise DISM meaningfully - the verification venue for this one is a real elevated run against the actual component store (or a VM snapshot), not a constructed fixture tree. Real-machine evidence: 22.32 GB component store, 14 reclaimable packages. Rebuild cost per piu rule 2: a superseded package DISM already flags reclaimable is normally cheap/irreversible-but-safe (Windows Update supersession, not user data), but this needs its own costClass story distinct from the other five finders' project-marker regeneration, since there is no package.json-equivalent here - the marker is DISM's own analysis output. Should register needsElevation $true on Register-Finder (see finders/_loader.ps1), which none of the piu finders needed.
notes:
KILLED 2026-09-04, measured rather than argued. Four findings, and the second
one alone would settle it.

1. WINDOWS ALREADY SHIPS IT, THREE WAYS. DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image
/StartComponentCleanup is the operation. Disk Cleanup exposes the same job as
'Windows Update Cleanup' -- VolumeCaches key 'Update Cleanup', CLSID
{606B3777-3051-401F-974A-E66ACA82A3A3}, handler scavengeui.dll, Autorun=3. And
Storage Sense is enabled on this machine, so it fires without a user.

2. THE FEATURE CLEANED UP AFTER ITSELF WHILE THE ISSUE SAT OPEN. This issue was
filed on 22.32 GB and 14 reclaimable packages, from HANDOFF-2026-08-21.
Measured today, nobody having touched it:

  Windows Explorer Reported Size of Component Store : 21.27 GB
  Actual Size of Component Store                    : 16.08 GB
    Shared with Windows                             :  8.21 GB
    Backups and Disabled Features                   :  7.84 GB
  Date of Last Cleanup    : 2026-09-02 18:58:57
  Number of Reclaimable Packages : 2
  Component Store Cleanup Recommended : Yes

Get-ScheduledTask \Microsoft\Windows\Servicing\StartComponentCleanup:
LastRunTime 09/02/2026 18:58:38, LastResult 0. Windows ran it unattended two
days ago and took 12 of the 14 packages. Free space on C: is 295.9 of 499.3 GB;
there is no pressure here either.

3. INV-1 CANNOT BE HONOURED, for a stronger version of the reason that cut 0ng.
pnputil destroys one FileRepository copy. Component cleanup deletes HARDLINKED
payload and commits a servicing transaction in the TrustedInstaller-owned
COMPONENTS hive. Measured: fsutil hardlink list on System32\kernel32.dll
returns both the System32 and the WinSxS name -- that fan-out IS DISM's own
'Shared with Windows: 8.21 GB' and the whole 21.27-vs-16.08 gap. There is no
file set the vault could hold that puts any of it back, because the
authoritative state is a registry hive and the mutation does not run in our
process. /ResetBase additionally makes every installed update permanently
non-uninstallable.

OUR OWN CODE ALREADY SAYS THIS BY NAME, verified: Test-ProtectedDestination
blocks %SystemRoot%\WinSxS (scanner.ps1:3560), quarantine asks the same
predicate rather than a copy of the list, and test/security-verify.ps1:404 pins
the refusal. Building the removal half means DELETING A SECURITY ASSERTION THAT
SHIPS TODAY.

4. NONE OF THE THREE ASSETS APPLIES. Servicing packages do not join the
installed-program map, so there is no 'belongs to something no longer
installed' claim to make. The vault refuses the location. And the tier/consent
half is already spent: ag0 shells dism /Online /Get-Packages today (189
packages measured, 103 Installed / 86 Staged) and reports Audit Mode's
inability with a displayable reason rather than silently shrinking the list.

ONE MORE HONESTY PROBLEM. DISM reports a package COUNT, not bytes, and there is
no reclaimable-size figure obtainable without performing the destructive
operation. The headline would have to read '2 packages, unknown size' -- and
per finders/_contract.ps1, costClass 'unknown' sorts last anyway.

NOT BLOCKED BY THIS KILL: the needsElevation parameter on Register-Finder
already exists and defaults false (finders/_loader.ps1:98). It stays available
for any future elevated finder.
close_reason: KILL. Windows ships it three ways and ran it unattended two days ago - the 14 reclaimable packages this was filed on measured 2 today with nobody touching it. INV-1 cannot be honoured for a stronger version of 0ng's reason: the payload is hardlinked and the authoritative state is the TrustedInstaller-owned COMPONENTS hive. Our own code already blocks WinSxS by name with a shipping test, so building it means deleting a security assertion.

title: Reclaim: orphaned WSL/VM images by age + no-user-files
description: From docs/history/HANDOFF-2026-08-21.md Module 1 (RECLAIM) table, deferred out of vanish-uninstaller-piu on purpose - needs elevation (wsl -l -v, and possibly disk-image mounting to check contents) and a different verification venue than piu's fixture-based finder suite (a real WSL install to test against, not a temp-dir fixture). Detect by: 'wsl -l -v' for distro list + age since last use, and 'contained no source' - i.e. no user-authored files inside, only OS/package content - before ever proposing removal, matching the piu rule-2 spirit (state the rebuild cost: a distro reachable via 'wsl --install -d <name>' is cheap to recreate, but ANY user file inside it that is not mirrored elsewhere is not, so this needs its own rebuild-cost story, not piu's). Real-machine evidence: 12 GB, cold 6 weeks, contained no source. Must reuse finders/_contract.ps1 and finders/_never-touch.ps1 (Test-NeverTouchPath, Find-ToolchainConsumers) exactly like the five piu finders do.
notes:
KILLED 2026-09-04, on real-machine evidence. Three findings, and the first one
alone retires the issue.

1. THE PREMISE HAS EXPIRED. This was filed on a 12 GB WSL distro, cold six
weeks, containing no source. Measured today: 'wsl --list --all' reports
'Windows Subsystem for Linux has no installed distributions',
HKCU:\...\Lxss exists with ZERO subkeys, and a sweep of every file over 1 GB
on C: and D: (51 files) found no ext4.vhdx at all. The operator unregistered it
before the finder was ever written. Hyper-V is Disabled at every feature with
an empty ProgramData store; VMware, Docker Desktop and VirtualBox are absent.
The ELEVATION this issue was deferred for buys nothing, because there is
nothing behind it to see.

2. THE JOIN IT WOULD MAKE, bu2 ALREADY MAKES. Running Vanish's own shipped
attribution pipeline read-only against this machine (238 top-level dirs, 150
installed apps) returns C:\Users\Anand\AppData\Local\Genymobile and
C:\ProgramData\Genymobile as state 'unattributed'. Both are already in
sizeCandidates, both are already measured, both are already quarantine-able
through the vault, with no new code. That is 2.103 GB, 1.70 GB of it a .vmdk
from a Genymotion install that is gone -- along with VirtualBox, which is why
~\.VirtualBox and VBoxNetAdp6.sys / VBoxNetLwf.sys also survive. A second,
image-specific finder to rediscover what bu2 already reports is the redundant-
nonsense case the scope standard names.

3. A CORRECT FINDER WOULD REFUSE EVERY OTHER IMAGE HERE, and one of the refusals
is a live hazard. 17.17 GB of Android AVDs plus 5.14 GB of system images belong
to Android Studio 2025.3, installed, with emulator -list-avds returning all
three and no .ini/.avd split-brain. And a 7.70 GB claudevm.bundle\rootfs.vhdx
belongs to installed Claude Desktop -- appearing at BOTH
AppData\Roaming\Claude\... and
AppData\Local\Packages\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\LocalCache\Roaming\Claude\...
while fsutil hardlink list returns ONE entry. VERIFIED DIRECTLY: it is one
physical file surfaced twice by MSIX AppData redirection. A path-walking image
finder double-counts 7.7 GB as 15.4 GB and could offer to remove 'the
duplicate', breaking a running program. A finder whose only correct output on
this machine is 'refuse everything, plus one thing bu2 already told you' is not
a feature.

INV-1 WAS CHECKED AND IS NOT THE BLOCKER, but it is not free. Get-VaultContentHash
caps at 256 MB / 2000 files for DIRECTORIES ONLY; a single file is hashed
unconditionally, measured at 717.5 MB/s against the real 1.701 GB system.vmdk,
so a 20 GB VHDX costs ~28.5 s to hash and ~28.5 s again to verify on restore.
Quarantining the folder instead exceeds the directory cap, so restore succeeds
but reports 'not verified' -- INV-1's letter holds, its spirit degrades. And
because the vault lives on C:, a cross-volume image falls to
Move-ItemTransactional's copy-verify-delete path, so reclaiming 20 GB from D:
makes C: 20 GB fuller, which is the opposite of the point.

IF THIS IS EVER REOPENED, the narrowest defensible version is not an image
finder at all. It is one positive test bolted onto bu2: a virtualisation
product registers a machine whose config file points at a path, and the product
is gone. ~\.VirtualBox\VirtualBox.xml's MachineRegistry on this machine still
points at the Genymotion .vbox -- a parseable, product-authored claim of
ownership, which is the evidence lib/attribution.js's honesty rule requires
before saying 'orphaned' rather than 'unattributed'. It would refuse: any image
under a product still installed; anything found by walking the filesystem for
*.vhdx or *.vmdk (shape-based detection is what would have eaten the Claude
VHDX); anything cross-volume from the vault; and any 'contains no user files'
claim that needs the image mounted, since a mount that fails must read as
could-not-look rather than clean.
close_reason: KILL. The 12 GB WSL distro this was filed on no longer exists - wsl reports no distributions and Lxss has zero subkeys. The one real orphan on the machine (2.1 GB of Genymotion residue) is already reported by bu2 as unattributed and already quarantine-able. Every other large image belongs to installed software, including a Claude VHDX that appears at two paths but is one physical file - a path-walking finder would double-count it and could break a running program.

title: Rules as data: new finding types are rule files, not edits to scanner.ps1
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, section 2, and it is the thing that keeps the seam from silently closing again.

Vanish ALREADY reads CleanerML (7sl, shipped 2026-08-19 - an MIT reader, definitions never vendored). Every finding in the hygiene suite should be a rule file consumed by that machinery, so a new artifact type is a DATA CHANGE rather than another few hundred lines in a file that is already 41% of the codebase.

The open question this issue exists to answer: CleanerML's own vocabulary covers file deletion by glob and walk. It has no vocabulary for "the package.json that regenerates this is visible", "this variable is unset", or "this repo cannot be read". So either the rule format is extended locally (a Vanish dialect, kept separate from anything GPL - the licence boundary in CLAUDE.md still applies), or these finders stay code and only the path-shaped ones become data. Decide with a real example in hand, after 5p5.
close_reason: Decided in adrs/0003-rules-as-data-only-where-the-rule-is-a-path.md, with real examples in hand as the issue required. TWO HALVES, and they got different answers. MECHANISM (yes, shipped): a finder is a FILE. finders/_loader.ps1 discovers finders/*.finder.ps1, each registers itself, and scanner.ps1 never learns a finder's name - nine finders were added and that file gained a dot-source block and two dispatch cases. That alone satisfies the handoff's stated requirement that a new artifact type not be a change to a 7,870-line file. RULE BODIES (no, on evidence): held against the nine finders now written, seven cannot be expressed as paths at all - git check-ignore exit codes, log @{u}..HEAD, size-then-SHA256 grouping, 'this variable is unset', 'this repo returned dubious ownership'. The two that nearly can (node_modules, *.zip beside an extracted dir) are a path PLUS a sibling-marker condition, and that condition is the entire safety property from Module 1 rule 1 - a format that could say 'node_modules' but not 'only when package.json is beside it' would express exactly the dangerous half, which is worse than no format. Extending CleanerML locally would also move the aeu three-state guarantee out of the type system (New-FinderResult having no -state parameter) and into an interpreter where a new rule kind can forget it. What stays data: CleanerML proper unchanged, the never-touch path list, and per-finder pattern tables at the top of their own file. GPL boundary untouched - no definitions vendored, no dialect published that invites them to be.

title: Module 4 REPORT: one artifact per run
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, Module 4.

One artifact per run, saying: "You can reclaim X GB. Here is the breakdown, the rebuild cost of each, and the N things that are wrong but free."

The last clause is the one that makes it different from every cleaner's summary screen. "Wrong but free" is Module 2's output - unset redirect variables, duplicate PATH entries, unreadable repos - none of which reclaims a byte and all of which is worth more than the bytes.

Depends on the rebuild-cost field from piu and the hygiene findings from pko. Rules as data (see the CleanerML reader, 7sl): a new finding type should be a rule file, not a change to a 7,870-line script.
close_reason: Shipped as lib/hygiene-report.js, a pure module (no fs, no Electron, no IPC), 39 assertions in test/hygiene-report-verify.js (verified independently by me: 39 passed, 0 failed). 'Wrong but free' is a first-class top-level section with its own count, rendered AHEAD of the reclaim breakdown - keyed on module='hygiene' rather than a bytes==0 heuristic, so unset redirect variables and duplicate PATH entries cannot be buried by a byte-ranked list. Sections are built by filtering the already-ranked findings without re-sorting, so there is no second place for a size sort to creep in. Unreadable locations appear in the headline, not a footer: a report claiming 'you can reclaim 40 GB' while eleven trees were unreadable is making a claim it cannot support. Disagreements render as a banner above the headline. formatBytes uses binary units, matching both PowerShell's 1GB/1MB (which produced the handoff's evidence numbers) and Explorer, with the reasoning in a comment. NOTE: the agent caught an inversion in my brief - I had written that cheap should rank BELOW irreplaceable; rankFindings sorts ascending so cheap-to-rebuild comes first, which is correct (the top of the list is what is safest to offer). It tested the real invariant in both size directions rather than my wrong wording.

title: Module 1 RECLAIM: detect by project marker, and state the rebuild cost
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, Module 1. Built THIRD, after rescue and hygiene.

TWO RULES THAT DECIDE THE DESIGN:

1. DETECT BY PROJECT MARKER, NEVER BY FOLDER NAME. Only propose deleting node_modules when the package.json that regenerates it is visible. Same for pubspec.yaml -> build/ and .dart_tool/, gradlew -> .gradle/ and android/app/build/.

2. EVERY PROPOSAL MUST STATE ITS REBUILD COST. "npm install, ~2 min" versus "re-download 12.9 GB". THAT NUMBER DECIDES, NOT THE SIZE. A 23 GB node_modules that rebuilds in two minutes and a 12 GB VM image that took a day to configure are not the same offer, and a cleaner that ranks by bytes gets it exactly backwards.

MEASURED ON THE REAL MACHINE:
  Node artifacts        23 GB in one repo, 614 MB after reinstall - 37x cruft
  Flutter/Dart          5.6 GB
  Gradle/Android        5.8 GB
  Package caches        npm 4.5 GB, Gradle 14.7 GB, pip 570 MB
  Orphaned WSL images   12 GB, cold 6 weeks, contained no source
  Redundant archives    1.8 GB (a *.zip beside an extracted dir of the same name)
  Installers for installed software  1.2 GB (filename matched to registry DisplayName)
  Windows standard      22.32 GB component store, 14 reclaimable packages via DISM

Split into per-finder issues once 5p5 has proved the shape. Filed as one issue because the two rules above are what make it a coherent module rather than eight cleaners.
notes: Implemented and verified 2026-08-27: finders/reclaim-node.finder.ps1, reclaim-flutter.finder.ps1, reclaim-gradle.finder.ps1, reclaim-package-caches.finder.ps1, reclaim-archives.finder.ps1, and test/finder-reclaim-verify.ps1 (43 assertions, 0 failed). All 5 register cleanly per finder-probe list (loadErrors: []). Rule 1 (marker, not folder name) has an explicit regression test per finder pair (node_modules/build without marker -> state 'nothing'). Rule 2 (rebuildCost) is enforced by New-Finding in code for non-audit actions and additionally self-imposed on every audit finding these 5 produce (asserted directly). aeu three-state discipline covered via an ACL-deny could-not-look fixture (SKIPs with a measured reason if the deny does not take effect on the running account, per the brief). Never-touch and Find-ToolchainConsumers wired per 4rn - package caches attach toolchain-consumer evidence rather than gating on it, since a cache's cost to refill does not depend on current consumers. WSL/VM images and DISM/WinSxS checks split into follow-ups as instructed: vanish-uninstaller-0h7 and vanish-uninstaller-cj9 (both need elevation + a different verification venue than fixture-based hygiene-scan). Files owned only; no shared files touched; no git commands run.
close_reason: Shipped as five finders (reclaim-node, reclaim-flutter, reclaim-gradle, reclaim-package-caches, reclaim-archives), audit-only, 43 assertions in test/finder-reclaim-verify.ps1 (verified independently by me: 43 passed, 0 failed, no skips - the could-not-look case ran for real via an ACL-deny fixture with the premise asserted first). BOTH RULES ENFORCED. Rule 1, detect by project marker never by folder name: the regression asserts that a node_modules with NO package.json beside it is NOT proposed, which is what stops this deleting somebody's data. Rule 2, every proposal states its rebuild cost: New-Finding THROWS when a removal-proposing finding omits rebuildCost, and the suite asserts the enforcement rather than the convention; every finding carries a costClass that is not 'unknown'. Ranking is by cost, not bytes - a 23 GB node_modules that rebuilds in two minutes and a 12 GB VM image that took a day to configure are not the same offer. Package caches are env-var-first then tool default, deliberately not marker-swept (a cache is not per-project), and use Find-ToolchainConsumers as EVIDENCE rather than as a gate. Archives corroborate with a top-level-entry-count check and state an honest caveat when it does not match. All helpers are per-file prefixed (PiuNode, PiuFlutter, ...) because every finder file shares one load scope. DEFERRED, as briefed, both needing elevation and a different verification venue: 0h7 (orphaned WSL/VM images) and cj9 (component store via DISM). LIMIT NOTED: default roots are $env:USERPROFILE rather than a machine-wide sweep, which is the issue's own 'split into per-finder issues once the shape is proved'.

title: Module 2 HYGIENE: find wrongness, not waste
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, Module 2. Built SECOND: cheap, high signal, zero risk. Nothing here deletes anything - it reports things that are wrong and free to fix.

Five checks, each with what it actually found on this machine:

  PATH hygiene - cross-scope duplicates, broken entries, entries under Downloads.
    Found: 27 user entries, 12 VERBATIM DUPLICATES of the machine PATH, 2 tools running from Downloads. After cleanup: 14 entries.
    Note the existing PATH cleaner (REQ-15) only finds entries whose directory does not exist. This is a different question and extends it.

  REDIRECT VARIABLES UNSET - GRADLE_USER_HOME, ANDROID_HOME, ANDROID_SDK_ROOT, npm_config_cache, PIP_CACHE_DIR.
    Found: ALL FIVE UNSET. Every dev tool had silently defaulted to C: since the machine was built. THIS SINGLE FINDING EXPLAINED MOST OF THE C: BULK. Highest signal-to-effort item in the whole document.

  REPO HEALTH - dirty, unpushed, and UNREADABLE.
    Found: 10 repos returning `dubious ownership` from a previous profile SID. Unreadable is the important state - see aeu, a repo that cannot be read is not a clean repo.

  ORPHANED ProfileList ENTRIES. Found: 12.

  DUPLICATE APP INSTALLS, both on PATH. Found: 2.4 GB - and one pair was INTENTIONAL. See 4rn before flagging any of these.
close_reason: Shipped as five separate finders (path-hygiene, redirect-variables, repo-health, profile-list, duplicate-installs), all audit-only, 78 assertions in test/finder-hygiene-verify.ps1 (verified independently by me: 78 passed, 0 failed, 1 named SKIP). Five files not one, because a finder is a file - that is what makes the sixth check a new file rather than an edit. PATH hygiene extends REQ-15 rather than duplicating it: the existing cleaner only finds entries whose directory is gone; this adds cross-scope verbatim duplicates against the machine PATH and entries running from Downloads, and the header states the difference. REDIRECT VARIABLES is the highest signal-to-effort item in the whole specification - it reports each unset variable WITH the default location the tool falls back to and the bytes currently sitting there, which is the finding that explained most of the C: bulk. DUPLICATE INSTALLS routes through Test-SameNameInstallsRedundant and always returns needs-confirmation, never redundant (4rn, the Antigravity case). Everything carries bytes=0 and costClass 'cheap' deliberately, so Module 4's 'wrong but free' section is not buried by a byte-ranked list. NAMED SKIP: reproducing a real dubious-ownership condition needs SeRestorePrivilege; the reason-naming branch is exercised via a deterministic forced git failure instead (a corrupt .git gitfile, verified against real git: 'fatal: invalid gitfile format', exit 128), so the code path runs, just not with that exact message. TWO POWERSHELL BUGS FOUND AND FIXED, both worth knowing: (1) 'if ($null -ne $override)' is FALSE for an empty array, because PowerShell's comparison operators filter element-wise and $null -ne @() returns @(), which is falsy - this silently made every empty-array override fall through to reading the real machine. Fixed with a membership test rather than a value test. (2) A [Parameter(Mandatory)] collection-typed parameter throws on an empty list without [AllowEmptyCollection()].

title: Module 3.3 RESCUE: content-hash dedup across trees, with a survivor manifest
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, Module 3. Used TWICE in the real cleanup: 41 duplicates inside phone backups, and 79 files duplicated between two trees.

Content hash, not name or size. The survivor manifest is the load-bearing half and is a hard requirement from the handoff:

  EVERY DESTRUCTIVE ACTION WRITES A MANIFEST - what was removed, and the path of the identical copy that survived.

That is what separates this from every dedup tool: after the run you can still answer "where did that file go" without restoring anything. It also satisfies aeu constraint 2 - the precondition (an identical copy really does still exist) is verified by comparison, in code, immediately before acting.
close_reason: Shipped as finders/duplicate-content.finder.ps1, audit-only, 30 assertions in test/finder-dedup-verify.ps1 (verified independently by me: 30 passed, 0 failed, no skips - the unreadable-file premise was constructible on this machine so assertions 3 and 4 ran for real). Two-pass by design: group by Length first, SHA256 only within size groups larger than one, because hashing every file on a drive to discover most are unique is the naive version and is unusably slow. Content decides identity, never name or size - a regression asserts that two files with the SAME name and SAME size but different content are NOT reported, which is the whole premise. THE SURVIVOR MANIFEST is the load-bearing half and round-trips: written, read back, survivor path and hash intact, so after a run you can answer 'where did that file go' without restoring anything. Survivor chosen by oldest LastWriteTimeUtc, tie-broken by shallowest path then ordinal compare, justified in a header comment rather than left as 'the tool picked one'. Assert-RemovalPrecondition is asserted to THROW on a missing survivor, a wrong size, and a matching size with a different hash. A never-touch copy is annotated removalEligible=false rather than dropped, so the refusal is visible. Also fixed a latent PowerShell bug in the finder's own evidence code: (X | Where-Object {...}).Count evaluates false-via-null when the pipeline collapses a single match to a bare object - the same scalar-unrolling class this project has been bitten by before.

title: Module 3.2 RESCUE: gitignored-and-unique - the true blast radius of a re-clone
description:
From HANDOFF-2026-08-21, Module 3. The generalisation of the credential scan (see the audit-only credential issue).

For any repo, list what the REMOTE DOES NOT HAVE. That set is the true blast radius of "just re-clone it" - the sentence everyone says before deleting a working tree, almost always without checking.

Audit-only in this release, same as its sibling. Obeys aeu's three-state contract: a repo whose remote cannot be reached is "could not look", never "nothing unique here".
close_reason: Shipped as finders/gitignored-unique.finder.ps1, audit-only, 35 assertions in test/finder-gitignored-verify.ps1 (verified independently by me: 35 passed, 0 failed, 1 named SKIP). Reports the true blast radius of 'just re-clone it': untracked-and-gitignored, untracked-and-never-added, uncommitted modifications, commits ahead of upstream, branches with NO upstream at all, and stashes - a stash being invisible to every other check and pure local-only work. Checks $LASTEXITCODE after every git call, never bare $?. No network fetch: it compares against the locally-known upstream ref and says so in the evidence, because a finder that silently goes to the network is a finder that hangs on a VPN. NAMED SKIP, not a silent pass: the dubious-ownership assertion needs SeRestorePrivilege to construct its fixture, so on an unelevated shell it reports SKIP with the measured reason. The detection branch is implemented and matches git's stderr text; only the fixture is elevation-gated. Same gap test/security-verify.ps1's z3s block already has.

title: Acceptance: run the definitions cleaner against a real BleachBit definitions set
description:
7sl shipped the CleanerML reader on 2026-08-19 with 61 engine assertions and 10 DOM assertions, all against fixture definitions this repo writes itself. What has never happened is a run against the real thing: BleachBit's own cleaners directory, several hundred files, written by people who did not have our reader in mind.

Needs a machine with BleachBit installed (the sandbox can install it via winget the same way it installs Chrome for 1qp).

What to look for, in order of how likely it is to be wrong:

1. VARIABLE COVERAGE. Our expansion handles ~, $foo, ${foo}, %foo%, $$foo$$ and the BleachBit pseudo-variables we know about. A definition using one we do not know resolves to nothing and the option silently does not appear. Count how many options come back with zero matches and check whether any of them SHOULD have matched.

2. THE WITHHELD LIST. Most real definitions use sqlite.vacuum, json or winreg somewhere, so expect a long 'not offered' note. Read it: if nearly every option is withheld, the honest conclusion is that this feature reaches less of the catalogue than it looks like it does, and PRE-RELEASE should say so.

3. SCALE. CleanerMlMaxMatches is 5000 per option. A browser cache will exceed it. Confirm the refusal reads as a refusal with a number, not as an empty section.

4. TIME. Every walk.* action is a recursive enumeration. Several hundred definitions on a real machine may take minutes; the scan reports progress but the number has never been measured.

Do NOT quarantine anything on a machine you care about without checking the restore first.
notes:
PARKED ON THE OPERATOR 2026-09-04, with the reason and the exact command.

BleachBit is not installed on this machine -- checked both Program Files paths.
This acceptance needs its real cleaners directory, several hundred definition
files written by people who did not have our reader in mind, which is the whole
point: our 61 engine assertions and 10 DOM assertions all run against fixtures
this repo writes itself.

I did not install it. Putting third-party software on the operator's machine
unasked is not mine to do, and it is a download besides.

TO UNBLOCK, one command and one suite:

  winget install --id BleachBit.BleachBit -e
  powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File test\cleanerml-verify.ps1

then point the reader at the installed cleaners directory (typically
C:\Program Files (x86)\BleachBit\share\cleaners) and read the three things
this issue lists, in order: how many options return zero matches and whether
any of them SHOULD have matched (a variable we do not expand resolves to
nothing and the option silently disappears); the withheld list, which will be
long because most real definitions use sqlite.vacuum, json or winreg somewhere;
and whether the honest conclusion is that this feature reaches less of the real
set than the fixtures suggest.

LICENCE BOUNDARY, unchanged and worth restating because it is easy to trip:
BleachBit's CleanerML definitions are GPL-3.0+ and this repo is MIT and public.
Running the reader against a copy on disk is fine. Copying any definition file
into this repository is not.

title: SEC-3 regression asserts on a fixture premise that does not hold when the interactive user is an administrator
description:
Diagnosed 2026-08-19 from test/logs/68A2CEC3-7F31-4/security-regressions.log. The remaining 2 of the 5 sandbox failures.

  FAIL  a child still owned by the interactive user is reported
  FAIL  a user-owned subtree is NOT called protected (the SEC-3 false positive)

The first four assertions in the block pass, including 'the DACL alone looks protected'. So the DACL half of the fixture built correctly and only the OWNER half did not.

test/security-verify.ps1:69-93 builds the regression by creating a scratch tree and assuming the objects come out owned by the interactive user - Test-VanishDataDirAcl (scanner.ps1:3784) treats S-1-5-32-544 and S-1-5-18 as trusted owners and everything else as foreign. Windows Sandbox runs as WDAGUtilityAccount, which is an administrator, so the fixture's premise ('the owner is a principal we do not trust') is not established there and foreignOwners comes back empty. The verdict protected=true is then CORRECT for what was actually on disk, and the test fails for describing a machine it is not running on.

Not a product defect as far as this log shows - but the test cannot currently tell the difference between 'the check regressed' and 'the fixture did not build', which is the same defect class as everything else this week.

Fix: measure the owner the fixture actually produced, and assert the regression only when the premise holds; otherwise SKIP with the measured owner SID printed, so the log says why. Do not weaken the assertion on machines where the premise does hold - it passes on the host today and must keep passing.
acceptance_criteria: The SEC-3 block reads the real owner of the scratch tree, states it, and either runs the regression or skips it with the reason. Host run still exercises the regression and passes. Sandbox run reports a skip with the owner SID, not a failure.
notes:
2026-08-19: fix landed. The SEC-3 block now reads the real owner SID of the scratch tree and its children, prints it, and branches: where an untrusted owner exists it runs the original two assertions unchanged; where every object is owned by a principal the check trusts by design it prints SKIP with the reason and asserts the positive case instead (no foreign owner invented, verdict protected).

GROUNDING: host run took the REGRESSION branch, not the skip branch - log shows '(fixture owned by S-1-5-21-479141868-1469886205-2683390752-1001)' followed by both original assertions passing. So the regression is not weakened on any machine where it can exist, which was the risk in this change.

STILL UNPROVEN: the skip branch itself. Needs a sandbox run to show it reporting SKIP with the owner SID rather than two FAILs - and that SID is also the answer to whether the hypothesis about the Administrators-group default owner was right.
close_reason: PROVEN in Windows Sandbox 2026-08-20, and the hypothesis was right: the log now reads '(fixture owned by S-1-5-32-544)' - BUILTIN\Administrators, because WDAGUtilityAccount is an administrator and the machine assigns ownership to the group. The block SKIPs with that reason and asserts the positive case instead of reporting two FAILs for a fixture it never built. The host still takes the regression branch, so nothing is weakened where the bug can exist.

title: Attribution join: say which INSTALLED PROGRAM a running process belongs to
description:
OPERATOR DECISION 2026-08-14, on ktt: option (a) plus the attribution layer. Do not bundle System Informer, do not vendor its source, do not build a third resource monitor.

THE ONE SENTENCE NOTHING ELSE ON THE MACHINE CAN ASSEMBLE, and the whole point of this issue:

  'This process is using 3.2 GB. It belongs to <program>, which you have not opened since <date>, it starts automatically, and it is reachable from your network on port N.'

Task Manager and System Informer both answer 'what is using CPU and RAM, and let me kill it' - that is a solved, commodity problem and Vanish must not build a third one. What neither has is an installed-program map, a startup inventory or a listener map. Vanish has all three (scanner.ps1 + corrections.json, Get-StartupItems, Get-Listeners). The join is the asset; the CPU/RAM numbers are the cheap part and are already half-present in the Task Manager tab.

SHAPE: this is ddx's shape applied to resources. Facts only, each traced to the command that produced it (see the verification-discipline memory). No score, no 'suspicious' label, no auto-kill - Rule 6, and tda's grouping amendment may not be widened by reflex.

WHAT THE JOIN NEEDS: process imagePath -> installLocation of a known program (prefix match), plus a fallback for processes under a path no uninstall entry claims, which must be REPORTED as unattributed rather than guessed at. bu2's owned/orphaned/unattributed split already exists for exactly this and should be reused, not re-invented.

WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: rendering an inferred attribution identically to a measured one. That is c0y, and it happened with install dates in this same renderer.
notes:
2026-08-20 BUILT. Host suite 1119/0 (1055 before).

SHIPPED: lib/process-attribution.js (pure, Node), IPC 'process-attribution-scan' in main.js (read-only, both tiers, five engine reads in parallel), preload, and the process details panel in renderer/quarantine-tasks.js. New suite test/process-attribution-verify.js, 63 assertions, registered in run-all.

REUSED not re-invented, as the issue required: bu2's lib/attribution.js supplies the owned/orphaned/unattributed/system split, the owner index, the recorded-install evidence and both name heuristics with their confidence levels. This module adds the ONE direction bu2 does not have - a binary running from INSIDE a registered install location - plus an ancestor walk capped at 'likely'.

FOURTH CLAUSE DELIBERATELY OMITTED: 'which you have not opened since <date>'. Nothing in this codebase knows it, Windows disables NTFS last-access updates by default, and the remaining routes are inference dressed as measurement - which is c0y exactly. Left out rather than invented. If it is wanted, it needs its own issue and its own evidence source (UserAssist is the only real candidate and it is per-user, opaque and rot-prone).

THREE THINGS IT GOT WRONG AGAINST REAL DATA, each found by running the join on this machine rather than by reasoning, each now a regression test:
1. Walking up from a Steam CEF helper, the Steam directory answered 'contains-install-location -> Dota 2', because Dota 2 installs underneath Steam. Refusing that was right; stopping there lost the answer that WAS available for the same directory (the folder is called Steam and Steam is installed). 11 processes affected. Fixed with a name-only re-ask of that directory.
2. Twelve Store-app processes came back 'Part of Windows itself' - C:\Program Files\WindowsApps is a system path to bu2, correctly. Fixed by feeding list-uwp into the same installedApps list; the package record carries the exact install location, which beats the system-path rule.
3. The first measurement said '63% unattributed'. 170 of 182 were no-image-path - Windows will not name a protected process's binary unelevated. Counted separately now. On this machine: 290 processes, 170 unnameable, and every one of the remaining 120 attributed (78 owned, 42 system, 0 unexplained).

MEASURED: five engine reads take ~20s wall clock, dominated by PowerShell starts. So the join is NOT on the 2-second sampling loop - it runs once when a process is first selected and is cached. Putting it on the loop would have made this the third resource monitor the operator said not to build.

RULE 6 held: no score, no risk field, no 'suspicious', ordering by memory used. Asserted in the suite by scanning the serialised output for those words.
close_reason: Built and grounded 2026-08-20. lib/process-attribution.js + IPC + the process details panel, 63 assertions, host suite 1119/0, and the join run against this real machine: 290 processes, every one Windows would name attributed. bu2's classifier reused rather than copied. The 'not opened since' clause was deliberately not built - see the notes.

title: Network panel: let the user act on a connection, not just look at it
description:
Operator, 2026-08-13, on the Network Activity process table: 'these should be closable here.'

Today the panel lists programs, their open connection counts and peer addresses, and offers exactly one action: the global background-transfer Hold. A user who sees something they do not want talking has to leave, find it in Task Manager, and end it there.

WHAT 'CLOSE' CAN HONESTLY MEAN, and this is the whole design problem: Windows has no supported per-connection kill for another process. SetTcpEntry can force a TCP connection to a delete state, but it is IPv4-TCP only, needs admin, and is a blunt instrument the OS does not really intend for this. The supported and honest actions are:
  1. End the owning process (already implemented and tier-gated: kill-process).
  2. Stop/disable the owning SERVICE where the process is one (startup-action already does part of this).
  3. Block it with a firewall rule - real, durable, reversible, and the one thing that actually stops it reconnecting.

RECOMMEND: wire the FIRST TWO from this panel, since both already exist behind the tier gate and would just gain a second entry point. Treat the third as its own decision - a firewall rule is persistent system state and belongs in the vault/restore model, not a button next to a row.

DO NOT implement SetTcpEntry as 'close connection'. A program whose connection is torn out from under it usually reconnects within seconds, so the button would appear to do nothing while having done something unsupported - the worst combination this app can offer.

Wording matters as much as the mechanism: 'End this program' is true; 'Close this connection' is not, when what happens is the process dies. Say the true one.

Pairs with ddx (show listeners, not just established connections) - together they answer 'who can reach this program' and 'what do I do about it' in the same place.
acceptance_criteria: At least one real action is reachable from a network row, tier-gated identically to its existing home; the label describes what actually happens; no unsupported per-connection teardown is introduced.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.6.2/0.6.3, from the operator's direct request 2026-08-14: 'the network activity items need a stop process button per row. safety warnings issued for reasonable activities, like "normal for so and so process" which is already shown. otherwise a generic warning so people knw what they are doing. still requires elevation.'

Delivered exactly that. A Stop button per row, elevation-gated, visible-but-inert in Audit Mode with the reason like every other destructive control (REQ-04).

THE CONFIRMATION ADAPTS, which is the part that was asked for. Where Vanish already knows what the program is - the same classifyNetProgram() knowledge that prints 'normal for a web browser' beside a high connection count - it says so BEFORE asking, because that is the fact most likely to change the answer. Where it does not know, it says so outright rather than inventing a reassurance or a warning it cannot support. Every dialog states what is actually lost: unsaved work, transfers that will not resume, and that this is NOT a removal so Quarantine cannot undo it.

Two things found while building it, both operator-reported and both real:

1. BITTORRENT LOOKED IDLE. Measured on their running qBittorrent: 4 TCP ESTABLISHED (all Vanish counted), 15 TCP across all states, 21 UDP sockets. BitTorrent moves data over uTP (UDP) and finds peers over UDP DHT, so a client saturating the link showed as a near-idle process with four connections - and the list SORTED on that number, so it ranked below a browser tab. UDP and non-established TCP are now counted and shown, reported separately and never added into the connection count. A UDP row is a socket, not a conversation.

2. THE RATE TILES CLAIMED SOMETHING THEY DID NOT MEASURE. 'Download'/'Upload' read as connection capacity; they are what crossed the wire in the last sample. Now 'Downloading now'/'Uploading now', with the negotiated link rate shown separately - 866.7 Mbps link against 10.2 Mbps actual line speed on this machine, numbers with nothing to do with each other.

Capacity itself is now measurable (0.6.3) behind its own consent, against speed.cloudflare.com, chosen by the operator after being shown the trade.

VERIFIED: full suite 750 passed, 0 failed; network-verify went from 41 to 47 assertions.

title: Task Manager details pane overlaps the process table when a row is selected
description:
Operator, 2026-08-13, with screenshots at two window sizes: 'task manager lets that space on the right remain that way permanently... indicators is hidden behind that space'.

TWO defects, one fixed and one not.

FIXED (this session): the pane reserved its width permanently, selected or not. index.css .process-details was 'width: 320px; flex-shrink: 0' unconditionally, so on a wide window it was dead space and on a narrow one it stole the table's width. Now width:0 when inactive, 320px on .active. Measured at the operator's own 1110x741: details pane 0px, Indicators column right edge 1102 inside a container ending at 1110, i.e. visible.

NOT FIXED: with a row selected, the pane paints OVER the table rather than the table compressing beside it - the Indicators header renders clipped mid-word at the pane boundary. Adding min-width:0 to .process-list-container (the standard flex fix, since a flex item defaults to min-width:auto and refuses to shrink below its content) plus overflow-x:auto did NOT resolve it, so the cause is something else and was not identified before running out of session. Next session should measure the container and table widths in the SELECTED state specifically - that measurement was attempted and the instrumentation edit failed, so it is genuinely unknown rather than inferred.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME BUG TWICE, and it is worth reading before fixing: index.css:761-768 carries this comment from ri6 -

    'ri6: before any selection this panel was invisible (opacity:0) but still
     claiming its full clamp() width from the workspace, permanently squeezing
     the app list for nothing. Collapse it to zero out of the layout instead -
     scoped to the All Programs sidebar specifically, since that is what was
     reported; Task Manager's process-details panel is unchanged.'

A previous session diagnosed this exact defect, fixed one instance, and deliberately scoped the fix away from the other because only one had been reported. The operator then reported the other one. Fixing the reported instance rather than the class is what produces the impression of a project repeating itself.

FIX DIRECTION: generalise rather than special-case again. Both panels are .details-panel; the collapse-when-inactive behaviour should belong to the class, with per-panel width overrides only where the widths genuinely differ. Do not add a third scoped rule.
acceptance_criteria: At 1110x741 with a process selected: the table compresses beside the pane rather than being covered, and the Indicators column is either fully visible or reachable by horizontal scroll within its own container. Verified by screenshot at that size, not only by measurement - the measurements reported this as fine while the screenshot showed the overlap.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0.5.0, and the cause was not what the issue assumed.
