CONSEQUENCE: Invoke-DeelevatedViaScheduledTask - the mechanism 9vp measured as
the only one of three that actually works - has never been exercised with an
argument vector. Packaged builds pass [] so shipping impact is nil; in a dev run
the de-elevated relaunch loses app.getAppPath() and starts bare Electron.

Correctness rather than security, but it sits in the middle of the privilege-drop
path, and the reason it went unnoticed is worth noting on its own: no strict
mode means an undefined variable in this 8,500-line file is a silent $null
rather than an error.

title: Partial byte sums render as totals, and zero renders as the word 'empty'
description:
ADVERSARIAL SWEEP 2026-09-04.

Get-FolderSize has four routes to a number and no way to say 'floor':

  $size = (Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
            Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum
  if ($size) { return [long]$size }
  return 0
  } catch { return 0 }

A denied subtree returns a partial sum with no marker. Total failure returns 0.
And Format-ByteSize renders 0 as the literal string 'empty' - so a Store data
folder whose contents could not be enumerated is labelled 'SomeApp - empty' in a
row the user is about to tick for quarantine. The renderer then sums those into
'That frees about N.'

Get-ItemSizeBytes is the same shape and worse placed: its result is written
into $row.sizeBytes - the QUARANTINE MANIFEST - immediately before the move.

THIS CONTRADICTS THE REPO'S OWN GOOD EXAMPLES, which is what makes it a bug
rather than a limitation: Measure-Paths returns sizeBytes = $null plus a reason
and never a number it cannot stand behind, and reclaim-package-caches labels its
floors in words.

ALSO, SAME CLASS, smaller:
* measuredCount is candidates.length - the number SUBMITTED to measure-paths,
  not the number measured - and is rendered as 'N folders were measured'. It
  overstates whenever the 20 s budget bites. The per-row 'not measured' display
  is honest, so only the summary line lies.
* measureDirectoryBounded skips junctions (correctly, 127o) but a skip does not
  affect complete, so an install folder with a junction to data elsewhere
  returns complete:true and a number that is a floor. Measure-FinderPathBytes in
  the contract does this correctly - a reparse point outside the root is added
  to unreadable and makes the total a floor.
* duplicate-installs.finder.ps1 wraps the HKLM PATH read in a bare catch { }, so
  a denied scope contributes zero directories and NO New-Unreadable - the finder
  then computes state 'nothing', the one state a decider may treat as clean. Its
  sibling path-hygiene.finder.ps1 does this correctly with an ok flag.
* main.js's audit fallbacks .catch(() => ({ items: [] })) supply a well-shaped
  empty, so the Array.isArray checks three lines below can never push to
  'missing' - the guard cannot detect the case its own comment describes.
close_reason: Folded into qkgu. Get-FolderSize returning 0 for both empty and failed is the same root, and the fix is the null-plus-reason shape Measure-Paths already uses.

title: lockFailuresFrom writes an uncapped path list into one oplog line
description:
FOUND 2026-09-04 in the h55 code shipped the same day. Minor, one-line fix,
filed because the asymmetry is the kind that goes unnoticed until a log stops
containing what someone needs.

lib/lock-failure.js's lockFailuresFrom returns EVERY locked failure in a
quarantine result, with no cap, and lib/vault.js writes all of them into
items.lockedPaths as a single oplog line.

The READ side is capped: store.lockedPaths(limit = 50) stops at 50 rows and
main.js asks for 50. So anything past the fiftieth entry in one record can
never be displayed by anything - it is written, never read, and still costs
space.

WHY THE SPACE MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY. The oplog rotates at 5 MB
(OPLOG_ROTATE_BYTES) and readOplog deliberately does NOT read rotated files.
One bulk purge of a few thousand items that all fail on locks writes on the
order of 150 bytes per entry into one line - a few hundred KB of a 5 MB budget
in a single record. What gets pushed out of the live log by that is the older
history, including the app-start and elevation records that
test/sandbox/collect-report.ps1 exists to print and that 69a and adg were
diagnosed from.

REACHABLE without anything pathological: the bulk uninstall queue and System
Clean both hand large item sets to one quarantine call, and a locked file is
the commonest failure there is.

FIX: cap in lockFailuresFrom, at or slightly above the reader's 50, and say in
the comment that the two numbers are related so they move together. Recording
'and N more' is optional and probably not worth it - the list is a convenience,
not an audit trail, and the audit trail is the failed COUNT beside it, which is
already exact and uncapped.

NOT A DEFECT IN WHAT IT SHOWS: the reader takes the newest 50 across records,
newest reason wins, so the user still sees the most recent problems. Nothing is
mis-reported. This is about what the log costs, not what the UI says.

CHECKED AND SOUND while looking at this: the change does NOT widen what a
diagnostic export contains. collect-report.ps1 filters oplog records by an
ALLOWLIST of actions (elevat|app-start|tier) and prints an allowlist of meta
fields, so quarantine records - the ones now carrying paths - are excluded by
construction rather than by having been remembered about.
close_reason: Folded into 2brn. Same root - a bound enforced on the read side and asserted on the write side.

title: The summary cards take MORE vertical space on a small window, not less
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-04 while adversarially checking a claim I had made without
measuring it. The claim was that 949's density work left the small-window case
alone. It did - and the small-window case was already inverted.

.dashboard-stats and .stat-card carry this comment in index.css:

  'Everything above the workspace is a fixed cost paid out of the same vertical
   budget the app list and the details panel share. At 1080x720 ... this row
   plus the header left the workspace 310px; at the 800x600 minimum it left
   190px ... Sizing this row in vh instead of px means it gives ground as the
   window shrinks rather than starving what matters.'

IT DOES NOT GIVE GROUND. It takes MORE:

  window      row    stats    workspace   rows visible
  800x600     48px   139px      250px         4
  1080x720    48px    94px      415px         7
  1440x900    48px    94px      595px        11

139px of a 600px window - 23% of the viewport - to show four rows of a program
list.

THE MECHANISM, measured rather than guessed. The vh clamps control PADDING and
ICON SIZE, which are height-ish properties. What actually sets the row's height
on a narrow window is TEXT WRAPPING, which is a function of WIDTH, and nothing
clamps that. grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr) gives each card:

  at 1440 wide:  card 274px wide,  66px tall, label 16px (one line)
  at  800 wide:  card 117px wide, 112px tall, label 32px (two lines)
                 and 'Total Disk Space' wraps to THREE lines, 48px

So the cards are 70% taller precisely when there is least room for them.

WHAT 949 ACTUALLY DID HERE, for the record: it helped and did not fix. The row
came down to 48px so 800x600 now shows 4 rows in 250px of workspace, against
the 190px the comment above recorded. Better, and still four rows.

THE FIX IS ABOUT WIDTH, NOT HEIGHT. Options, cheapest first: let the grid
reflow (auto-fit with a sensible minmax) so four narrow cards become two rows
of two readable ones, or better, collapse to a single inline strip below some
width - the System Overview line on Health Advisor is the precedent, and it was
collapsed for exactly this reason. Do NOT reach for smaller text; the labels
are already 11-12px.

WORTH DECIDING AT THE SAME TIME whether four summary cards earn a fixed slot at
all. Two of the four duplicate things already on screen: 'Total Disk Space'
restates the Storage panel one tab away, and 'Read-only / System Safety'
restates both the persistent Audit Mode banner at the top of every screen and
the badge in the sidebar. That is the 470o question asked of a different
surface, and it is why this is filed as one issue rather than two.

REPRODUCE: scratchpad adv-smallwindow.js, one window size per process
(creating a second offscreen BrowserWindow in the same run does not settle).

title: Decide: nine nav destinations, and whether any of them should merge
description:
SPLIT OUT OF 949 on 2026-09-04, when the three measured items in that issue
(s4cx icons, mp31 Date/Size, density) all closed and this was the only thing
left in it. 949 had already recorded it as 'a bigger and harder-to-reverse
change than this issue' and said it needs its own decision, so it gets one.

WHAT WAS ALREADY ESTABLISHED, and it is the reason this is not a quick win:

A control census found the panels are NOT over-buttoned -- 1 to 10 controls
each. The load is STRUCTURAL, and the census named three specific overlaps:

  * Force Uninstall as a peer nav entry means the user has to know IN ADVANCE
    that their uninstall will fail. Nobody knows that in advance.
  * System Clean and Machine Hygiene both answer 'what can I remove'.
  * Quarantine is UNDO, not a destination. It is where you go after something
    went wrong, which is not the same kind of thing as the other eight.

WHY IT IS STILL OPEN RATHER THAN OBVIOUS. Every merge moves something the
operator has already learned to find, and this app's user is the operator. A
reorganisation that is defensible in the abstract and annoying every day is a
net loss. So the decision needs the operator, not an audit.

DO NOT start by drawing a new sidebar. Start by answering, for each of the
three overlaps above, what the user was actually trying to do when they got
there -- Force Uninstall is reached after a failure, Quarantine after a
removal, and Machine Hygiene and System Clean from the same question asked
twice. A destination that is only ever reached FROM somewhere else does not
need to be a peer of the place people start.

title: Tree hashing is 20x slower inside the engine than the identical function standalone
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-03 while implementing cihg, and left unexplained rather than guessed at.

Get-VaultContentHash on the SAME 2,000-file tree:

  standalone, spawned powershell.exe, same function text   ~270 ms
  inside scanner.ps1 during a real quarantine             ~6,300 ms

Phase instrumentation inside the engine puts effectively all of it in the streaming loop:

  P-enumerate    76 ms (2000 files)
  P-sizeloop      3 ms
  P-stream     6302 ms

WHAT IT IS NOT, each checked rather than assumed:
- Not the move. A tree moved into a vault-shaped nested path and hashed immediately after, having never been read before, takes ~267 ms standalone.
- Not first-read or antivirus. Fresh files hashed in place: 273 ms. Moved then hashed: 209 ms. Moved into <lab>/vault/<guid>/files/1/: 267 ms.
- Not enumeration or the size loop, per the phase numbers above.
- Not the cap logic. An earlier isolation harness accidentally excluded the two $script: cap variables, so the function returned the cap message in 75 ms with an empty algo - that harness was invalid and was corrected. With the caps present it hashes correctly in ~324 ms.
- Not Set-StrictMode or Set-PSDebug; scanner.ps1 sets neither.

REMAINING SUSPECTS, untested: deep call-stack variable resolution inside PowerShell (the engine calls this from Invoke-QuarantineItems inside a switch, several frames down, while the harness runs it at top-level script scope), or something about the engine process's loaded state after 8,400 lines of definitions.

WHY IT IS ONLY P3: the cap is set from the SLOW number, so the unknown cannot hurt anyone. 2,000 files is ~6.5 s worst case and single files are free regardless (250 MB adds ~200 ms). If this is ever explained the cap can rise, and tree verification would cover far more of the vault.

Reproduce: instrument Get-VaultContentHash's three phases with [Console]::Error.WriteLine and quarantine a 2,000-file directory through scanner.ps1, then run the same function text standalone against the same tree.
notes:
ANSWERED 2026-09-04, and the answer is that there is no engine-side slowdown.

All three suspects measured and all three wrong. Same 2,000-file tree, one
process per row: top level 253 ms, four frames down 256 ms, scanner.ps1
dot-sourced 248 ms. Dot-sourcing all 8,500 lines costs 115 ms once and is not
in the hash. The move is not it either -- a full engine quarantine, spawn and
protected-destination checks and Move-ItemTransactional included, is 352 ms
above baseline against a WARM tree and 3,024 ms against a COLD one.

The original pair of numbers (270 ms standalone, 6,300 ms in the engine)
compared a warm standalone read with a cold engine read. Nothing else was ever
wrong.

WHERE THE COLD TIME GOES: the file OPEN. Of a 2,734 ms cold pass, 2,616 ms is
inside [System.IO.File]::OpenRead; enumerate 90, sort 57, size loop 6, and the
reads and SHA256 transforms are identical cold and warm.

It tracks FILE COUNT, not bytes, which is what separates a per-file on-access
scan from a page-cache miss:

  2000 x 400 B   0.77 MB   cold open 2569 ms  1.29 ms each   warm 70 ms
   200 x 4 KB    0.76 MB   cold open  561 ms  2.81 ms each   warm  7 ms
  2000 x 40 KB  76.30 MB   cold open 4364 ms  2.18 ms each   warm 67 ms

Same bytes, a tenth of the files: 4.6x less time. 100x the bytes at the same
count: 1.7x more. And the verdict is cached machine-wide -- a DIFFERENT process
reads the same tree 35x faster -- so it is not this process's cache.

That is a filesystem filter evaluating each file on first open. This machine
has klif.K4W-21-26 attached at altitude 320400 with Defender not running.
Recorded as the SHAPE of the cost, not as a proven attribution: the filter was
not disabled to confirm it, because changing a machine's security posture to
make a benchmark look better is not a measurement.

THE CAP STAYS AT 2000 and the reasoning is now the right one rather than a
guess. A quarantine is by definition a first touch, so the cold path is the
only one that matters. There is nothing to optimise: verifying content means
opening every file once, the opens ARE the cost, and the reads are already
free. The only lever is parallel reads to overlap the filter's latency, which
in PS 5.1 means runspaces inside an 8,500-line script to save a couple of
seconds on an action that already shows a spinner.

And the number is a property of the operator's machine, not of Vanish, which is
the reason NOT to raise the cap on one machine's figures.

docs/BENCHMARKS.md Run 005. Reproduce with
test\sandbox\vault-hash-cost-probe.ps1 (elevated for step 2).
close_reason: Not a defect. The 20x was a warm standalone read compared against a cold engine read; the cost is the first open of each file, charged by a filesystem filter, and the engine adds nothing. Cap stays at 2000 with the measured reasoning behind it.

title: Two Health Advisor panels are strictly-worse mirrors of Windows Settings
description:
ADVERSARIAL PASS 2026-09-02, measured against this project's own standard: 'Solve problems that are not solved... Do not build redundant nonsense.'

The standard is applied WELL elsewhere in the same file. index.html on the attribution panel: 'Deliberately not a treemap -- what is big is answered by WinDirStat, WizTree and Windows own Storage page, and the half none of them can answer is whose bytes these are.' That is the test passing.

Two panels do not pass it.

1. STORAGE (Health Advisor). Renders two bars: '201.2 GB used of 499.3 GB - 298.1 GB free - 40.3% full'. Settings > System > Storage shows the same numbers PLUS a breakdown by category (Apps, Temporary files, Documents) PLUS cleanup actions. Vanish's version is a strict subset. A user who checks Vanish instead of Settings learns less.

2. WINDOWS UPDATES, IN PLAIN WORDS. The panel's own copy says it: 'Vanish does not remove updates and will not pretend it can reverse one -- that is Windows own job, through wusa.exe or the Settings page, and both are one click away on any row.' So it is a read-only mirror that points at the better tool on every row. The 'in plain words' framing is the only thing it adds.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not an argument to delete them. The operator's stated goal is a suite they never have to leave, and consolidating a glance-level view is legitimate even when Windows also has one. The test that matters is narrower: IS VANISH'S VERSION WORSE THAN THE BUILT-IN? For both of these, today, it is.

So the choice per panel is one of:
  a. Add the half Windows cannot answer, the way the attribution panel did. For Storage that is plausibly 'which of this is attributable to programs you have uninstalled' -- which bu2 already computes and which Settings cannot know.
  b. Demote it. It does not have to leave the app to stop occupying the landing page.
  c. Keep it and write down why, so the next person does not re-litigate this. That is a valid answer and it is what the attribution comment does.

Related and already done 2026-09-02: System Overview was six cards of hardware specification (OS, uptime, CPU, RAM, GPU, motherboard) at the top of the landing page. Same failure -- msinfo32 answers that -- and it is now one collapsed line. See 949.
notes:
ANSWERED 2026-09-04. Option (c) for both -- kept, with the why written down -- and
the reasons are now ASSERTED rather than only asserted in a comment, because a
comment is what the next adversarial pass will not read.

STORAGE. The panel is a subset of Settings > System > Storage and that is
deliberate, because it is not a storage manager: it is THE VERDICT'S INPUT.
renderDiskBars' own 90% threshold is what auditReportWork counts into the
headline at the top of the page. Delete the bars and the verdict still counts
drives while nothing on screen shows which. So the honest fix was not to add a
category breakdown (Settings is better at that and is one click away) but to
say what the panel is not, and point at the half nothing else answers:

  'How full each drive is, and nothing more - Settings > System > Storage
   breaks the same numbers down by category and offers the cleanup, and it is
   better at that than Vanish would be. The question none of them answer is
   WHOSE bytes those are: Where your disk space went matches folders against
   the programs you actually have.'

That last phrase is a working link now, not a promise. A delegated
data-goto-tab handler in setupSidebarNavigation navigates any element carrying
it, so the next panel that stops short needs no wiring of its own.

WINDOWS UPDATES. The issue's premise is wrong, and this is the finding rather
than a defence. It read the note that says 'Vanish does not remove updates' and
concluded the panel adds nothing. Not removing is the CUT -- a removal engine
for Windows Updates is permanently cut in PRE-RELEASE.md -- not the feature.
The feature is every field Settings does not give you and this list does: what
KIND of thing each update is, what removing it would COST, an install date that
says 'not recorded' with a reason instead of a blank, and newest-first because
the question people arrive with is 'what changed just before this started going
wrong'. Settings > Update history > Uninstall updates gives a bare KB list
several clicks deep and none of that.

It also contributes NOTHING to the verdict, on purpose, which is the other half
of why it is defensible: a panel that counted updates into 'N things need a
look' would be claiming they are the user's problem.

TESTS: test/landing-panels-verify.js, 12 assertions. The two load-bearing ones
pull in opposite directions and that is the point -- Storage MUST count into
the verdict, Windows updates MUST NOT. If either stops being true the written
justification is stale and the suite says so. Three mutants, all killed; set now
41/41.

Screenshot: dist/screenshots/470o-storage-note.png.
close_reason: Both kept, option (c), with the reasons asserted rather than only commented. Storage is the verdict's input and now says what it is not and where the rest lives; Windows updates was misread - not removing is the cut, the legible list is the feature.

title: Date and Size say Unknown on a quarter of rows, and a fifth of those are recoverable
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-02, 150 real desktop entries from scanner.ps1 -Action list-desktop.

  no size          39 of 150   26.0%
  no install date  40 of 150   26.7%
  installDateSource: 110 'recorded', 40 none -- no entry on this machine used 'key-name' or 'folder-created'

A table where a quarter of two columns reads 'Unknown' looks broken even when it is being honest, and honesty is the point here: renderer/core.js already has a full install-date provenance model (INSTALL_DATE_SOURCES) that distinguishes a date the program recorded from one Vanish worked out, and shows the inferred ones as approximate with a note. The model is good. It is just not being fed.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY RECOVERABLE, and it is less than it first looks:

  no date BUT has installLocation   13 of 150    8.7%
  no size BUT has installLocation   27 of 150   18.0%

Only 34.7% of entries carry an installLocation at all, so folder-derived answers cannot fix the majority. Stating that up front because the obvious reading of '26% Unknown' is that a folder walk fixes it, and it does not.

THE TWO MECHANISMS ALREADY EXIST AND ARE NOT APPLIED HERE:
1. 'folder-created' provenance is implemented and used ONLY for Store apps (scanner.ps1:832). A desktop entry with an installLocation could take the same treatment and the same 'Approximate' label -- the note would need rewording, since it currently says 'A Store app records no install date'.
2. The shared directory sizer (lhf) can measure a folder. Size currently comes from the registry EstimatedSize alone, which is a value the installer chose to write or not.

THE COST, which is why this is P3 and not P2. Sizing 27 folders on demand is not free and this is the LIST view, which loads in seconds today. Anything here has to be lazy and cancellable, must never block first paint, and an unmeasured size must keep saying Unknown rather than showing a spinner forever. A 10-second list is a worse product than a list with 27 Unknowns in it.

Do not fill either column with a guess that does not admit itself. bu2 and the install-date work both exist because a rendered value that mixed measurements with inferences let people sort by a column that meant two different things.
notes:
BOTH HALVES DONE 2026-09-04, and the live numbers beat the estimate because the
Store apps were not counted in it.

THE DATE HALF, synchronous in the engine. Get-InstallFolderCreated reads the
InstallLocation's creation time when the entry recorded no date and the key
name is not a date either. 'folder-created' already existed for Store apps
since c0y; nothing had wired it up for desktop entries.

  before  40 of 150 Unknown  26.7%   sources: 110 recorded, 40 none
  after   27 of 150 Unknown  18.0%   sources: 110 recorded, 13 folder-created

Costed before shipping: probing all 40 dateless entries took 22 ms and reading
the 13 real creation times took 3 ms. Three refusals, each a fabricated date
avoided: a path that does not exist (a leftover registry entry is not dated
from a folder that is gone), a relative path (it would resolve against the
ENGINE's working directory), and a UNC path. The renderer's folder-created note
was reworded, since it said 'A Store app records no install date' and now has
to be true of both.

THE SIZE HALF, lazy in the MAIN PROCESS. A PowerShell round trip costs ~470 ms
of spawn before reading a byte, and this is asked once per row, so the walk
lives in main.js behind measure-install-size. The IntersectionObserver pattern
is s4cx's, unchanged: only rows that scroll into view ask.

Budgeted at 1500 ms and 200,000 files. A folder that cannot be measured
completely returns NO number - not a partial one - and the row keeps saying
Unknown. Same for an unreadable subtree and a junction (skipped, 127o).

LIVE, real machine, real observer, All Programs:

  on arrival        156 rows  103 Unknown  92 pending   1 measured
  after scrolling   156 rows   56 Unknown  41 pending  48 measured

47 rows recovered, Office at 3.7 GB among them, and 41 still pending because
nobody scrolled to them - which is the laziness working rather than a gap. Most
of the recovered rows are Store apps, which the estimate in this issue did not
count at all.

A measured size SAYS so: a mark in the table, '(measured)' plus a sentence in
the details pane. Not because it is worse than a recorded one - EstimatedSize is
frequently stale or absent - but because a sortable column that silently mixes
what the installer claimed with what Vanish walked is the defect c0y fixed for
dates.

TESTS: install-date-source-verify.ps1 20/20 (new, engine-side, via a new
install-date-probe action), install-size-verify.js 17/17 (new), and
install-size-render-verify.js 19/19 (new). Nine mutants added, all killed; full
set 38/38.

Three of those assertions could not fail when first written and mutation
testing said so: the UNC refusal (the drive-letter rule already refused it
first), a recorded date being overwritten (nothing checked which source won -
fixed with a planted HKCU pair), and a PARTIAL total being rendered (the stub's
default refusal carried bytes:null, so a renderer checking only 'is there a
number' passed too).

Live probe kept at test/sandbox/install-size-live-probe.js.
close_reason: Dates: 40 Unknown -> 27, synchronous, 3 ms. Sizes: 103 Unknown -> 56 on the real list, lazily and budgeted, with every measured value marked as measured. 38/38 mutants.

title: Network Activity ranks talkers by socket count, so the top rows are the ones talking to nobody
description:
FOUND 2026-08-30 answering an operator question about the panel.

The process table takes processes.slice(0, 6) from the engine, and the engine
orders by socketCount. socketCount counts idle UDP sockets. Live reading from
this machine, the six rows the panel would show, in order:

  svchost   pid 7100   sockets 12   connections 0   peers 0
  avp       pid 11044  sockets 11   connections 0   peers 0
  avp       pid 5348   sockets 10   connections 9   peers 7
  System    pid 4      sockets  9   connections 0   peers 0
  svchost   pid 2448   sockets  8   connections 0   peers 0
  svchost   pid 7684   sockets  6   connections 0   peers 0

Five of the six rows in a table headed by "who is using the network" have zero
connections and zero peers. The one row with real traffic - avp pid 5348, nine
connections to seven distinct peers - is third, and would fall off the list
entirely on a machine with a few more idle UDP listeners.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE AS y72j's decision bar and lib/findings.js's
ranker, and it should be fixed with the same rule: rank by the quantity that
answers the question, never by the one that is easiest to count. Here the
question is "who is talking to something", so the sort key is peerCount and
connectionCount; socketCount is at best a tiebreak.

NOT a data problem. The engine returns everything needed - peerCount,
connectionCount, otherTcpCount, processId - and the renderer already displays
processId, so rows with the same program name are distinguishable. It is
purely the ordering and the slice.

WORTH DECIDING AT THE SAME TIME: whether a process with zero connections and
zero peers belongs in this table at all. "svchost has twelve UDP sockets open"
is true and is not what the panel claims to answer. If they stay, they should
sort below everything that is actually connected.

CHECK BEFORE FIXING: whether the engine's sort or the renderer's slice is the
right place. Sorting in the engine changes what every consumer sees; sorting
in the renderer keeps the payload neutral. bfh.1's suite asserts on this
payload, so check what it already pins before moving the sort.
notes:
DO NOT RE-SORT THIS. Investigated 2026-08-30; the fix proposed in the description is WRONG, and so is the obvious alternative.

THE THREE CANDIDATE KEYS, and why each fails:

1. connectionCount (established TCP). ALREADY TRIED AND REJECTED - the comment in Get-NetworkActivity says so: 'Sorting on established alone is what put a saturating torrent client below a browser tab.' BitTorrent moves data over uTP, which is UDP, so a client saturating the link shows about four connections.

2. peerCount as a magnitude. Same failure, same reason. peers are collected ONLY where a remote address exists, i.e. established TCP - the hashtable is filled in the same block that does connections++. UDP contributes sockets and never peers.

3. peerCount > 0 as a GATE, then socketCount within each group. This is what I was about to ship, and live data killed it. With a game running: dota2 held 55 UDP sockets, 0 connections, 0 peers, while the link was quiet at 0.5 KB/s - idle in a menu, and the gate correctly demoted it. But IN A LIVE MATCH it looks IDENTICAL: still UDP, still no remote address in the socket table, still zero peers. The gate would bury an actively transmitting game.

THE PROBLEM IS THE DATA, NOT THE ORDER. An active UDP talker and an idle UDP holder are indistinguishable in what Get-NetworkActivity collects - both are 'many UDP sockets, zero peers'. No ordering over these fields separates them. The current socketCount sort errs toward showing what COULD be busy, which is the safer error.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX IT:
  * cheap and probably right: change what the panel CLAIMS. It reads as though it ranks who is using the network; it ranks who holds the most sockets. Say that, keep the peer and connection columns visible, and let the reader judge.
  * expensive: per-process network bytes. Windows does not expose it cheaply - Get-Counter '\Process(*)\IO Data Bytes/sec' is ALL I/O including disk, and a real per-process network figure means ETW.

MEASURED EVIDENCE FOR THE ORIGINAL COMPLAINT still stands: on an idle machine 4 of the 6 visible rows had zero connections and zero peers, and msedge with 6 connections to 5 peers was sixth. That is real, and it is a labelling problem rather than a sorting one.

P2 -> P3.
close_reason:
Fixed the half that is fixable. The ORDER is unchanged and must stay unchanged: connectionCount was already tried and rejected (a uTP torrent shows about four connections), peerCount as a magnitude fails identically because peers are only collected from established TCP, and peerCount>0 as a gate would bury an actively transmitting game - verified live, dota2 holding 55 UDP sockets with zero peers looks identical whether it is mid-match or idle in a menu. No ordering over the fields the engine collects separates an active UDP talker from an idle socket holder; only per-process byte counters would, and on Windows that means ETW.

What shipped instead is the honest half: the panel now says it is ordered by sockets held, that this is not the same as how busy a program is, that a program can hold sockets and be connected to nothing, and that heavy UDP users show no connections at all - so read the two right-hand columns rather than the order. The measured complaint that started this (4 of 6 visible rows with zero connections and zero peers, msedge with 6 connections pushed to sixth) is real and is now explained on screen instead of being silently misleading.

title: package-lock.json still says version 0.3.0
description:
NOTICED 2026-08-29 while bumping to 0.9.3.

package-lock.json lines 3 and 9 both read "version": "0.3.0". package.json has
moved through 0.4 to 0.9.3 since; the lockfile root version was never bumped
with it. Pre-existing drift, not introduced by any recent change.

HARMLESS TODAY: electron-builder reads package.json, and npm does not use the
lockfile's own root version for anything at install time. So this is a
cosmetic lie, not a broken build -- which is exactly why it has survived nine
minor versions unnoticed.

WORTH FIXING because a lockfile that disagrees with package.json is a thing a
reader has to work out is safe, every time. The fix is either two edited
fields or `npm install --package-lock-only`, and the second is preferable
because it also refreshes anything else that has drifted.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE AT RELEASE TIME: regenerating a lockfile produces churn
in the same commit as a verified behaviour change, and the whole point of
that commit was that its diff is reviewable. Do this on its own.

While in there, decide whether the version bump should be scripted at all --
docs/RELEASING.md lists package.json but says nothing about the lockfile, and
that omission is why this drifted.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-02. package-lock.json said 0.3.0 against package.json's 0.9.4 -- six releases of drift. Both the root version and packages[""] are now 0.9.4.

Hand-editing it would drift again next release, so the actual fix is the guard: test/repo-invariants-verify.js asserts package.json and package-lock.json agree on version AND name, in both places npm writes it (the root key and the packages[""] entry are written by different code paths and can disagree with each other as well as with package.json). Verified by planting 0.3.0 back:

  FAIL  package-lock.json root version matches package.json (0.3.0 === 0.9.4)

This mattered beyond tidiness because npm ci installs from the lock, so the version stamped into a packaged build came from the file nobody was watching.

title: Health Advisor should link to Machine Hygiene, and show its last verdict
description:
Health Advisor is the landing page and Machine Hygiene is the differentiator, and right now the landing page does not mention it exists. Someone who opens Vanish and does not click the second sidebar entry never learns the app can tell them what a delete would destroy.

Small: a card on the dashboard that either says 'these checks have not been run' with a link, or shows the last decided verdict and when it was taken.

Requires deciding where a last-run result lives. It is NOT free to keep: a stale verdict presented as current is worse than no verdict, so it has to carry its timestamp and be visibly stale after some interval, or not be kept at all and the card just links.

Depends on the scan-duration issue: a card offering a run that takes ten minutes is a trap.
notes:
CORRECTION to the close note above. I claimed test/repo-invariants-verify.js 'now checks that every fa- token referenced has a rule'. It briefly did, and that was a mistake: test/icon-verify.js has owned this check since the FontAwesome CDN was dropped, scans the same way (every fa- token, not just fa-solid fa-x pairs), and is registered in run-all.ps1. It would have caught all four the moment it ran.

It passed when I finally ran it only because I had already added the glyphs. The check was never broken; I never ran it between writing the card and screenshotting it, which is the entire reason four squares reached a screenshot.

The duplicate has been removed from repo-invariants-verify.js. Two files checking one property is worse than one, because they drift and each makes the other look redundant. repo-invariants-verify.js keeps only what nothing else owns: package.json/package-lock.json version agreement, and every suite registered in run-all.ps1 existing on disk.
close_reason:
SHIPPED 2026-09-02. A Machine Hygiene card on the Health Advisor landing page, between System Overview and Storage.

WHERE THE LAST RUN LIVES, which the issue said had to be decided: in memory, for this session only, never persisted. renderer/hygiene.js sets window.VanishHygieneLastRun at exactly one place -- the line where a verdict becomes legitimate -- so no partial decision rendered during progress can reach it. Persisting across launches was rejected: a verdict that survives a restart is a claim about a machine that has been installed to, uninstalled from and rebooted since, and the hygiene panel's whole premise is that it makes no claim it has not just earned.

BOTH RULES FROM THE ISSUE ARE ENFORCED BY TESTS, not by intent:
- A stale verdict presented as current is worse than none. Past 30 minutes the card stops leading with the verdict and leads with the AGE ('Last checked 1 hour ago'), reports what that run said as history, says the machine may have changed, and is toned as the dullest card on the page rather than the brightest. Under 30 minutes it leads with the headline and still carries its age.
- A card offering a ten-minute run is a trap. The invitation names the cost -- read-only, works in Audit Mode, can take several minutes on a disk with many repositories -- in the same paragraph as the offer.

13 assertions in test/hygiene-panel-verify.js (133 passed, 0 failed), including that the never-run state makes NO claim about the machine, and that the recording point is singular.

FOUND WHILE SCREENSHOTTING IT: four icon names had no rule in assets/icons.css and were rendering as solid filled squares. That is a property of the mechanism, not a slip -- the base .fa-solid rule paints a 1em block in currentColor and masks it with var(--vi), so a name with no rule has no mask and the block paints in full. A missing icon is LOUDER than a present one, with no console warning and no layout break. The four glyphs were added in the house 24x24 / 2px style, and test/repo-invariants-verify.js now checks that every fa- token referenced in index.html or renderer/*.js has a rule. It scans every fa- token rather than 'fa-solid fa-x' pairs, because all four of these were built as fa-solid ${icon} from a variable and a pair-matching scan called the codebase clean while four squares were on screen.

title: Elevation mismatch marker is silently discarded after 5 minutes
description:
Found while closing adg, 2026-08-28. Not the cause of adg, but it is the gap that would let adg's symptom recur invisibly.

main.js writes a one-shot marker just before quitting on the relaunch success path, and the next boot compares the tier it LANDED in against the tier it WANTED. A mismatch is written to the oplog as relaunch-elevated-mismatch / relaunch-deelevated-mismatch. That instrumentation works - the operator's oplog contains two real relaunch-deelevated-mismatch records.

THE GAP: the marker only counts as evidence when msSinceAttempt < 5 minutes. Beyond that it is deleted and ignored. That is correct for a stale marker from a crash, but it means a relaunch that fails by NOT RESTARTING AT ALL - the app reports success, never quits, and the user reopens it an hour later - is indistinguishable from a clean boot. The one case where the app never got a chance to notice is the one the window excludes.

SUGGESTED, not decided: keep the 5-minute window for the mismatch verdict, but record an 'elevation-attempt-unresolved' oplog line when a marker is found stale, so the evidence exists even though the verdict does not. That preserves the current behaviour's caution - an old marker is genuinely weak evidence about the current boot - while making the invisible case visible.

Low priority because the direction that actually failed on this machine (de-elevation) is caught, and because the elevated path is now proven live by test/sandbox/relaunch-live-probe.ps1.
close_reason:
FIXED 2026-09-02. main.js now writes a 'relaunch-attempt-unresolved' oplog record when a marker is found outside the 5-minute window, instead of deleting it unread.

The verdict rule is UNCHANGED and deliberately so: a stale marker is still weak evidence about this boot, still produces no mismatch record and no diagnostic banner. What changed is that 'too old to judge' and 'never happened' are no longer the same thing on disk. The case the window excludes is the worst one -- a relaunch that reports success and then never restarts at all, so nothing is running to notice within five minutes -- and it was the only one with no trace anywhere.

outcome is 'unknown', not 'error'. Whether that attempt failed genuinely cannot be determined from a later boot, and calling it a failure would be the same overreach as reporting a could-not-look as a nothing. The record carries attemptedAt, trigger, direction, wantedTier, landedTier, msSinceAttempt and a 'why' that distinguishes an old marker from a future-dated one (clock skew).

test/elevation-intent-verify.js's model is updated to match and now covers both stale shapes. Because that model is a MIRROR of main.js and can pass while main.js drifts away from it, two structural checks were added against the real file -- that it contains the action and that the action is recorded with outcome unknown. Verified by planting the drift: renaming the action in main.js turned both red, restoring it green. 25 passed, 0 failed.

title: D-2: it does not feel modern, and the visual pass comes AFTER the seam
description:
OPERATOR-REPORTED, 2026-08-21. Recorded verbatim in HANDOFF-2026-08-21 section 1 as the MORE IMPORTANT of the two reports:

  "the app doesn't feel modern, advanced or futuristic."

His stated intent: Vanish is to be his STANDING SUPPORT SYSTEM for this and future machines - depended on, smooth, and free of exactly the class of error D-1 is an instance of. A tool held to that bar is judged on feel, not just correctness.

THE HANDOFF IS EXPLICIT ABOUT THE ORDER: seam first, visual pass second. "Modern" comes from a UI that always knows which state it is in, not from styling. Reskinning a flow that still guesses at zero-result states produces a better-looking guess.

No done-criteria yet, deliberately. This needs the operator to say what specifically reads as dated - the two candidates already visible are that renderer/audit.js (1,675 lines) and renderer/queue-clean.js (1,159) are doing view AND flow control, which is where "the screen does not know what it is" comes from.
notes:
LANDING VERDICT SHIPPED 2026-09-02. This issue said it needed the operator to say what specifically reads as dated. Three things now have numbers attached instead of opinions, and the first is done.

DONE -- Health Advisor had no answer on it. The landing page opened with six cards of hardware specification (OS, uptime, CPU, RAM, GPU, motherboard) above everything actionable, then eight sections each rendering itself and none saying anything about the whole. It now opens with one of the four states lib/findings.js already decides for Machine Hygiene: work / clear / incomplete / checking. System Overview is one collapsed line -- it is identity, not health.

The rule that keeps it honest: it aggregates ONLY judgements the sections had already made and already badge. 90% is renderDiskBars' own danger threshold; broken startup entries are the number already on the 'N broken' pill; redundancy already subtracts what you waived. It scores nothing new. Listeners and Windows Update contribute nothing on purpose, asserted against the source -- counting listeners into a headline would rank them by placement, which is the claim that panel explicitly refuses to make.

STILL OPEN, all measured against this machine:
  s4cx  87 of 150 rows (58%) carry a real icon path and 0 render one
  mp31  Date and Size read Unknown on 26.7% and 26.0% of rows
  density  seven rows visible in a 900px window for a 152-item list; the
           'Windows Apps' toolbar segment wraps inside its own control

NOT DONE and deliberately not attempted: collapsing the 9 nav destinations. A control census found the panels are NOT over-buttoned (1-10 controls each) -- the load is structural. Force Uninstall as a peer entry means the user must know in advance that their uninstall will fail; System Clean and Machine Hygiene both answer 'what can I remove'; Quarantine is undo rather than a destination. That is a bigger and harder-to-reverse change than this issue, and it moves things the operator has already learned to find. It needs its own decision.

THE THING TO KEEP RESISTING: every finding above is the interface failing to show something it ALREADY KNOWS -- an icon it collected, a date it could derive, a verdict it ranked wrongly. Restyling a screen that discards 87 icons produces a prettier screen that discards 87 icons.
DENSITY DONE 2026-09-04. All three measured items in this issue are now closed;
what remains is the nav-collapse question, which the note above already sends
to its own decision.

  s4cx   87 of 150 rows carry an icon and 0 render one   -- shipped
  mp31   Date and Size read Unknown on ~26% of rows      -- shipped today
  density  seven rows visible for a 152-item list        -- this

MEASURED, 1440x900, the real 156-row list:

                         before    after
  row height              70 px    48 px
  rows visible                7       11
  list container top     318 px   273 px
  list container height  550 px   595 px

NOTHING WAS REMOVED. Same icon, same publisher line, same badges, same columns.
Two measurements decided it:

1. THE ICON WAS SIZING THE ROW. 70px was 14px of padding around a 40px icon
   TILE while the two lines of text beside it needed about 30. Tile to 30px,
   padding to 8. The explicit line-heights on .app-title-name and
   .app-publisher-name are load-bearing now rather than cosmetic, because the
   text pair decides the row height instead of the icon.

2. THE SUMMARY CARDS HAD A FLOOR AND NO CEILING. .dashboard-stats and
   .stat-card were already sized in vh clamps, written so the row gives ground
   on a SMALL window -- measured at the time as leaving the workspace 190px at
   800x600. Nothing stopped them GROWING: at 1440x900 every clamp sat at its
   maximum and four cards took 110px off a list that could show seven rows.
   Only the ceilings moved. The floors and the vh scaling are untouched,
   because the small-window problem they were written for has not changed.

Also from the same report: 'Windows Apps' wrapped onto two lines INSIDE its own
segment, stretching all three to 50px. white-space: nowrap -- a segmented
control's labels are fixed strings we choose.

HELD UNDER TEST: test/list-density-verify.js, 13 assertions. Bounds are loose
on purpose (row <= 56px, at least ten visible) because font rasterisation
differs between machines and an exact pixel assertion would be a flaky test
wearing a design badge. It also asserts every row is the SAME height, so a long
name cannot reintroduce this one row at a time. Three mutants: the padding, the
tile size, the nowrap.

docs/BENCHMARKS.md Run 007. Screenshots: dist/screenshots/949-density-before.png
and 949-density-after.png.
close_reason: All three measured items closed: s4cx (icons render), mp31 (Date/Size Unknown filled in and labelled), density (7 -> 11 rows visible, 70px -> 48px). The un-measured half - collapsing the nine nav destinations - is split out as p171, which is what this issue said it needed.

title: network-verify has at least one assertion that flakes under load (837/1 in a batch run, 51/0 alone)
description:
OBSERVED 2026-08-14, twice-clean before and after: the full suite reported 'Network attribution (bfh.1) 50 passed 1 failed' in a batch run, and the same suite run alone immediately afterwards reported 51 passed, 0 failed. Nothing in that change touched network code (the diff was test/elevated-confirmations.ps1, test/vault-ipc-verify.js, test/phase4-ipc-verify.js), and the batch summary does not preserve which assertion failed.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN A SHRUG: a suite that fails one-in-N under load teaches everyone to re-run until green, which is how a real regression gets waved through. It also means 'npm test: 838 passing' is not reproducible on a busy machine, and that number is quoted in CHANGELOG entries and close reasons.

MOST LIKELY CANDIDATE, not confirmed: test/network-verify.ps1:186 asserts totalBytesPerSecond EQUALS the sum of gateway adapter rates. Those are live counter deltas sampled over a window; under load (the batch run has Electron suites downloading nothing but scanning heavily in parallel) a difference between the headline figure and the per-adapter sum is plausible without anything being wrong. Line 155's verdict assertion and 178's negative-rate check are the other environment-dependent ones.

WHAT TO DO, in order:
1. Make the failure identifiable: run-all.ps1 should keep each suite's FAIL lines in the summary, or the per-suite log should be written to disk unconditionally. Right now a batch failure cannot be diagnosed at all without re-running.
2. Then decide whether the assertion is wrong or the code is. If it is a sampling-window comparison, it should assert agreement within a tolerance and SAY it is a tolerance - not silently loosen to always-true.

Do not 'fix' this by removing the assertion. bfh.1's whole point is that the headline rate is honest about which adapters it counts.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-08-16, and the issue's own 'most likely candidate' was wrong - which is why it was measured rather than accepted. The rounding comparison at network-verify.ps1:186 CANNOT flake on this machine: it has exactly one gateway adapter (Wi-Fi; Ethernet 3 and 4 are down and non-gateway), so headline and sum are the same expression. The real flake was the timing assertion 'the whole read stays well under the time a person will wait' at < 8s. Measured: bare powershell.exe start 0.75s, check-admin 1.45s, get-network-activity cold 7.6s, warm 2.4-2.9s. A 3x spread on an IDLE machine against an 8s ceiling is a coin toss, and a batch run adds load. (1) IDENTIFIABILITY, which was the more serious half: run-all.ps1 now writes every suite's full output to test/logs/<slug>.log unconditionally and before parsing, collects FAIL and WARN lines per suite, and prints a 'Failures, named' block under the TOTAL naming the suite, every failing assertion and its log path. Grounded by inducing a real failure in icon-verify and confirming it is named at the bottom with its log and exit 1. (2) The timing assertion is now a HANG guard at 30s that states its tolerance and what the wall clock includes, plus a new DETERMINISTIC assertion that the read takes at least its own sample window (a faster answer would not be a measurement), plus a WARN - not a failure - above 8s so slowdown stays visible. Not loosened to always-true: 30s is far outside anything measured. (3) Found in passing and fixed: the headline totalBytesPerSecond summed UNROUNDED per-adapter rates while each row displays a rounded one, so Round(a)+Round(b) != Round(a+b) - on a machine with two gateway adapters up the panel would contradict itself. Now accumulates the rounded per-adapter figure. Invisible here for the same reason the rounding assertion cannot flake here. Suite: 845 passed 0 failed (838 before; +6 qof, +1 the new sample-window assertion).

title: measure-paths returns sizeBytes 0 with error null for a FILE path (latent, same class as c0y)
description:
Found in passing 2026-08-14 while proving the -ParamsBase64 fix (bkn), not by a user report. LATENT, not live - filing it so it is not rediscovered as a mystery later.

EVIDENCE, one command:
  scanner.ps1 -Action measure-paths -ParamsBase64 <{paths:['D:\...\package.json']}>
  -> {"success":true,"results":[{"path":"...package.json","sizeBytes":0,"fileCount":0,"skippedDirs":1,"partial":true,"timedOut":false,"error":null}]}

package.json is ~2 KB. The answer is 0 bytes, and error is NULL.

CAUSE: Measure-Paths (scanner.ps1:5809) treats every target as a directory. 'New-Object System.IO.DirectoryInfo <a file>' succeeds, then EnumerateFiles() throws, the per-directory catch increments skippedDirs, and the walk ends with total=0. The only signal that anything went wrong is partial=true.

WHY IT MATTERS DESPITE BEING LATENT: the function's own comment says 'A wrong number is worse than no number' and that unmeasured things come back with sizeBytes = null and a reason. This path violates both - it returns a NUMBER (0) with error null. That is c0y's failure exactly: an inference rendered with the confidence of a measurement.

WHY IT IS NOT LIVE: the only caller is main.js:1671 (attribution-scan), whose candidates come from attribution.sizeCandidates() over install-snapshot's dirs - directories by construction. Nothing in the app passes a file path today.

FIX, when it is worth doing: at the top of the per-target loop, if the target is a file, either return its Length as sizeBytes with fileCount 1, or return sizeBytes = null with error 'Not a folder'. Either is defensible; returning 0 is not. Whichever is chosen, assert it - the existing attribution suite (test/attribution-verify.js) is the natural home.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-08-16. Measure-Paths now branches on Test-Path -PathType Leaf before the directory walk: a file reports its real Length with fileCount 1, skippedDirs 0, partial false; an unreadable file reports sizeBytes null with a reason. Verified against the real engine - package.json returns 2114, which is its exact size on disk; a directory still walks (lib/ = 61191, 6 files); a missing path still returns null + 'No longer on disk'. Pinned by 6 new assertions in test/attribution-verify.js (36 -> 42) that call scanner.ps1 the way main.js does, so the engine half of 'never a false zero' is now defended by a test rather than by a comment.

title: All Programs now has two Type controls; decide whether the header toggle stays
description:
Introduced by 5b0 (0.6.5), and flagged rather than resolved unilaterally because it is a UI-surface call.

The All Programs header has had an All / Desktop / Windows Apps toggle since 0.1.0 (filterType). 5b0 added a Type column filter offering Desktop / Windows App / Feature. Both filter the same column and they AND together, so it is possible to set the toggle to Desktop and the column filter to Feature and get an empty table. That state is LEGIBLE - the caption names both and the empty state says which filters emptied it, asserted in test/column-filter-verify.js - so nothing is hidden. But two controls for one column is still redundancy of the kind CLAUDE.md's standard is written against.

THREE OPTIONS:
(a) Leave both. Zero risk, and the toggle is a one-click shortcut the popover cannot match. Redundant.
(b) Drop the header toggle, let the column filter own Type. Frees header width; costs the one-click path and touches an old control several tests reference.
(c) Make them one control - the toggle writes into the column filter's state.  Least redundancy, most code, and the popover would then have to render 'Desktop only' set from outside itself.

RECOMMENDATION: (a) for now, revisited only if the header runs out of room. The cost of the redundancy is one confusing empty state that already explains itself; the cost of (b) is removing a control an operator may be used to.
close_reason: DECIDED: option (a), leave both controls. The empty state that the two can produce together already names both filters and says which emptied the table (asserted in test/column-filter-verify.js), so nothing is hidden - the cost of the redundancy is one self-explaining empty state. The cost of (b) is removing a header control that has been there since 0.1.0 and that several suites reference, to save width the header does not yet need; (c) buys least redundancy for most code and would make the popover render state set from outside itself. Revisit only if the All Programs header runs out of room.

title: Decide: process-stop mechanism and resource-hog scoring (both currently refused)
description:
Carried out of ktt so closing it does not lose the two questions the operator raised on 2026-08-14 and that were deliberately NOT started:

1. 'A mechanism to stop such suspicious processes.' An automatic or semi-automatic killer acting on heuristics is the confident-wrong-answer failure this project keeps fixing, but with teeth: killing the wrong process loses a user's unsaved work. Note that a MANUAL kill already exists in the Task Manager tab, with a denylist and a typed double-confirm for svchost/explorer/dwm. So the honest question is not 'can Vanish stop a process' - it can - but 'should Vanish ever choose which one', and the default answer is no.

2. 'An intelligence model to detect resource hogs.' Scoring processes as suspicious is precisely what Rule 6 forbids. tda's amendment permits a trusted-publisher allowlist for GROUPING ONLY and says explicitly that it may not be widened by reflex.

A DEFENSIBLE VERSION OF BOTH EXISTS and it is 0bi: state facts (this is using 3.2 GB, it belongs to X, you have not opened X since <date>, it autostarts, it listens on port N) and let the user act. That is a resource hog identified without anything being scored.

This issue is a DECISION, not an implementation. It should be closed with a verdict either way rather than quietly implemented.
notes:
VERDICT 2026-09-04. Both refused, and the second one is already built in the
form that is defensible.

1. SHOULD VANISH EVER CHOOSE WHICH PROCESS TO STOP? No.

The capability is not the question -- a manual kill already exists in Task
Manager, with a denylist and a typed double-confirm for svchost, explorer and
dwm. The question is whether Vanish picks the target, and there is a reason to
refuse that is stronger than Rule 6 and specific to this product:

  EVERY DESTRUCTIVE ACTION IN VANISH GOES THROUGH A VAULT THAT CAN PUT IT
  BACK. That is INV-1, and it is the invariant the whole app is built around --
  quarantine may only take what restore can return, asked of the same predicate
  from both sides. A killed process's unsaved work cannot be put back by
  anything. An automatic kill would therefore be the ONLY destructive action in
  the product with no undo path, chosen by the software rather than the person,
  on the strength of a heuristic.

That is not a close call. Rule 6 would forbid the scoring anyway; INV-1
forbids the consequence even if the scoring were perfect.

2. AN INTELLIGENCE MODEL TO DETECT RESOURCE HOGS? No -- and the honest version
of it shipped on 2026-08-20 as 0bi.

Scoring processes as suspicious is what Rule 6 exists to prevent, and tda's
amendment permits a trusted-publisher allowlist for GROUPING ONLY with an
explicit instruction not to widen it by reflex. What 0bi does instead is state
facts and let the user act: this process is using 3.2 GB, it belongs to X, it
starts automatically, it is reachable on port N. Nothing is ranked, and the
resource hog is identified anyway -- by the reader, from evidence, which is the
difference this product exists to make.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS, stated so the refusal is a decision rather than a
dogma:

  * A user-authored rule is the user choosing, not Vanish scoring. 'Kill
    anything named X over Y GB' written BY the operator would not violate
    either principle. Nobody has asked for it, and building it before someone
    does would be inventing the demand.
  * Nothing else. In particular, a better heuristic is not an argument -- the
    objection is to the missing undo, and no amount of accuracy supplies one.

Closed as a decision, per the issue's own instruction that it should be closed
with a verdict either way rather than quietly implemented.
close_reason: Both refused. Automatic process-stop: INV-1 has no analogue for unsaved work, so it would be the only destructive action in the product with no undo path, chosen by software. Resource-hog scoring: Rule 6 forbids it and 0bi shipped the defensible version - state the facts, let the reader identify the hog. A user-authored rule would reopen the first; a better heuristic would not.

title: Detect an existing System Informer install and hand off to it
description:
OPERATOR DECISION 2026-08-14, on ktt: option (a). System Informer is MIT (verified against LICENSE.txt), so bundling would be LEGAL - it is refused on cost, not licence. Its deeper capabilities need KSystemInformer, a signed kernel driver: driver signing, Microsoft attestation, conflicts with security products, a much heavier install, for an app whose pitch is that it is honest and light. The kernel driver is out of scope.

SCOPE, deliberately small: if System Informer is installed, Vanish points at it for deep process work (handles, tokens, kernel-level detail) instead of pretending to offer that itself. If it is not installed, Vanish says nothing about it - no bundled download, no nag, no 'recommended tools' list.

DETECTION: it ships portable as often as installed, so an uninstall-entry lookup alone will under-detect. Check the uninstall map first (it is already scanned), then a running process named SystemInformer.exe. Do NOT go hunting the filesystem for it.

WHAT THIS MUST NOT BECOME: an affiliate-style recommendation surface, or a place where Vanish claims another tool is 'safe'. State that the tool is present and what it is better at. Nothing else.

Depends on nothing. Pairs with 0bi (the attribution join), which is the substantive half of the same decision.
notes:
SHIPPED 2026-09-04, at the scope the issue set and no wider.

DETECTION uses only what is already in the renderer's memory, which is exactly
what the issue asked for ('do NOT go hunting the filesystem for it'):

  1. a running process named exactly SystemInformer.exe -- checked FIRST,
     because it is the stronger signal and it is the one that catches a
     portable copy, which is the common case for this tool
  2. failing that, an uninstall entry whose name contains 'system informer'

Neither costs a query: Task Manager already holds the process list and
allApps already holds the uninstall map. If the program list has not loaded
yet the note simply does not appear, which is the correct reading of 'we have
not established it' rather than a wrong one.

THE NOTE says the tool is present, says HOW it knows, and says what it is
better at (handles, open files, tokens, kernel-level detail) alongside what
Vanish itself will not do -- it reads process information the way Task Manager
does and loads no kernel driver, so there are questions about a process it
cannot answer. When the tool is absent the element is hidden and holds no text
at all: not a placeholder, not a greyed-out row.

WHAT IT MUST NEVER BECOME is asserted rather than reviewed. The suite fails the
note if it ever contains 'safe', 'trusted', 'recommend', 'download', 'install
it', a URL, or an anchor element of any kind. Vanish does not make claims about
software -- it will not say that about its own startup entries, and buying an
exception here would be the affiliate-recommendation surface this issue
forbids.

TESTS: test/system-informer-verify.js, 19 assertions, including that a process
merely NAMED like it (NotSystemInformer.exe, systeminformer.exe.bak) does not
trigger the note, and that closing the tool hides the note again on the next
refresh -- it is a live reading, not a one-time verdict. Three mutants: the
exact match becoming a substring, the note not being re-evaluated, and the note
appearing when the tool is absent.

NOT VERIFIED ON A MACHINE THAT HAS IT. System Informer is not installed here,
so the present-path is exercised by fixtures rather than by a real detection.
The absent-path IS the live behaviour on this machine and is correct: nothing
appears.
close_reason: Shipped: Task Manager names System Informer when it is running or installed, says how it knows and what it is better at, and is completely silent when it is absent. 19 assertions, most of them refusals (no 'safe', no 'recommend', no download, no anchor). Detection uses only lists already in memory.

title: UAC diagnostics: distinguish 'UAC disabled, changeable' from 'UAC disabled/locked by domain Group Policy'
description:
Operator, 2026-08-11: 'uac disabled status is visible to vanish, and it should be able to discern vanish being disabled against it being perm locked, as is common in perm locked corporate machines.'

Get-UacDiagnostics (scanner.ps1) already reads EnableLUA and reports enableLua:false when UAC is off, but treats every disabled case identically. On a domain-joined, GPO-managed corporate machine, EnableLUA is very often force-set to 0 (or force-set to 1 and unable to be turned off) by Group Policy and will silently revert on the next policy refresh if a local admin changes it by hand - materially different from a home/personal machine where the SAME registry value was just switched off once and stays that way. The elevate-toggle's own behavior (trigger UAC if enabled, silently elevate if disabled) does not need to change - Start-Process -Verb RunAs already does exactly this correctly, confirmed live this session (kt0). This is purely a DIAGNOSTIC/MESSAGING improvement: telling the user WHY UAC reads as off, and whether they can expect to change it themselves.
design:
No clean single registry flag distinguishes 'set by GPO' from 'set by hand' for classic UAC values - Windows does not tag policy-origin on these keys. Best achievable, honestly-caveated signal (matches Rule 24 - unknown is not zero):
1. Check domain membership: (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).PartOfDomain.
2. If domain-joined, test whether the current (already-admin) token can actually WRITE to HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA (a scratch Set-ItemProperty + revert, or Get-Acl against the key checked against the current identity).
3. Domain-joined AND not writable by an admin token -> report a new cause 'uac-disabled-locked' (or similar) distinct from the existing 'uac-disabled'. Domain-joined but writable, or not domain-joined at all -> keep the existing plain 'uac-disabled'.
Explicitly not attempting: reading actual GPO RSOP data (gpresult /nsopping is slow, not scriptable cheaply, and overkill for a UI hint) or claiming certainty this IS GPO-enforced when the heuristic can only really say 'this looks locked down, likely by policy'. Wording in the UI must say 'likely locked by your organization's policy' or similar, never a flat, overconfident claim.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.5.0. Get-UacDiagnostics now returns partOfDomain, policyWritable and lockLikely; a new 'uac-disabled-locked' cause carries wording that says the setting is LIKELY enforced by organisation policy and points at whoever administers the PC, instead of telling a corporate user to turn UAC back on (which reverts at the next policy refresh).

TWO DELIBERATE CHANGES FROM THE DESIGN AS FILED, both about not overclaiming:

1. The writability probe only runs when the process is ALREADY ELEVATED. The design said to test whether 'the current (already-admin) token' can write EnableLUA, but nothing enforced that. An unelevated process cannot write HKLM under any circumstances, so running the probe from Audit Mode would report 'locked by policy' on every ordinary home machine in the world - confident, plausible, and completely wrong, which is the exact failure mode this issue exists to prevent. Unelevated leaves policyWritable null. Verified live on this machine: partOfDomain false, isElevatedNow false, policyWritable null, lockLikely false - it correctly claims nothing.

2. It writes a SCRATCH value (VanishWriteProbe) and removes it in a finally block, rather than setting and reverting EnableLUA as the design suggested. Same key, same ACL, same answer, but a failure halfway through leaves a stray registry value instead of a machine with UAC switched off. test/uac-lock-verify.js asserts nothing in the engine ever writes EnableLUA.

WORDING IS PART OF THE CONTRACT and is asserted, not just written: the message must say 'likely', must never assert Group Policy did this (Windows does not record policy-origin on these values), must point at the administrator, and must NOT repeat the personal-machine advice. The unmanaged case still says 'turn UAC back on'.

Verified: test/uac-lock-verify.js 19/19, wired into run-all. Full suite 660 passed, 0 failed.

title: Indicators column and general filtering: add Excel-style column filter/category list across views
description: Operator wants the Task Manager Indicators column (and process/app views generally) to support more categories plus an Excel-like filter list - click a column header, get a checklist of the distinct values present, select which to show. This is a real, larger feature (a reusable column-filter UI component), not a one-line fix - scope which columns/views it applies to first (Indicators in Task Manager is the explicit ask; All Programs type/publisher columns are an obvious extension) before building.
design:
SCOPED 2026-08-09 (the issue's own instruction was to scope before building). Not built yet - deliberately, see the sequencing note at the end.

WHERE IT APPLIES. There are exactly four real column-header tables in the app, all sharing the .apps-table class (confirmed by grep - System Clean and Force Uninstall are div-based item lists with no header row, so they are out of scope by construction):
- Task Manager: Indicators (the explicit ask), plus Process name. NOT CPU/GPU/Memory/Disk - those are continuous numeric values where a distinct-value checklist is meaningless; they want a threshold filter, which is a different control and should not be smuggled into this one.
- All Programs: Type (Desktop/Windows App/Feature - only 3 values, high value) and Publisher (long tail, needs search-within-filter).
- Health Advisor startup table: Source and Status - both small closed sets, cheap wins.
- Network Activity process table: not worth it, the list is already capped at the top 6 rows.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE.
- One function, buildColumnFilter(tableEl, columnIndex, { getRows, onChange }), attached to a header via a small funnel icon that only appears on filterable columns. No framework, no new dependency - matches how the rest of this renderer is written.
- Popover lists DISTINCT VALUES PRESENT IN THE CURRENT DATA with a count each, not a hardcoded enum, so it cannot drift out of sync with what the engine actually returns.
- Search-within-filter box appears only when distinct values exceed ~12 (covers Publisher, stays out of the way for Type).
- Select all / none / invert. Active filters shown as removable chips above the table so a filtered view can never be mistaken for an empty one - this app has a documented history of exactly that confusion (7oo epic, the silent-filter bug).
- Filter state per (view, column), held in renderer memory only. NOT persisted to settings: a filter the user forgot they set, restored silently on next launch, is the same class of bug as the silent filter above.
- Interaction with existing search: AND, and the row count caption must state both ('Showing 12 of 158 - filtered by Type, Publisher').

WHAT TO WATCH.
- Indicators is multi-valued per row (a process can carry several chips), so the filter is 'row matches ANY selected indicator', not equality. Getting this wrong silently under-reports, which is the honesty failure mode this project keeps hitting.
- Sticky headers shipped in h0i - the popover must be positioned against the sticky header's live position and needs a z-index above it (th is z-index 2).
- The empty result state must say 'no rows match this filter' with a clear-filters action, never the generic empty-list copy.

SEQUENCING. Build 5rz (multi-select + 'Add N to queue') FIRST, then this. The pair is what creates the real value - filter to a publisher, select all, queue - and 5rz defines what 'select all' must mean against an active filter. Building this one first risks a select-all semantic that 5rz then has to change.
close_reason:
Shipped in 0.6.5. One shared control (renderer/column-filter.js, 8th renderer script) on all three real column-header tables: All Programs (Publisher on the NAME header, since that is the column publishers are rendered in; Type), Task Manager (Process, Indicators), Health Advisor startup (Source, Status). CPU/GPU/Memory/Disk/PID deliberately excluded - a distinct-value checklist is meaningless for a continuous number, and hiding a threshold control behind the same funnel would misrepresent both.

FOUR DECISIONS THAT ARE THE ACTUAL DESIGN, each failing towards showing too much:
1. State is the set of EXCLUDED values, never the selected ones. With live data (a process starts, a program is removed, a new indicator kind ships), selected-set semantics would withhold a value that did not exist when the filter was set. Hiding something new is the failure this app cannot afford.
2. The checklist is built from the view's whole pool, not the surviving rows - an option list that shrinks as you uncheck is a trap with no way back.
3. A multi-valued row survives while ANY of its values is shown. The two-indicator process stays visible when one is hidden and leaves only when both are; equality would under-report exactly the processes carrying the most warnings. Rows with no value get one synthetic None bucket.
4. Nothing persisted. Asserted, not assumed: setSettings call count is 0 after the whole suite.

Also: the checklist offers the words the CELLS show, via appTypeLabel()/startupSourceLabel()/startupStatusLabel() extracted so the cell and the filter cannot drift - Type reads 'Windows App' not 'UWP', Source reads 'Task' not 'TaskScheduler'.

ACCOUNTABILITY, which is most of the work: caption names the columns ('Showing 12 of 158 programs - filtered by Publisher, Type'); removable chips above each table; empty states name the filter that emptied them and offer a way out. Task Manager and the startup table had NO caption row before this - Task Manager re-samples every 2s, so a filtered list read as a quiet machine.

ONE REAL DEFECT FOUND BY THE TESTS: updateBulkSelectUI tested only filterText/filterType, so with only a column filter set the bulk-selection caption dropped the filter sentence - the 2026-08-05 silent-filter bug through a new door. Fixed in queue-clean.js. Found by asserting the RULE, not the two filters that existed when the rule was written. Second find: fa-filter did not exist in the vendored icon set, and an undefined glyph here paints a blank square rather than throwing (icon-verify caught it).

VERIFIED: test/column-filter-verify.js, 81 assertions, registered in run-all.ps1. Full suite 838 passed / 0 failed (was 757). details-panel-layout-verify (52 assertions, several widths) confirms the funnels did not truncate a header or overflow the process table - clippedHeaders empty, container client 620 = scroll 620 at the operator's 1110x741. Offscreen screenshots of All Programs (popover + chip + caption) and Task Manager narrow reviewed.

NOT VERIFIED BY A HUMAN AT A REAL CONSOLE: mouse-driven use of the popover (hover states, wheel scrolling inside a long Publisher list). Nothing here is tier-gated or destructive, so this is the ordinary UI-polish gap, not the elevated-confirmation class.

title: Network Activity: beautify upload/download(/ping) into a proper visual instead of inline text

Depends partly on kp0s outcome for whether ping is included at all; upload/down alone can be redesigned independently as small stat tiles or a compact sparkline-style widget.
close_reason: Replaced the up/down text fragment (previously just another entry in the 'Looked at:' inline note) with three tiles under the verdict: Download, Upload, and a de-emphasised adapter/link tile carrying the adapter name, Wi-Fi/Wired and signal % when known. Grid is auto-fit minmax(150px,1fr) so it reflows to one column on a narrow window. Adapter name and the two rates were removed from the 'Looked at:' line so the same numbers are not printed twice. Built independent of kp0 as that issue allows - no ping, and the layout takes a fourth tile without rework if that decision later lands. Deliberately did NOT express the rates as a percentage of link speed: linkSpeedBps is the negotiated rate to the router, not the speed of the internet connection behind it, so a percentage would be a confident wrong answer against the wrong denominator. Caught by this project's own test/icon-verify.js while verifying: fa-arrow-down, fa-arrow-up and fa-ethernet were not in the vendored icon set, so all three tiles rendered a blank 1em square with nothing thrown and nothing logged - exactly the failure mode that test exists for. Added the three glyphs to assets/icons.css on the same 24x24/2px grid (55 defined, 55 referenced, 0 missing) and re-captured the panel to confirm they paint. npm test 395/0.

title: Game platform size detection: verify and add GOG Galaxy, Ubisoft Connect, EA App, Battle.net
description: Add-GamePlatformSizes now uses an extensible provider array (GamePlatformSizeProviders) with Steam (live-verified) and Epic (documented format, not live-tested) implemented. GOG Galaxy got real research this session: it does write a per-game goggame-<id>.info JSON file with what looks like a depots array carrying per-depot size fields, matching what a content-manifest download-time format uses - but every source found describes the DOWNLOAD manifest, not confirmed against the actual local post-install file contents on a real machine. Implementing from research alone risks a wrong field name silently attaching a plausible-but-incorrect size to a real game, which is worse than the current unknown-size status quo. Needs a real GOG install to verify field names before writing Get-GogLibrarySizes. Ubisoft Connect and EA App/Origin/Battle.net were not researched at all this session - lower priority, add if a user reports the same unknown-size gap for one of them.
notes: BLOCKED ON HARDWARE, not on effort - checked 2026-08-18. None of the four platforms is installed on this machine: GOG Galaxy, Ubisoft Connect, EA Desktop and Battle.net all absent from their registry keys, and a recursive search for goggame-*.info across C: and D: found zero files. So the exact thing the bead says is required - verifying the real field names in a real post-install goggame-*.info rather than in download-manifest documentation - cannot be done here. Implementing from research alone would attach a plausible-but-wrong size to a real game, which the bead already judged worse than the current honest 'unknown size'.
